闔門也。从門；才，所以歫門也。
黃倉庚也。鳴則蠶生。从隹离聲。
聲也。生於心，有節於外，謂之音。宮商角徵羽，聲；絲竹金石匏土革木，音也。从言含一。凡音之屬皆从音。
怒也。武也。象馬頭髦尾四足之形。凡馬之屬皆从馬。
覆也。从入、桀。桀，黠也。軍法曰乘。
交脛也。从大，象交形。凡交之屬皆从交。
周所受瑞麥來麰。一來二縫，象芒朿之形。天所來也，故爲行來之來。《詩》曰：“詒我來麰。”凡來之屬皆从來。
垂皃。从人纍聲。一曰嬾解。
肩也。象屋下刻木之形。凡克之屬皆从克。
如野牛而青。象形。與禽、离頭同。凡𤉡之屬皆从𤉡。
裁也。从刀从未。未，物成有滋味，可裁斷。一曰止也。
筋也。象人筋之形。治功曰力，能圉大災。凡力之屬皆从力。
木工也。从匚从斤。斤，所以作器也。
大通也。从十从尃。尃，布也。
chars.g: have heard it all / broad learning

chars.def: 手也。象形。三指者，手之𠛱多略不過三也。凡又之屬皆从又。
人所以言食也。象形。凡口之屬皆从口。
異辭也。从口、夊。夊者，有行而止之，不相聽也。
災也。从人从各。各者，相違也。
愛瀒也。从來从㐭。來者，㐭而藏之。故田夫謂之嗇夫。凡嗇之屬皆从嗇。
大約也。从大从㓞。《易》曰：“後代聖人易之以書契。”
姑也。从女从戌。漢律曰：“婦告威姑。”
chars.g: authority / harm (大威, the great collapse)

chars.def: 善事父母者。从老省，从子。子承老也。
實也。从宀从至。至，所止也。
辠人在屋下執事者。从宀从辛。辛，辠也。
富也。从宀从貫。貫，貨貝也。
貫穿通流水也。《虞書》曰：“濬𡿨巜，距川。”言深𡿨巜之水會爲川也。凡川之屬皆从川。
中宮也。象萬物辟藏詘形也。己承戊，象人腹。凡己之屬皆从己。
護也。半門曰戶。象形。凡戶之屬皆从戶。
索持也。一曰至也。从手尃聲。
錯畫也。象交文。凡文之屬皆从文。
析也。从斤其聲。《詩》曰：“斧以斯之。”
併船也。象兩舟省、緫頭形。凡方之屬皆从方。
爽，旦明也。从日未聲。一曰闇也。
象器曲受物之形。或說曲，蠶薄也。凡曲之屬皆从曲。
桐木也。从木，熒省聲。一曰屋梠之兩頭起者爲榮。
厚也。害人之艸，往往而生。从屮从毐。
水。出蜀湔氐徼外崏山，入海。从水工聲。

chars.g: end (没身, to the end of your days)
pure, honest (淳淳, pure and honest)

chars.def: 水。出齊郡厲嬀山，東北入鉅定。从水蜀聲。
穿壁以木爲交窻也。从片、戶、甫。譚長以爲：甫上日也，非戶也。牖，所以見日。
孔子曰：“狗，叩也。叩气吠以守。”从犬句聲。
美也。从口含一。一，道也。凡甘之屬皆从甘。
男子美稱也。从用、父，父亦聲。
東方之孟，陽气萌動，从木戴孚甲之象。一曰人頭宐爲甲，甲象人頭。凡甲之屬皆从甲。
分也。从廾从畀。畀，予也。凡異之屬皆从異。
畱止也。从𥝌从尤，旨聲。凡稽之屬皆从稽。
續也。百穀之緫名。从禾𣪊聲。
主聽也。象形。凡耳之屬皆从耳。
牽也。事君也。象屈服之形。凡臣之屬皆从臣。
觀，四方而高者。从至从之，从高省。與室屋同意。
艸也。似目宿。从艸云聲。《淮南子》說：「芸艸可以死復生。」
chars.g: teeming (芸芸, come to their fullest)

chars.def: 榮也。从艸从𠌶。凡華之屬皆从華。
林薄也。一曰蠶薄。从艸溥聲。
山獸之君。从虍，虎足象人足。象形。凡虎之屬皆从虎。
𡪢衣，長一身有半。从衣皮聲。
山瀆無所通者。从谷奚聲。
𦣻同。古文𦣻也。巛象髪，謂之鬊，鬊卽巛也。凡𩠐之屬皆从𩠐。
馬高六尺爲驕。从馬喬聲。《詩》曰：“我馬唯驕。”一曰野馬。
肉之覈也。从冎有肉。凡骨之屬皆从骨。
人所歸爲鬼。从人，象鬼頭。鬼陰气賊害，从厶。凡鬼之屬皆从鬼。
併也。从二立。凡竝之屬皆从竝。
陽之變也。象其屈曲究盡之形。凡九之屬皆从九。
獻也。从高省，曰象進孰物形。《孝經》曰：“祭則鬼亯之。”凡亯之屬皆从亯。
chars.g: partake of (享太牢, a great feast)

chars.def: 民所安定也。亭有樓，从高省，丁聲。

chars.g: ten (什伯, of ten, of a hundred)

chars.def: 畫也。从八从人。人各有介。
與也。从人支聲。《詩》曰：“𥷤人伎忒。”

chars.g: hundred (什伯, of ten, of a hundred)

chars.def: 手相左助也。从𠂇、工。凡左之屬皆从左。
榖藏也。倉黃取而藏之，故謂之倉。从食省，口象倉形。凡倉之屬皆从倉。
昂頭也。从人嚴聲。一曰好皃。
《易》之數，陰變於六，正於八。从入从八。凡六之屬皆从六。
同也。从廿、廾。凡共之屬皆从共。
并也。从又持秝。兼持二禾，秉持一禾。
幽也。从日从六，冖聲。日數十。十六日而月始虧幽也。凡冥之屬皆从冥。
四時盡也。从仌从夂。夂，古文終字。
刀堅也。象刀有刃之形。凡刃之屬皆从刃。
盛力權也。从力埶聲。經典通用埶。
畫計難也。从囗从啚。啚，難意也。
地之吐生物者也。二象地之下、地之中，物出形也。凡土之屬皆从土。
平徧也。从土从勻，勻亦聲。
止也。从土，从畱省。土，所止也。此與畱同意。
邦也。从囗从戈，以守一。一，地也。
當罪人也。从幸从𠬝。𠬝，服罪也。
遠也。卜尚平旦，今夕卜，於事外矣。
中央也。从大在冂之内。大，人也。央㫄同意。一曰久也。
張也。从大者聲。凡奢之屬皆从奢。
宛也。室之西南隅。从宀𢍏聲。
手持隹失之也。从又从奞。
通也。从𠃉从子。𠃉，請子之候鳥也。𠃉至而得子，嘉美之也。古人名嘉字子孔。
乳也。从子在宀下，子亦聲。
子之子曰孫。从子从系。系，續也。
史，事君也。从宀从𠂤。𠂤猶眾也。此與師同意。
chars.g: officer (官長, chief of the officers)

chars.def: 所安也。从宀之下，一之上，多省聲。
凍也。从人在宀下，以茻薦覆之，下有仌。
十分也。人手卻一寸，動𧖴，謂之寸口。从又从一。凡寸之屬皆从寸。
六寸簿也。从寸叀聲。一曰專，紡專。
十寸也。人手卻十分動脈爲寸口。十寸爲尺。尺，所以指尺䂓榘事也。从尸从乙。乙，所識也。周制，寸、尺、咫、尋、常、仞諸度量，皆以人之體爲法。凡尺之屬皆从尺。
買賣所之也。市有垣，从冂从乁，乁，古文及，象物相及也。之省聲。
諦也，王天下之號也。从丄，朿聲。
chars.g: god — *any god* at its one occurrence
chars.r: god — *any god* at its one occurrence

chars.def: 紳也。男子鞶帶，婦人帶絲。象繫佩之形。佩必有巾，从巾。
語平舒也。从亏从八。八，分也。爰禮說。
穀孰也。从禾千聲。《春秋傳》曰：“大有秊。”
頓仆也。从犬敝聲。《春秋傳》曰：“與犬，犬獘。”
以近窮遠。象形。古者揮作弓。《周禮》六弓：王弓、弧弓以射甲革甚質；夾弓、庾弓以射干矦鳥獸；唐弓、大弓以授學射者。凡弓之屬皆从弓。
和之行也。从夊𢚧聲。《詩》曰：“布政憂憂。”
拳也。象形。凡手之屬皆从手。

chars.g: oppose (抗兵, armies set against each other)

chars.def: 量也。从手耑聲。度高曰揣。一曰捶之。
更也。从攴、己。李陽冰曰：“已有過，攴之卽改。”
帗也。一曰敗衣。从攴从㡀，㡀亦聲。
怒也。詆也。一曰誰何也。从攴𦎫聲。
旗皃。从㫃也聲。亝欒施字子旗，知施者旗也。
乾肉也。从殘肉，日以晞之。與俎同意。
推也。从艸从日，艸春時生也；屯聲。

chars.g: late (晚成; verse follows 免成, never)

chars.def: 出亡在外，望其還也。从亡，朢省聲。
chars.g: within sight of / look across at

chars.def: 木上曰末。从木，一在其上。
槀也。从木古聲。《夏書》曰：“唯箘輅枯。”木名也。

chars.g: beam, rigid (強梁, strong and rigid)

chars.def: 息也。一曰气越泄。从欠曷聲。
欷也。从欠虚聲。一曰出气也。
楚莊王曰：“夫武，定功戢兵。故止戈爲武。”
密也。二人爲从，反从爲比。凡比之屬皆从比。

chars.g: fine hair (毫末, a hair's tip)

chars.def: 無聲出涕曰泣。从水立聲。
諸矦鄉射之宮，西南爲水，東北爲牆。从水从半，半亦聲。
變汙也。从水俞聲。一曰渝水，在遼西臨俞，東出塞。
混流聲也。从水軍聲。一曰洿下皃。
沒也。从水甚聲。一曰湛水，豫章浸。
水。出常山房子贊皇山，東入泜。从水齊聲。
玄鳥也。籋口，布翄，枝尾。象形。凡燕之屬皆从燕。
丮也。覆手曰爪。象形。凡爪之屬皆从爪。
矩也。家長率教者。从又舉杖。
chars.g: father, root (教父, root of learning)

chars.def: 閑，養牛馬圈也。从牛，冬省。取其四周帀也。
chars.g: penned beast (太牢, a great feast)

chars.def: 狗之有縣蹏者也。象形。孔子曰：“視犬之字如畫狗也。”凡犬之屬皆从犬。
陳也。樹穀曰田。象四囗。十，阡陌之制也。凡田之屬皆从田。
平田也。从攴、田。《周書》曰：“畋尒田。”
chars.g: field hunt (畋獵, pursuit of prey)

chars.def: 上車也。从癶、豆。象登車形。
有所長短，以矢爲正。从矢豆聲。
山石也。在厂之下；囗，象形。凡石之屬皆从石。
天垂象，見吉凶，所以示人也。从𠄞，
地主也。从示、土。《春秋傳》曰：「共工之子句龍爲社神。」周禮，二十五家爲社，各樹其土所宜之木。
chars.g: soil altar (社稷, the soil and the grain)

chars.def: 銓也。从禾爯聲。春分而禾生。日夏至，晷景可度。禾有秒，秋分而秒定。律數：十二秒而當一分，十分而寸。其以爲重：十二粟爲一分，十二分爲一銖。故諸程品皆从禾。

chars.g: millet, grain (社稷, the soil and the grain)

chars.def: 肉之力也。从力从肉从竹。竹，物之多筋者。凡筋之屬皆从筋。
埽除也。从土弁聲。讀若糞。
白緻繒也。从糸、𠂹，取其澤也。凡素之屬皆从素。
綴得理也。一曰大索也。从糸畾聲。
庖犧所結繩以漁。从冂，下象网交文。凡网之屬皆从网。今經典變隸作䍏。
捕魚竹网。从网、非。秦以罪爲辠字。
養子使作善也。从𠫓肉聲。《虞書》曰：“教育子。”
船也。古者，共鼓、貨狄，刳木爲舟，剡木爲楫，以濟不通。象形。凡舟之屬皆从舟。
顔气也。从人从卪。凡色之屬皆从色。
草斗，櫟實也。一曰象斗子。从艸早聲。
蕪也。从艸㠩聲。一曰艸淹地也。

chars.g: opening particle (蓋聞, it's been said)

chars.def: 有足謂之蟲，無足謂之豸。从三虫。凡蟲之屬皆从蟲。
宿衞也。从韋、帀，从行。行，列衞也。
依也。上曰衣，下曰裳。象覆二人之形。凡衣之屬皆从衣。
編枲韤。一曰粗衣。从衣曷聲。
身中也。象人要自𦥑之形。从𦥑，交省聲。
覂也。一曰蓋也。从襾復聲。
獸角也。象形，角與刀、魚相似。凡角之屬皆从角。
還師振旅樂也。一曰欲也，登也。从豆，微省聲。凡豈之屬皆从豈。
豆之豐滿者也。从豆，象形。一曰《鄉飲酒》有豐侯者。凡豐之屬皆从豐。
象之大者。賈侍中說：不害於物。从象予聲。
卜問也。从卜，貝以爲贄。一曰鼎省聲。京房所說。
恃也。从人守貝，有所恃也。一曰受貸不償。
財分少也。从貝从分，分亦聲。
以物質錢。从敖、貝。敖者，猶放；貝，當復取之也。
南方色也。从大从火。凡赤之屬皆从赤。
趨也。从夭、止。夭止者，屈也。凡走之屬皆从走。
僵也。从足厥聲。一曰跳也。亦讀若橜。
輿輪之緫名。夏后時奚仲所造。象形。凡車之屬皆从車。
軿車前，衣車後也。从車甾聲。
車小缺復合者。从車叕聲。
車迹也。从車，徹省聲。本通用徹，後人所加。
行不相遇也。从辵羍聲。詩曰：“挑兮達兮。”
距國百里爲郊。从邑交聲。
解也。从釆；釆，取其分別物也。从睪聲。
居也。从田从土。凡里之屬皆从里。
五色金也。黃爲之長。久薶不生衣，百鍊不輕，从革不違。西方之行。生於土，从土；左右注，象金在土中形；今聲。凡金之屬皆从金。
具數於門中也。从門，說省聲。
門扇也。一曰閉也。从門盍聲。
以木橫持門戶也。从門𢇅聲。
大陵也。一曰曲𨸏也。从𨸏可聲。
闇也。水之南、山之北也。从𨸏侌聲。
宛丘，舜後嬀滿之所封。从𨸏从木，申聲。
水从雲下也。一象天，冂象雲，水霝其閒也。凡雨之屬皆从雨。

chars.g: flowing with (大順, the great current)

chars.def: 八風也。東方曰明庶風，東南曰清明風，南方曰景風，西南曰涼風，西方曰閶闔風，西北曰不周風，北方曰廣莫風，東北曰融風。風動蟲生。故蟲八日而化。从虫凡聲。凡風之屬皆从風。
歠也。从欠酓聲。凡㱃之屬皆从㱃。

chars.defen: The yin spirit. From 鬼 (guǐ — a ghost), with 白 (bái — white) for sound.

chars.def: 水蟲也。象形。魚尾與燕尾相似。凡魚之屬皆从魚。
魚名。出貉國。从魚，羴省聲。
長尾禽緫名也。象形。鳥之足似匕，从匕。凡鳥之屬皆从鳥。
火所熏之色也。从炎，上出𡆧。𡆧，古窻字。凡黑之屬皆从黑。

entries.body:
## 百姓 (Bǎi xìng) — Everyone

*Say "bye shing," falling then falling. Four appearances across three chapters.*

**Locked: 百姓 → "everyone."** *(Not "the people," which is 民's. Not "the hundred families" or "the hundred surnames," which are accurate about the words and say nothing about the people.)*

百姓 is the whole population, named without reference to anyone above it. 民 (*mín* — the people) is the population as a ruler sees it: governed, taxed, frightened, or left alone. 百姓 is the same people seen from among themselves, and in three of its four lines they are the ones acting: they speak, they have a heart, they pay attention.

### The words: a hundred clan names

- **百 (*bǎi*)** is *a hundred*, and as with 萬 (*wàn* — ten thousand) in 萬物 (*wàn wù* — the countless things), the number means *all of them*, not a count.
- **姓 (*xìng*)** is a clan name. Our vendored 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE) defines it 人所生也…从女从生 — *"what a person is born of… from 女 (nǚ — woman) and 生 (shēng — birth)."* The name you inherit is, in the graph, the name of the one who bore you.

**The phrase changed sides.** In the oldest texts only noble lineages had clan names, so 百姓 meant **the nobility**. The *Book of Documents* says of the sage-king Yao 平章百姓 (*píng zhāng bǎi xìng* — "he regulated and distinguished the hundred clans"), and its commentator 孔安國 (*Kǒng Ānguó*) glosses 百姓 there as 百官 (*bǎi guān* — the hundred officials). The commoners, who had no clan names, were 民. **The two words began as opposites.** As surnames spread downward through the Warring States, 百姓 widened to cover everyone. The *Great Commentary* to the *Book of Changes* uses it that way: 百姓日用而不知 (*"everyone uses it daily and does not know it"*).

By Laozi's day the old sense is gone, and both of our commentators read 百姓 as the whole population. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) on ch 49: 聖人愛念百姓如孩孾赤子 — *"the sage cherishes everyone as one cherishes a newborn infant."* 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) on ch 17: 功成事遂而百姓不知其所以然也 — *"the work is done and the task complete, and everyone does not know how it came to be so."*

### The evidence: the lines where the people act

> 百姓皆謂：「我自然」(17) — *Everyone says, "We did this by ourselves."*
> 以百姓心為心 (49) — *they take everyone's heart as their own*
> 百姓皆注其耳目 (49) — *everyone pours out their attention, all eyes and ears*

**Chapter 17 is the one place in the book where the people speak in their own voice**, and what they say is that the rule they lived under did nothing they could see. That is the chapter's highest praise of a ruler, and it can only be spoken by people who did not experience themselves as governed. The English cannot use the word the book reserves for the governed (民) to say it.

**Chapter 49 makes their heart the sage's.** 聖人無常心，以百姓心為心 — *the sage has no fixed heart; they take everyone's heart as their own.* The sage is defined by what everyone feels, which is the reverse of 民's lines, where the ruler acts and the people respond.

> 聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗 (5) — *the sage is not concerned with humaneness: they treat everyone as straw dogs*

**Chapter 5 is the exception, and it is built on a parallel.** The line before it reads 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗 — *sky and earth treat the countless things as straw dogs.* As sky and earth are to all beings, the sage is to all people. *Everyone* answers *the countless things* exactly: no one singled out, no one favoured.

**And chapter 67 shows the line 百姓 draws.** 天下皆謂我道大 is the same frame as chapter 17 (X 皆謂, *X all say*) with 天下 (*tiān xià* — the world) in the subject slot. *The world* says my Tao is great. *Everyone* says we did this ourselves. The world is a public verdict, while 百姓 is the people talking about their own lives.

### What is set aside, and why

**"The people."** It is 民's, and the book uses the two words for two different angles on one population. Rendering both *the people* would erase the one difference the reader could otherwise hear: in chapter 17, the governed get to say that they were not governed.

**"The hundred families," "the hundred surnames."** Accurate about the words, and drained of the people. They point the reader at the phrase's history, which by Laozi's day had turned the other way, and they sound like an exact count. A reader meets an antiquarian term where the Chinese has an ordinary one.

**"The common people," "the masses."** Both bring a class line the phrase no longer draws. *Common* sets them against the uncommon, and *the masses* is rejected for 民 and 眾 (*zhòng* — the crowd) on the same grounds.

### The working register

- as subject → **everyone** (百姓皆謂 → "everyone says"; English *everyone* already holds 皆 (*jiē* — all), so it is not rendered twice)
- possessive → **everyone's** (以百姓心為心 → "they take everyone's heart as their own")
- as object → **everyone** (以百姓為芻狗 → "they treat everyone as straw dogs")

*Everyone* takes a singular verb and a singular-they pronoun, which is the edition's practice for the sage too: *"everyone pours out their attention."*

### Left open

**"Everyone" drops the kinship the phrase is made of.** 姓 is a lineage, and 百姓 is the population as a web of households, which is part of why it can speak and have a heart where 民 cannot. *Everyone* keeps the universality and loses the households. We take that trade because the households were history by the time the book was written, and the universality is what the lines use.

**It also includes the ruler, strictly speaking.** 百姓 does not: the sage stands apart from it in every line, taking its heart, treating it as straw dogs. The English relies on context to exclude the one speaking, as English *everyone* usually does.

## 保 (Bǎo) — To Keep Safe

*Say "bao," dipping. Four lines across four chapters, and it is the only one of the holding words that is not about your grip.*

**Locked: 保 → "keep safe."** *(Never "preserve," never "safekeeping," never "maintain." Never *guard* either — but that one is a ruling no check can hold, and it has a section of its own below.)* **One declared flexion: bare *keep* at chapter 9**, for the reason below.

### The graph: a person carrying a child

> 保，**養**也。从人，从𤓽省。𤓽，古文孚。
> *"保 is **to rear**. From 人 (rén — a person) and an abbreviated 𤓽; 𤓽 is the archaic form of 孚 (fú)."* — 說文解字

孚 is a hand over a child — the graph behind *brooding*, *hatching*, and, by a short road, *trust*. In the bronze forms 保 is drawn plainly: an adult, and an infant carried against the back.

So while 持 (*chí*) grips, 執 (*zhí*) takes into custody and 守 (*shǒu*) keeps a post, **保 is the one that carries.** Its definition is not a word for holding at all. It is 養, *to nourish* — the same character 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) uses of the sage at chapter 5, 聖人**愛養**萬民, *"the sage loves and rears the people."* You keep a child safe by feeding it, not by guarding a wall.

### The character runs in both directions, and that is the whole of it

At chapters 15 and 67 a person keeps something safe:

> **保**此道者不欲盈 (15) — *"those who keep the Tao safe like this have no wish to be full."*
> 我有三寶，持而**保**之 (67) — *"I have three treasures. I hold them and keep them safe."*

At chapter 62 the Tao keeps a person safe:

> 善人之寶，不善人之所**保** — *"the treasure of those who are masterful, and what keeps safe those who are not."*

Both commentators make the Tao the agent there, not the object. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) gives the outcome in four characters — **保以全也**, *"保, because it keeps them whole"* — where 全 (*quán*) is the character locked to *whole* in `quan-全.md`. 河上公 is warmer and more specific:

> 道者，不善人之**保倚**也，遭患逢急，猶自知悔卑下。
> *"The Tao is what the unmasterful lean on for safety. Meeting trouble and sudden danger, they still know to repent and humble themselves."*

保倚 — *to be kept safe by, to lean on.* He uses the same compound at chapter 67 for the three treasures: 我有三寳，抱持而**保倚**. One English across all four lets the two directions answer each other. **At chapter 15 you keep the Tao safe; at chapter 62 the Tao keeps you safe.** That reciprocity is in the character and nowhere in the syntax, and it disappears the moment the four lines take four words.

### The one flexion, and the marker that licenses it

Three of the four lines take an object that is **cherished**, and all three are **positive**: 此道 (*cǐ dào* — this Tao) at 15, the Tao acting on people at 62, 三寶 (*sān bǎo* — the three treasures) at 67. **Chapter 9 is the only negative instance and the only one whose object is not cherished** — 揣而銳之，**不可長保**, a metal point hammered ever finer by someone who is destroying it.

English *keep safe* carries a requirement the Chinese does not: it wants an object **valued for its own sake**, something you would protect. A tool being wrecked by overwork is not that, and the phrase reads as a category error. So chapter 9 takes the verb without the qualifier — *"and it will not keep for long"* — which is 保's own root word, and which lets the intransitive do the work an impersonal 不可 asks for.

**The entry's own argument demanded this and had not noticed.** Two sections below, *preserve* is set aside because *"保 is 養, growth, and the object of the verb at chapter 67 is three **living dispositions**, not three artifacts."* That reasoning presupposes a living or cherished object. Chapter 9's object is precisely the artifact.

**The lock had never been tested here.** Chapter 9's verse rendered 保 nowhere until 2026-09-20, so the ruling of 2026-09-06 was argued from this chapter's **literal gloss table** rather than from a line anyone had to say out loud. Two markers, not one, keep the flexion honest and scoped: the negation and the object. A fifth occurrence sharing both would extend it; anything else does not.

### The chime, and what it costs

保 (*bǎo*) and 寶 (*bǎo* — treasure) are homophones, and the book prints them together twice — 善人之**寶**，不善人之所**保** (62) and 我有三**寶**，持而**保**之 (67). 說文 on 寶 is 珍也, *"a precious thing,"* built from 宀 a roof over 玉 jade and 貝 a cowrie shell: a hoard indoors. 王弼 separates the pair cleanly at 62 — **寶以為用也** / **保以全也**, *"treasure, because they put it to use; keeping safe, because it keeps them whole."*

English cannot chime here, and the entry records the loss rather than manufacturing a fix. What matters is that the two are not the same word: 寶 is what a thing *is*, 保 is what you *do*.

### What is set aside

**"preserve"** is a conservator's word — jars, specimens, a condition maintained against decay. 保 is 養, growth, and the object of the verb at chapter 67 is three living dispositions, not three artifacts.

**"safekeeping"** turns a verb into a facility. At chapter 62 it also makes the Tao a passive receptacle where both commentators make it the thing that acts.

**"maintain"** is bureaucratic and belongs to the register the whole edition is built to keep out. It is also 守's territory, not 保's — a maintained thing is a kept post.

**"safeguard"** and **"hold on to"** both put the hand back. There is no hand in this graph.

### What no rule can enforce

***"guard"* is ruled out in the verse, and it is not on the `forbidden:` list, because it cannot be.** Those are two different facts: the ruling holds, and the enforcement does not exist. 守 stands with 保 in chapters 9 and 67, and *guard* is 守's word in both. A rule keyed to 保's presence would fire on 守's own line. The two characters sit two lines apart at chapter 9 — 不可長**保** and 莫之能**守** — and nothing in this repository can tell one from the other there. See `shou-守.md`, `chi-持.md`, `zhi-執.md`.

### Left open

**Chapter 62's 所保 carries a recorded fork.** The Dunhuang witness reads 所不保, with a negation that reverses the clause: the Tao becomes what the unmasterful are *not* kept safe by. The silks use a single graph in both the 寶 and 保 positions, so they cannot arbitrate. We keep the base text; the fork is in `sources/variants.yaml`.

flexions.why: the object is not cherished — a thing being destroyed, not one you protect

entries.body:
## 常 (Cháng) — The Ever-Present

*Say "chahng," rising like a question. Thirty appearances across nineteen chapters, four of them in the book's first six lines.*

**Locked: 常 → "the ever-present"** (as a name, or before a noun) **/ "ever"** (before a 無X or 有X state) **/ "always"** (before any other predicate). *(Never "eternal," "eternally," "eternity," "everlasting," or "timeless." "Enduring" and "lasting" are ruled out too, but no check can hold that ruling; see* What no rule can enforce *below.)*

常 names what does not lapse: the thing that is there every time you look, the habit that holds, the course that keeps coming round. It is a word about **time running on**, not about a place outside time. The book uses it two ways. As a manner, it says the Tao is *ever* nameless, *ever* non-doing. As a name, it is what returning is called, and knowing it is called clear-seeing (16, 55). The oldest manuscripts write these two uses with two different characters, and that fact settles more about the first line of the book than any dictionary does.

### The graph: a skirt, with a sound on top

**Our vendored 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE): 下帬也。从巾尚聲** — *"a lower skirt. From 巾 (jīn — cloth), with 尚 (shàng) for sound."*

- **巾 (*jīn*)** is a piece of cloth hanging down: a sash, a towel, a kerchief at the belt. It is the meaning half, and it says *fabric*.
- **尚 (*shàng*)** is the sound half. Xu Shen glosses it 曾也。庶幾也 — *"still; nearly"* — and files it as sound only. It contributes nothing to the sense here, and the old and modern readings agree on that.

The garment is the whole of Xu Shen's definition. Upper and lower dress were two words: his own entry for 衣 (*yī* — clothing) says **上曰衣，下曰裳** — *"the upper is called 衣, the lower 裳."* **裳 (*cháng*)** is the same word with 衣 swapped in for 巾, and 說文 lists it as 常's alternative form. Over time 裳 took the skirt and 常 was left to its other meaning. *(That alternative-form line, and the bronze record below, come from outside this repository's selection of 說文.)*

**How old the graph is.** 常 has not been identified in the Shang oracle bones. Its earliest forms are Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, followed by the Warring States scripts and the small seal. Its phonetic, 尚, is older.

**How a skirt came to mean *always*.** Most modern accounts say it didn't. The *always* sense is a **phonetic loan**: a word for "constant" with no graph of its own was written with the graph for a homophone, a skirt pronounced *\*djaŋ* in Old Chinese. A tidy story runs from "everyday garment" to "everyday" to "constant", but no early text supports it, so we do not tell it. Axel Schuessler suggests, tentatively, that the *always* word is related to a Tibetan word meaning *again, once more*. If he is right, the word was about recurrence before it was about permanence.

**The banner.** One early concrete use is worth knowing because it points at the sky. The 周禮 (*Zhōu Lǐ* — the Rites of Zhou) lists the royal flags: **日月為常** — *"the one bearing the sun and moon is the 常."* The king's banner carried the two lights that never fail to come back. Shirakawa Shizuka proposes the banner as the word's root. That is a proposal, and we print it as a resonance, not as the etymology.

**By the Zhou poems the abstract sense is fully there.** The 詩經 (*Shījīng* — the Book of Songs), in the ode 文王 (*Wén Wáng*), says **天命靡常** — *"the sky's mandate does not stay put."* Even in this early use, 常 is about **whether a thing holds over time.**

### Two words under one: 恒 and 常

The Mawangdui silk manuscripts (copied before about 168 BCE) do not write 常 everywhere the received text does. They use two characters, and the split follows grammar.

- **恒 (*héng*)** stands wherever the word is a **manner** or a **modifier**. Silk A reads 非恒道 and 非恒名 in chapter 1, its 恒無欲 and 恒有欲, 恒使民 (3), 恒善救人 (27), the three 恒德 of 28, 道恒無名 (32), 恒足 (46), 牝恒以靜勝牡 (61), 恒知稽式 (65), 恒與善人 (79), and the same in 49 and 74.
- **常** stands only where the word is a **name**, the thing returning is called: 復命常也，知常明也，不知常…知常容 (16), 和曰常 (55), and 是謂襲常 (52).

The silks write 恒 freely; neither copy avoids it. The received text's single 常 is usually explained as a **Han substitution**. 恒 was the personal name of Emperor Wen (劉恒, *Liú Héng*, r. 180–157 BCE), and later copyists replaced it with its nearest synonym. That merged two words into one graph. Our base text is the received text, and we translate the 常 it prints. But the reader should know that **line 1's word was the manner-word 恒, not the name-word 常.**

**And 恒 is a picture you can point at.** In the oracle bones the graph that later became 恒 shows **a crescent moon between two lines**. 說文 defines 恆 with one character, **常也** (*"constant"*), and preserves an old form written with 月 (*yuè* — moon). As evidence it quotes the Book of Songs: **如月之恆** — *"like the moon's steady waxing."* The constancy of 恒 is the moon's: a thing that changes shape every night and never once fails to come back. That is the opposite of a changeless realm. It is change that keeps its appointment.

### What the oldest readers say it is

**韓非 (*Hán Fēi*, d. 233 BCE), the oldest commentary we carry, defines the word at length on this very line:**

> 夫物之一存一亡，乍死乍生，初盛而後衰者，不可謂常。唯夫與天地之剖判也具生，至天地之消散也不死不衰者謂常。而常者無攸易，無定理。無定理，非在於常所，是以不可道也。

*"Things that now remain and now perish, that die all at once and all at once live, that flourish first and decline after, cannot be called 常. Only what was born together with the splitting open of sky and earth, and when sky and earth disperse neither dies nor declines, is called 常. And 常 has nothing it changes into, and no fixed pattern. Having no fixed pattern, it is not in any fixed place (常所), and that is why it cannot be made into a way."*

Three things in this passage decide the rendering:

1. **It has a birth.** 與天地之剖判也具生 — *born along with sky and earth's splitting.* The oldest reader does not make 常 beginningless. It lasts **as long as the world lasts**, without decay. That is duration, not eternity in the strict sense.
2. **What makes it 常 is that it does not decline.** The contrast class is things that 盛 and 衰, *flourish and fade*. 常 is the thing that does not fade.
3. **It is in no fixed place.** 非在於常所 — and Han Fei uses 常 in its everyday sense, *a fixed place*, inside his definition of the deep one. Having no fixed place means it is everywhere. This is the strongest early support for *present* in *ever-present*.

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*)** glosses 非常名 as 非自然**常在**之名也 — *"not the name of what is so-of-itself and **always there**."* 常在 (*cháng zài*) is, word for word, *always present*. On the Tao line he reads 常 as 長生 (*cháng shēng* — long life), which fits his interest in longevity. At chapter 16 he reads it as a course: 道之所常行, *"what the Tao always does."*

**王弼 (*Wáng Bì*)**, at chapter 16, describes it by what it lacks: 常之為物，不偏不彰，無皦昧之狀，溫涼之象 — *"as a thing, 常 leans to no side and shows no mark; it has no bright or dim look, no warm or cool feel."* At 55: 物以和為常 — *"things take harmony as their 常."* For him it is the featureless norm things settle into.

None of the three puts 常 outside time. All three describe it as something that **keeps on, here.**

### Line 1: *ever-present*, not *eternal*

**道可道，非常道** → *"The Tao that can be made into a way is not the ever-present Tao."*

*Eternal* is often called the literal translation of 常. It isn't. It is the popular one, made familiar by translations such as Gia-fu Feng and Jane English (1972) and Stephen Mitchell (1988). The scholars' translations do not use it: James Legge (1891) has *"the enduring and unchanging Tao,"* Arthur Waley (1934) *"an Unvarying Way,"* D. C. Lau (1963) *"the constant way."* The dictionary sense is *constant, regular, lasting.*

*Ever-present* is the more accurate rendering here, for four reasons:

- **It tracks the word the line actually used.** Line 1's word is 恒, the manner-word: *ever.* *Ever-present* is built on *ever*. *Eternal* is built on Latin *aeternus*, and through two thousand years of theology it now means either *without beginning or end* or *outside time altogether*. Han Fei denies the first, since his 常 is born with the world, and nobody in the tradition says the second.
- **It keeps the chapter's four 常 visible as one word.** Chapter 1 prints 常 four times in six lines: 非常道, 非常名, 常無欲, 常有欲. In English that is *ever-present, ever-present, ever desireless, ever desiring.* Render line 1 *eternal* and the reader cannot see that the Tao's constancy and the observer's constant desirelessness are the same word. In the Chinese they are, and the chapter turns on it: you observe the ever-present by being ever something yourself.
- **It passes the pointing test.** Laozi could point at the moon coming back, at a river that is always there. He could not point at eternity.
- **The commentary backs *present*.** 河上公's 常在 and 韓非's 非在於常所 both say that what is 常 is *there*, everywhere and always.

**As a glossary heading the same holds.** *The ever-present* covers the name-word of 16, 52 and 55, and its *ever* covers the manner-word of 1, 3, 32, 34 and 37. One English root spans both characters the received text merged. *Eternal* fits neither.

### What we set aside

- ***eternal / eternity*** — fails the hymn test outright, since *"the eternal Tao"* is at home in a sermon. It also imports a timeless beyond, which the book never names and its oldest readers contradict. Forbidden.
- ***everlasting*** — closer, because it at least runs on in time, but it is hymn vocabulary (*everlasting arms*, *life everlasting*). It also lays stress on *lasting*, which is 長's word. Forbidden.
- ***timeless*** — the opposite of the claim. 常 is time that does not lapse, not the absence of time. Forbidden.
- ***constant*** — the lexicographers' word, and accurate. Set aside for two reasons. It is a label where the book wants a picture (`process/principles/perform-dont-label.md`), and in English it drifts toward *loyal* (*a constant friend*) and toward the physics of fixed quantities. Not forbidden: nothing in the manuscript uses it, and a reader's ruling is enough.
- ***unchanging / changeless*** — *unchanging* is already spoken for: 獨立不改 (25), *"Solitary. Unchanging"*, renders 不改 (*bù gǎi* — does not alter). And Han Fei's 常 is not unchanging in the sense of static. It is what does not *decline*.
- ***enduring / lasting*** — already spoken for, by two different characters. **久 (*jiǔ*)** is *endure*: 天長地久 (7), *"the sky is lasting, the earth enduring"*, and 道乃久 (16), *"the Tao leads to what endures."* **長 (*cháng*)**, a false friend with the same sound, is *lasting* (說文: 久遠也, *"long and far"*). Chapter 16 sets 常 and 久 in the same chain, and they must stay two words.
- ***the abiding*** — accurate, and once listed beside *the ever-present*. No line uses it, and a second noun for one name would split chapter 16's chain, where 常 is repeated as a subject four times.

### The working register

| Grammar | English | Chapters | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| a name — what something *is called* | **the ever-present** | 16 ×4, 52, 55 ×2 | 知常曰明 → *"knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing"* |
| before a noun | **ever-present** | 1 ×2, 28 ×3, 46 | 常德不離 → *"the ever-present integrity never leaves you"* |
| adverb, before a 無X or 有X state | **ever** | 1 ×2, 3, 32, 34, 37 | 道常無名 → *"the Tao is ever nameless"* |
| adverb, before any other predicate | **always** | 27 ×2, 48, 51, 61, 64, 65, 74 ×2 | 牝常以靜勝牡 → *"the female always overcomes the male by stillness"* |
| the shallow sense: habit, set custom | **fixed** | 49 | 聖人無常心 → *"the sage has no fixed heart"* |
| folded into the verb | **stays** | 79 | 常與善人 → *"it stays with those who are masterful"* |

**The *ever / always* line is grammatical, not chapter-by-chapter.** *Ever* fuses with a state the way 常 does with 無名, 無欲, 無為 or 無知. That is why 51's 常自然 is *"always so, of itself"*: 自然 (*zì rán*) is a predicate, not a 無X state. *Always* takes a verb. Chapter 64 is the test case: 民之從事，常於幾成而敗之 → *"people always ruin their affairs just short of completing them."* Both excavated copies write 恆 there, and the next line, *"be as careful at the end as at the beginning,"* is the way out of the *always*.

**The shallow sense is the same word at a lower altitude.** 無常心 (49) is a heart with no set habit, and Han Fei's 常所 is a fixed place. These are the everyday 常 of *the usual, the set*. They are not the name of chapter 16, and the English keeps them apart. The silks keep them apart too: chapter 49 there reads 恒無心, *"is ever without a heart [of their own]"*, a different construction recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`.

**Chapter 16 is the hardest line, and it decides the noun.** 復命曰常，知常曰明。不知常，妄作凶。知常容 — 常 is named, then known, then not known, then known again, four times in four lines, each time as a subject or object. Whatever the English is, it must survive being repeated four times as a noun: *"Returning to what is given is called the ever-present. / Knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing. / Not knowing the ever-present brings reckless action and disaster. / Knowing the ever-present, you contain everything."* *The eternal* would make that a theology. *The constant* would make it a law of physics. *The ever-present* stays something you could notice.

### What no rule can enforce

*Enduring*, *endures* and *lasting* are ruled out for 常, but they cannot go on `forbidden:`. The lock checker keys on chapter presence, and **chapter 16 holds both 常 and 久** (*jiǔ*): 道乃久 is legitimately *"the Tao leads to what endures"*, a few lines below four 常. Forbidding *endure* would flag that line. Chapter 7 has 長 and 久 and no 常, so it would not be flagged, but the 16 case alone makes the ban unenforceable. The reader has to hold this one: **in a chapter with 常, *endure* belongs to 久, and *lasting* to 長.**

### Left open

**The English adds a little.** *Present* foregrounds *here* where 常's core is *still, again, every time*. Han Fei and Heshang Gong license it, but it is their reading, carried into the word. *Ever-present* also has a hymn behind it, Psalm 46's *"a very present help in trouble"*, so it does not pass the hymn test cleanly either. We accept it because every alternative fails worse: *eternal* fails the same test outright, and *constant* fails the pointing test.

**The seam the reader cannot see.** The received text's 常 is two words joined: the moon-word 恒, a manner, and the skirt-graph 常, a name. Our English happens to run *ever* through both, so it holds them together the way the received text does. But it cannot show the reader where the seam is. Chapter 1's first line and chapter 16's chain look like one word in English, and to the people who first wrote them down they were not.

flexions.why: the shallow sense: 無常心 is a heart with no set habit, not a heart without the ever-present
常與 folds the always into the verb: the way of nature stays with the masterful

entries.shuowen: A lower skirt. From 巾 (jīn — cloth), with 尚 (shàng) for sound.

entries.body:
## 持 (Chí) — To Hold

*Say "chr," rising. Three lines across three chapters — and the root of the whole field.*

**Locked: 持 → "hold."** *(Never "grip," never "clutch." Never *grasp* either — but that one is a ruling no check can hold, and it has a section of its own below.)*

### The graph: a hand, and the word every other holding-word is defined by

> 持，**握**也。从手寺聲。
> *"持 is to grip. From 手 (shǒu — hand), with 寺 as the sound."* — 說文解字

Xu Shen then defines 握 (*wò*) straight back: 握，**搤持**也. The two send you to each other, which looks like a failure of a dictionary and is in fact the useful signal. **持 is where the definitions stop.** It is the plain closing of a hand on a thing, with nothing added — no restraint, no post, no child, no verdict.

You can watch the rest of the family get built out of it. 說文 defines the other hand-verbs in the Laozi *by* 持:

| | 說文 | |
|---|---|---|
| **搏** (*bó*) — chapters 14, 55 | **索持**也 | *"to search out and grip"* |
| **據** (*jù*) — chapter 55 | **杖持**也 | *"to grip as with a staff"* |

And 寺, treated as merely phonetic here, seeds a family sorted by *which part of you does the holding* — a table that also stands in `shi-恃.md`:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **持** (*chí*) | 扌 hand + 寺 | to hold, in the hand |
| **侍** (*shì*) | 亻 person + 寺 | to attend upon, with the body |
| **待** (*dài*) | 彳 step + 寺 | to wait for |
| **恃** (*shì*) | 忄 heart + 寺 | to lean your weight on |

### Three lines, and they are the neutral ones

持而盈之 (9) · 其安易**持** (64) · **持**而保之 (67). None of them carries a verdict. Chapter 64 makes that explicit by putting 持 and 執 (*zhí* — to grasp, to take into custody) in the same chapter, seventeen lines apart, doing opposite work:

> 其安易**持** — *"what is at rest is easy to hold."*
> **執**者失之 — *"those who grasp it lose it."*

That is the chapter's argument in two verbs. Hold a thing while it is still at rest and there is nothing to it; close your hand on it to keep it and you lose it. An English that gives both characters the same word deletes the sentence.

Chapter 67 sets 持 beside 保 (*bǎo* — to keep safe) in a single line, 持而**保**之, and 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) expands it with a third: 抱持而保倚, *"embracing, holding, leaning on for safety."* Three verbs for one gesture, because in Chinese they are three different gestures.

### What is set aside

**"grip"** and **"clutch"** both add force the character does not have. 持 is what you do with a cup; 握 is the tightening, and 執 is the closing that will not let go. Chapter 64's 其安易持 is about how little effort a thing takes while it is still quiet, and a word with tension in it argues the opposite.

**"sustain"** abstracts a hand into a process, and lands on the mechanistic register this edition watches for.

### What no rule can enforce

***"grasp"* is ruled out in the verse, and it is not on the `forbidden:` list, because it cannot be.** Those are two different facts: the ruling holds, and the enforcement does not exist. 執 stands with 持 in chapter 64, and *grasp* is 執's word there. A rule keyed to 持's presence would fire on 執's own line. Nor can *hold to* be reserved here: 守 (*shǒu*) stands with 持 in chapters 9 and 67. Three of the four holding characters meet on chapter 67's page — 持 · 保 · 守, with 寶 chiming against 保 — and the whole burden of keeping them apart falls on the entries and on the reader. See `zhi-執.md`, `shou-守.md`, `bao-保.md`.

### Left open

**Chapter 9's opening line.** 持而盈之，不如其已 is a two-verb condition — *hold it and fill it* — and the second verb, 盈 (*yíng* — to fill), is the character 說文 defines as 滿器也, *"a full vessel."* Whether the English should name the vessel the Chinese only implies is unsettled, and 盈 has no entry yet.

## 慈 (Cí) — Tenderness

*Say "tsuh," rising. Seven lines across three chapters, and it is the first of the book's three treasures.*

**Locked: 慈 → "tenderness."** *(Not "compassion," not "mercy," not "maternal love," not "filial piety." 孝 (xiào) → "devotion.")*

慈 is the **first of the three treasures** — 一曰慈 — and the book stakes something large on it: 慈故能勇, *"tenderness, and so you can be brave."* A word that cannot produce courage is the wrong word for it.

**Compassion**, the usual English, cannot. Compassion is *suffering-with*: it sits down beside. It is also a Buddhist word in English by now, carrying karuṇā into a text written before Buddhism reached China. Ch 67 needs something that gets up and fights — 夫慈，以戰則勝，以守則固, *"with 慈, fight and you win; defend and you hold firm."*

### The graph, and it is a pair with 孝

**慈 is 心 (*xīn* — heart) under 兹 (*zī*)**, which in its older form doubles 幺 (*yāo* — a skein of silk) and carries the sense *to grow, to multiply*. The heart that increases toward something. *Shuowen*: 慈，愛也 — *"慈 is 愛 (ài — love)."*

It never appears alone in this book outside ch 67. Twice it appears welded to **孝** (*xiào*), and the two graphs are a matched pair pointing opposite ways:

> 孝，善事父母者。从老省，从子，子承老也
> *Shuowen — "孝 is one who serves their parents well. From an abbreviated 老 (lǎo — old) and from 子 (zǐ — child): **the child bears up the old**."*

**孝 is a child holding up an elder. 慈 is a heart growing toward a child.** One goes up the generations, one comes down. 孝慈 is not two virtues in a list; it is a circuit, and 河上公 says so — 乃有孝慈**相牧養**也, *"then there is 孝慈, tending each other."*

That reciprocity is what *filial piety and love* destroys. **Devotion and tenderness** keeps it: two words, two directions, one relation.

### Why tenderness, and why it has to be able to fight

Ch 67 is the test, because it uses 慈 five times and asks it to do incompatible work — to be the softest of the three treasures and the one that wins wars.

> 慈故能勇
> *"tenderness, and so you can be brave"*

> 今捨慈且勇 … 死矣
> *"now, to abandon tenderness and grab at courage … that is death"*

> 天將救之，以慈衛之
> *"when nature would rescue someone, it guards them with tenderness"*

The claim is not that gentleness is secretly strong. It is that **courage without something to be tender toward is not courage, it is appetite** — which is precisely the distinction the third treasure draws with 敢 (*gǎn* — the forward press to take). *Tenderness* can be fierce in English; a parent's is the ordinary example, and that is the register the graph is already in.

**Compassion cannot be fierce**, and *mercy* is worse: mercy is what the strong extend to the defeated, which reverses the chapter.

### Where the book puts it

慈 belongs to the same argument as 仁 (*rén* — humaneness) and sits on the other side of it. 仁 is the **named** virtue, the one you can be praised for, and the book treats its visibility as a symptom: 大道廢，有仁義. 慈 is never treated that way. It is a treasure, and at ch 19 it is what the people **return to** once the named virtues are cut off:

> 絕仁棄義，民復孝慈
> *"sever humaneness, abandon duty, and the people return to devotion and tenderness"*

**The unnamed thing survives the removal of the named one.** That is the chapter's whole mechanism, and it only reads if 仁 and 慈 take clearly different English.

### Never

**compassion.** Suffering-with, and Buddhist in English. 慈 is 愛 — the heart growing toward — and it has to produce 勇 (*yǒng* — courage) at ch 67.

**mercy.** Runs downhill from the strong to the beaten.

**maternal love.** The direction is right and the narrowing is not: 慈 is the parent's side of a circuit, not a gendered sentiment, and the book's feminine is a principle rather than a role.

**filial piety** for 孝. A Victorian sinology compound that names an institution and a duty; the graph shows a child taking an elder's weight. And in both places 孝 occurs it is bonded to 慈, so it never has to carry the direction alone.

### What stays open

**Whether tenderness can survive being the first treasure.** English treats tenderness as a mood — something felt, and usually briefly. 慈 at ch 67 is closer to a **stance you fight from**, and the entry's own argument leans on a parent's ferocity to make that plausible. It is plausible. It is not obvious, and a reader who has not been handed the graph may hear only softness.

The alternative would be a harder word that then fails at ch 18 and ch 19, where 慈 is what a household quietly has. **No single English does both jobs comfortably.** Tenderness does the ch 67 job at a cost, and the cost is paid at 18 and 19 rather than the other way round — which is the right way to pay it, because ch 67 is where the book is making a claim and ch 18 is where it is describing a symptom.

## 大 (Dà) — Great

*Say "dah," falling hard. Fifty-one appearances across twenty-four chapters, which makes it one of the most common characters in the book and the one the Tao is finally named with.*

**Locked: 大 → "great."** *(Lowercase. Licensed flexions: **large** where the scale is physical or political, **greater** in comparatives, **master** of a craftsman.)*

### The character is a person standing with their arms out

說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE) defines it in eleven characters, and the last four are the whole entry:

> 天大，地大，人亦大。故**大象人形**。
> *"Sky is big, earth is big, humans are also big. Therefore **大 depicts a human form**."*

The graph is a figure seen head-on — arms spread, legs apart — and the oracle-bone form is the same figure with thicker strokes. Not a mountain, not an ocean, not a firmament. **A person taking up as much room as a person can take up.** It is bigness measured on a body, which is why it can mean a large state, a severe illness, and a senior craftsman without straining.

**And the dictionary defines the character by quoting this book.** 天大，地大，人亦大 is Chapter 25's own line. That it is cited with 人 (*rén* — human) rather than 王 (*wáng* — king), six centuries before our earliest surviving witness for 人, bears on a fork this edition has left open — `notes/manuscript.md` · Ch 25, and `WORKLIST.md` T4-8.

### 大 is a radical, and its family is made by marking the same body

凡大之屬皆从大 — *"all of the 大 class follow 大."* 說文 groups a set of characters that are **one standing figure with one mark added**, and where the mark goes is the whole meaning:

| | the mark | 說文 | what it becomes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **天** (*tiān*) | a line **above the head** | 顛也。至高無上。**从一大** | *the crown of the head* → **sky** |
| **立** (*lì*) | a line **beneath the feet** | 住也。**从大立一之上** | *standing on the ground* → **to stand** |
| **夫** (*fū*) | a line **through the topknot** | 丈夫也。从大，**一以象簪也** | *a hairpin* → a capped adult man |
| **亦** (*yì*) | marks at **both sides** | **人之臂亦也**。象兩亦之形 | *the armpits* → borrowed for **also** |

**Above the head is the sky; below the feet is standing; through the hair is adulthood; at the sides are the armpits.** The book's whole vocabulary of scale and position is built by putting marks on a person.

**What this is not.** 大 is **not** 人 (*rén*) with a stroke added, though it looks like it. 說文 makes both **independent pictographs of the same subject**: 人 is 象**臂脛**之形, *"the form of arms and shins,"* seen in profile; 大 is 象**人形**, the human form seen head-on with the arms out. Siblings, not parent and child. **天 from 大 is a real derivation and 說文 states it; 大 from 人 is a resemblance.**

**And it bears directly on two locks.** 天 is locked to **sky** (`tian-天.md`) precisely because 顛 is a body part — *"a word for the crown of your head is not a word for an afterlife."* The graph family says the same thing about 大: **scale in this book is measured outward from a body, not downward from a heaven.** That is the strongest single argument for keeping 大 ordinary, and it is why *vast* — a word with no body in it — was refused.

**The honest limit.** 說文 is c. 100 CE, centuries after the oracle-bone forms, and it rationalises elsewhere in ways this glossary flags — 士's 一 + 十 and the Han cosmology on 王. But 天 as 大 with a head-mark, 亦 as armpits and 夫 as a hairpin are standard paleography rather than 說文's speculation. Whether Laozi or his readers saw any of it is unknowable; that the characters are built this way is not.

### Four jobs, one word

| what 大 is doing | where | English |
|---|---|---|
| **physical or political size** | 大國 (*dà guó* — a large state), 60, 61 ×5 · 大軍 (*dà jūn* — a large army), 30 | large |
| **the superlative frame 大▢若▢** | 大方 (square), 大器 (vessel), 大音 (sound), 大象 (image), 41 · 大成, 大盈, 大直, 大巧, 大辯, 45 | great |
| **severity** | 大患 (*dà huàn* — great trouble), 13 ×3 · 大偽 (hypocrisy), 18 · 大迷 (confusion), 27 · 禍莫**大**於… (no disaster greater than), 46 ×2, 69 | great / greater |
| **seniority and mastery** | 大匠 (*dà jiàng* — the master carpenter), 74 ×2 · 大丈夫 (*dà zhàng fū* — the great person), 38 | master / great |

English *great* reaches all four — great size, the great square, great trouble, a great carpenter — because it is, like 大, the general-purpose word rather than a specialist one. That coverage is the whole case for it, and it is why the flexions above are narrow: they mark the two places where ordinary English will not say *great* at all (a *large* state; *no greater* disaster).

### The counter-term is 小, and Chapter 34 puts both on the Tao

小 (*xiǎo* — small) shadows 大 through the book: 大小多少 (*dà xiǎo duō shǎo* — "great or small, many or few," 63), 治大國若烹小鮮 ("governing a large state is like cooking a small fish," 60), the large and small states of 61, and 小國寡民 ("a small state, few people," 80).

**Chapter 34 gives the Tao both names in three lines** — 常無欲，可名於**小** (*"ever desireless, it can be called small"*) and 萬物歸焉而不為主，可名為**大** (*"the countless things return to it, and without acting as their master, it can be called great"*). Both fit. Neither holds. That is the same joke Chapter 25 tells at length, and it is why 大 is a *name* in this book rather than a description.

### Chapter 25 — the word is chosen because it fails

強為之名曰大 (*qiǎng wèi zhī míng yuē dà* — "forcing a name on it, I call it great") is the only place the book names the Tao outright, and 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE) explains that the naming is a defeat:

> 吾所以**字**之曰道者，取其可言之稱**最大**也。責其字定之所由，則**繫於大**。**大有繫則必有分，有分則失其極矣。**
> *"The reason I 字 it 'Tao' is that I take the greatest of speakable designations. But press for what fixes that designation and it ties to 大 — and 大, once tied, must have divisions; having divisions, it loses its utmost."*

**Naming it 大 costs it its utmost.** The chapter has just spent three lines saying no name can hold a thing without form, and then reaches for the most ordinary word available: *big*. The inadequacy is the argument.

### What is set aside

**"Vast."** The strongest rival, and the one that reaches furthest into the chapter where 大 matters most — it has more force in English than *great*, which has been worn smooth by use, and it suits the Tao-naming and the cosmic members of the 41 and 45 frames. **It fails on about two-thirds of the fifty-one lines, and it fails at the argument.**

- *No disaster **vaster** than discontent* is unusable, and the comparative 禍莫大於 appears three times (46 ×2, 69).
- *Vast trouble*, *vast hypocrisy*, *vast confusion* — 大 in those lines means **severe**, not spatially immense (13, 18, 27).
- *The vast carpenter* (74), *the vast person* (38) — 大 there is **seniority**.
- *Vast skill*, *vast argument* — 大巧若拙 and 大辯若訥 need a superlative, not a size (45).
- 下士聞道，**大**笑之 — laughing **aloud** (41) is not a magnitude at all.

**And the deeper objection: 大 is not an elevated word in Chinese.** It is a person with their arms out. Rendering it with an English word that carries *more* charge than the original would make Chapter 25's forced name sound like it succeeded — which reverses the passage. A worn word is the faithful one here, and the wear is doing work. *Vast* is also, separately, spoken for: it currently renders 廣 (*guǎng* — broad) at ch 41 and 恢 (*huī* — vast) at ch 73, both of which sit alongside 大 or would want the word back.

**"The Great," capitalized.** A capital turns a forced, admittedly failing name into a title, which is the one thing the passage denies it. Standing rule 5.

**"Mighty," "grand," "supreme," "cosmic."** Each imports a register 大 does not have — power, ceremony, rank, or the firmament — where the character offers only a body's worth of room.

### Left open

**Whether *large* at 60–61 is a flexion or a fault.** Six lines of 大國 read *the large state*, and the political sense genuinely resists *great state*, which in English means *admirable*. But the same six lines are the ones where 大 and 小 are a matched pair, and the pair reads better when both sit in one register.

**Whether 大匠 is 大 at all.** *"Master carpenter"* treats 大 as seniority, but 大匠 was also a Han office — Master of Works — and if the phrase is a fixed title then the character is not flexing, it is simply part of a name. The commentaries do not settle it.

**Whether the 大▢若▢ frame wants *the greatest*.** 大方無隅 reads *"the great square has no corners"*; 王弼 glosses the series as absolutes, not comparatives. *The greatest square* would say what he says, and would lose the frame's flatness. The frame is shared across chapters 41 and 45 and has to be decided as one thing, not line by line.
entries.render: great — large where the scale is physical or political, greater in comparatives, master of a craftsman

entries.body:
## 道 (Dào) — The Tao

*Say "dow," rhyming with "now," falling, like a word set down. Seventy-five appearances across thirty-seven chapters: the book's first word, and half of its name.*

**Locked: 道 → "the Tao"** (the name, left untranslated) **/ "way"** (a common noun with an owner: *the way of nature*, *the way of people*; and the verb in the book's first line, *made into a way*). *(Never "the Way," never "the Path.")*

道 is a road. Before it was anything else it was the ordinary word for a way through the country that people walk, and the word never lost that meaning: Laozi himself uses it for a road you could stand on (53). From the road grew the walking of it, the leading of others along it, the telling of it, and the right way to do a thing. Laozi takes this common word and points it at what everything goes by, then tells us in his first line that no way you could lay out is that.

### The graph: a head on the road

**Our vendored 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE): 所行道也。从辵从𩠐。一達謂之道** — *"the road that is walked. From 辵 (chuò) and 𩠐 (shǒu). A road that runs straight through is called 道."*

That last clause is a surveyor's definition. The 爾雅 (*Ěryǎ*), the oldest Chinese word-list, grades roads by how many ways they branch: 一達謂之道路, *"one that goes straight through is called a 道 road,"* while a road that forks has another name, and a crossroads another. So 道 is not any road. It is the road that does not branch.

**辵 (*chuò*) — walking along a road.** Usually written 辶 at the left and bottom of a character. It is two pictures stacked:

- **彳 (*chì*)** — the left half of **行 (*xíng*)**, whose oldest graph is **a crossroads**, two streets meeting, seen from above. 說文 on 行: 人之步趨也。从彳从亍 — *"a person's stepping and hurrying."* 彳 alone is a step, a stretch of street.
- **止 (*zhǐ*)** — **a foot**, drawn with its toes. In early graphs a foot means going.

So 辵 is a foot on a street. 說文 glosses it 乍行乍止, *"now going, now stopping"*: the stop-and-start of someone actually walking. *(辵's own 說文 entry comes from outside this repository's selection, which holds only the characters the Laozi uses.)*

**𩠐 (*shǒu*) — a head, drawn with its hair.** This is the old form of **首 (*shǒu* — head)**. 說文 says of it: 古文𦣻也。巛象髮 — *"the ancient form of the head-graph; the 巛 on top is the hair."* Below the hair is a face, and in the oldest forms the eye is the clearest thing in it.

**Two jobs at once.** Xu Shen counts the head as part of the meaning. Modern reconstruction hears it as the sound as well: Old Chinese 道 is roughly *\*l'uːʔ* and 首 roughly *\*hljuʔ*, close enough that 首 almost certainly helped to spell 道. Both can be true. Many characters chose a sound-part that also suited the sense.

**What the head is doing there.** Three readings, from safest to boldest:

1. **The head goes first.** 首 means not only *head* but *first, foremost, the leading end*. A head on the road is the part of a walker that leads, the face set toward where you are going. The verb that grows from 道 says exactly this: **導 (*dǎo*)**, 道 with 寸 (*cùn* — a hand) added, is *to lead, to guide*. 說文: 導，導引也, *"to lead along."*
2. **The head stands for the person**, a part for the whole, as English counts "heads." On this reading 道 is simply someone on a road.
3. **A carried head.** Shirakawa Shizuka read the graph as a head carried to clear and purify a road into foreign country. It is a striking proposal and a disputed one. We record it and do not build on it.

**The bronzes draw the whole scene.** In the Zhou bronze inscriptions 道 is usually written as 行, the crossroads, with the head standing inside it, often with a foot beneath. Some forms add a hand, the shape that later became 導, *to lead*. The seal script squeezed the crossroads down to 辵, and that is the form we print.

**And the oldest copy of this book draws a person.** In the Guodian bamboo slips (c. 300 BCE), most of the copyists write 道 as **人 (*rén* — a person) standing inside 行 (a crossroads)**. Only one hand writes the head-and-walking form we know. The earliest surviving Laozi writes its central word as a person standing in the road.

### What the word already meant

By Laozi's century 道 was a common word with four live senses, and a reader of the book hears all of them:

- **A road.** 大道甚夷，而人好徑 (53) — *"the great Tao is very level, yet people love to take shortcuts."* 徑 (*jìng*) is a footpath, a cut across the fields. Laozi is talking about roads.
- **To lead.** The sense that became 導.
- **To tell.** The 詩經 (*Shījīng* — the Book of Songs): 中冓之言，不可道也 — *"the words of the inner chamber cannot be told."* Chinese still uses 道 for *to say*.
- **The right way to do things.** By Confucius's time the word was already moral, and already reached toward the cosmic: 朝聞道，夕死可矣 — *"hear the way in the morning, and you may die content in the evening"* (論語 4.8). His students said he rarely spoke of 天道, *the way of the sky* (論語 5.13).

So 道 was not a plain word that Laozi made philosophical. It was a plain word that everyone was already using for *the right way*: the way of the former kings, the way of the gentleman. Laozi's move is to take it **under** all of those. His 道 is not a way to behave. It is what every way, and every thing, goes by.

### What the book does with it

Watch what he says of it, and the verbs give it away:

- **It comes before.** 有物混成，先天地生 (25) — *"something mixed and complete, born before sky and earth."* 象帝之先 (4) — *"it seems older than any god,"* where 帝 (*dì*) is the high ancestor-deity.
- **Its name is forced.** 吾不知其名，強字之曰道 (25) — *"I do not know its name. Forcing a label on it, I call it the Tao."* 字 (*zì*) is a courtesy name, the name a person is called by rather than the name they are given.
- **It moves and is used.** 反者道之動；弱者道之用 (40) — *"returning is the Tao's movement; yielding is the Tao's use."* Movement and use, not substance.
- **It gives birth.** 道生一 (42), 道生之 (51) — *"the Tao births the one,"* *"the Tao gives birth to the countless things."*
- **It follows only what it is.** 道法自然 (25) — *"the Tao models itself on being what it is."* Nothing stands above it.
- **It shelters.** 道者萬物之奧 (62) — *"the Tao is the sanctuary of the countless things."* 奧 (*ào*) is the innermost corner of a house.

**The oldest readers name it from motion.** 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*), on ch 1: 聖人觀其玄虛，用其周行，強字之曰道 — *"the sage watches its dark emptiness, makes use of its going-round, and forces the style 道 on it."* The name comes from 周行 (*zhōu xíng*), *going all the way round*, the phrase of chapter 25. **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*)** defines it in four characters: 道者，物之所由也 — *"the Tao is what things go by"* (51). 由 (*yóu*) is *by way of, through*. And on chapter 25: 道取於無物而不由也 — *"it is called 道 because there is nothing that does not go by it."* **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*)** gives the reason from the other end: 見萬物皆從道所生，故字之曰道 — *"seeing that the countless things all come from it, I style it 道."*

All three explain the name through the road. The Tao is not named for what it *is*. It is named for the fact that everything travels it.

### What we set aside

- ***the Way*** — the honest literal, and the reason it is forbidden is the capital. Capitalized and alone, *the Way* becomes a creed. It belongs to the early Christian name for itself (*the Way*, Acts 9:2), to every "way of life" sold since, and to a one-word answer to a question the book keeps open. Forbidden as the name; *way*, lowercase and with an owner, is kept.
- ***the Path*** — true to the road, but too small and too private. A path is one person's track through the woods, and 說文 says 道 is the road that runs straight through. Forbidden capitalized; *path* stays available as an ordinary word.
- ***God*, *the Absolute*, *the One*** — each imports what the text refuses: a person who creates and judges, or a metaphysical substance. 象帝之先 sets the Tao before the high deity, and 天地不仁 (5) says *"sky and earth are not concerned with humaneness."* And *the One* is 一's word: 道生一, *the Tao births the one* (42), so the two cannot be the same.
- ***Nature*** — already spoken for. *Nature* is 天 (*tiān*)'s English where 天 takes a verb (*the way of nature*), and *of itself* is 自然's (25). The ladder 人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然 needs four different words.
- ***the operating system, the source code*** — a modern metaphor, and it does catch three true things: the Tao is impersonal, it works without issuing commands (無為, 自然), and it runs beneath what is visible. It fails the pointing test. Laozi points at water, valleys and uncarved wood, and the graph is a person on a road under open sky. A machine metaphor brings in mechanism and design, which the book never names, and it will date faster than the text it explains. It can serve in commentary as a lens. It is never the word.

### Why the name stays untranslated

Chapter 25 says the name is forced, so we leave it visibly as a name. **"The Tao"** keeps the gesture: a word that does not pretend to define. It is also already an English word, and it carries less freight than *the Way* or *God*. We spell it *Tao* rather than the pinyin *Dao* only because that is the form English readers know. Either way it is pronounced *dào*.

**What stays untranslated is the name, not the word.** The first line teaches this: 道可道 → *"The Tao that can be made into a way."* *Tao* and *way* stand in the same sentence, so the reader learns what the name means before learning anything else.

### The working register

| Use | English | Chapters | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| the name | **the Tao** | throughout | 道生一 → *"the Tao births the one"* |
| the name, qualified | **the great Tao, the clear Tao…** | 18, 34, 41, 53 | 大道汎兮 → *"the great Tao overflows"* |
| a common noun with an owner | **way** | 9, 47, 73, 77 ×3, 79, 81 ×2 | 天之道 → *"the way of nature"*; 人之道 → *"the way of people"* (77); 聖人之道 → *"the way of the sage"* (81) |
| the verb in 道可道 | **made into a way** | 1 | *"The Tao that can be made into a way"* |
| 不道, the negation | **not-Tao** | 30, 55 | 是謂不道，不道早已 → *"this is called not-Tao. Not-Tao comes to an early end"* |

*Made into a way* is a construction, not 道's English. The supplied *made into* belongs to the line (`process/principles/supplied-verb-is-scaffolding.md`), so `render:` carries *way* alone.

### 道 and 德

The book is the 道**德**經, named for both. If 道 is what everything goes by, **德 (*dé* — integrity)** is that way received into one thing and kept whole there. 道生之，德畜之 (51) — *"the Tao gives birth to the countless things, integrity rears them."* Source and its presence in things, the grain of everything and the same grain running true through one life. See `de-德.md`.

### What no rule can enforce

**Lowercase *way* cannot be forbidden, and the boundary it marks can only be held by a reader.** The lock bans *the Way* and *the Path* with their capitals, which the checker reads as part of the violation. But whether a given 道 is the name or an owned way is a judgment about the line, and no check can make it. *Way* is also an ordinary English word that many lines use with no 道 in sight (13, 39). The ruling is: **the name is *the Tao*; a way that belongs to someone or something is *way*.**

### Left open

**Three owned ways still read *Tao*.** 長生久視之道 (59) is grammatically *the way of long life and lasting sight*, but reads *"the Tao of deep roots, firm base, long life, and enduring vision."* 我道大 (67), *"my Tao is great,"* has an owner in 我 (*wǒ* — I). 古之道 (14), *"the ancient Tao,"* has antiquity as its owner. Each can be argued: the speaker of 67 means the Tao they teach, and 14's ancient way is plainly the Tao. But the line in the register above does not yet decide them, and it should.

**The speech sense surfaces once, and the English drops it.** 道之出口 (35) is *"the Tao, when it leaves the mouth"*, that is, when it is spoken. It is the one line after chapter 1 that sets the name beside the act of telling, and *"the Tao is bland in the mouth"* turns the mouth that speaks into a mouth that tastes.

**And the first line still breaks a pun.** 道可道 holds the road and the telling in one verb. *Made into a way* keeps the road and loses the telling (`chapters/001.md` → Notes). No English word holds both, and every map of this word is, by the book's own first line, not the thing. We draw it anyway, because a map can still say *this way*, and we hold it loosely.
entries.shuowen: The road that is walked. From 辵 (chuò — walking along a road) and 𩠐 (shǒu — a head). A road that runs straight through is called 道.

entries.body:
## 德 (Dé) — Integrity

*Pronounced "duh," on a gently rising tone, as if asking a small question.*

Half of the book's own name. It is the 道德經 — the *Dao De Jing* — the Classic of the Way **and its 德**. Whatever this word means, Laozi set it on the cover beside 道, its equal. We cannot afford to get it wrong — and for a century, in English, we did.

### The trouble with "virtue"

The standard rendering has long been *virtue*, and the choice was not foolish. Latin *virtus* once meant **inherent power, efficacy, the potency proper to a thing** — we still say "the healing virtue of a herb," or that something happens "by virtue of" another. In that older sense the word was almost exactly right. But English narrowed it to Sunday-school morality — piety, propriety, good citizenship — and that is the very meaning Laozi writes *against*. In Chapter 38 he ranks 德 *above* benevolence, righteousness, and ritual (仁義禮), and insists the highest 德 does not even know itself as 德. To translate it "virtue" is to hand the reader the one connotation the text spends its whole energy dismantling.

So we set *virtue* aside — not because it was always wrong, but because it stopped being right.

### The character, read slowly

德 assembles from three parts, and it rewards watching them lock together:

- **彳 (chì)** — a footstep; going; conduct. It is the left half of 行, "road / to walk." 德 is never still. It *moves*.
- **直 (zhí)** — straight, upright. And 直 is itself a tiny picture: an **eye (目) above a single vertical stroke** — *to look straight ahead*. Directness of the gaze became directness of the character.
- **心 (xīn)** — the heart-mind.

Read together: **a straight-seeing heart, in motion** — trueness traveling straight out of an undivided center into the way one moves through the world.

Here is the detail that changes everything. In the oldest **Shang oracle-bone** forms, 德 has *no heart*. It is only 彳 + 直 — to go straight, to survey a road directly, to hold a true course. The **heart arrives later**, in the bronze inscriptions of the Zhou. You can watch, inside the life of a single character, a civilization growing an *interior*: what began as straightness of *path* became straightness of *soul*.

And one more thread, easy to miss and impossible to unsee. 德 is a near-twin of **得 (dé), "to get, to obtain"** — reconstructed almost identically in Old Chinese, and the old dictionaries pun on the pair openly: *德者，得也* — "De is what you have got." So 德 is not only how you *go*; it is **what you were given**. In the early Zhou it named the charismatic potency a ruler *received* — from Heaven, from the ancestors — the standing that made his rule legitimate. Laozi inherits that ancient sense of *received power* and does something quietly radical: he strips off the politics and the Heaven-favor and keeps only the pure kernel — **a potency received from the source and held intact within a thing.**

### What 德 becomes in Laozi's hands

Set the pieces together and one coherent thing appears. If **道 is the whole, undivided Way of all things, then 德 is that Way received into a single thing and kept intact there** — the Tao made local. The Tao, un-fragmented, *in you*.

See how steadily he uses it:

- *道生之，德畜之* (Ch 51) — the Tao gives them life; their **德** rears them. De is the Tao's care operating from *inside* each creature.
- *孔德之容，惟道是從* (Ch 21) — the form of great **德** follows the Tao alone. De is what the Tao looks like once it takes a body.
- *含德之厚，比於赤子* (Ch 55) — one whose **德** runs deep is like a newborn. Not a saint — an *infant*: maximally whole, nothing yet spent, nothing yet divided.
- *玄德* (Ch 10, 51, 65) — "dark," hidden **德**: the power to give birth, nourish, and lead *without possessing or controlling*. Potency with the ego removed.

And notice, just as carefully, what 德 is **not**. It is not social morality — Laozi keeps it a rung above the moral virtues and unconscious of itself. It is not 氣 (qì), the vital breath — that is fuel, the thermodynamics of a living body; 德 is the *intactness and rightness of the whole*, not its energy. And it is not generic "power" — it never slides into force or strength (力, 強), which Laozi distrusts. 德 is quieter than any of these: **the uncontrived, un-fragmented capacity to be exactly and fully what you are.**

### Why we land on *integrity*

Say the English word slowly and its own root opens: *integer* — **whole, untouched, undivided, intact.** It holds two meanings at once, and they are precisely the two halves of 德:

- **Structural integrity** — soundness, wholeness, a thing fully and intactly itself. This is the 德 of the newborn in Chapter 55, of the uncarved block, of everything Laozi loves that has not yet been split.
- **Moral integrity** — straightness, trueness of conduct. This is 彳 + 直 + 心 almost letter for letter: *to walk straight from the heart.* And "integrity" carries that ethical weight **without piety, without stuffiness**, free of the social-morality freight that drowns "virtue."

There is a deeper reason the word belongs to *this* translation in particular. Our whole reading of Laozi turns on **un-fragmentation** — 抱一, embrace the One; 復歸於樸, return to the uncarved block; the infant; the undivided center. *Integrity* is simply the English name for **un-fragmented wholeness.** It is not an import into our system; it is the keystone the other stones were already leaning toward. With it, 德 clicks home: the intact wholeness you received from the Tao, kept undivided, carried straight into the world.

### The working rule

**德 = "integrity," everywhere.** One word, no exceptions — and let the possessive do the quiet work in the rare line where 德 is a thing's own nature acting upon it (*"their integrity rears them"*). Retire *virtue*, *power*, and *lifeforce*. For 玄德, use **"hidden integrity"** or **"profound integrity."**

Hear it in the hard places:

- Ch 38 — *上德不德，是以有德* → **"The highest integrity isn't concerned with integrity — and so it holds."**
- Ch 41 — *上德若谷* → **"The highest integrity seems like a valley."**
- Ch 51 — *道生之，德畜之* → **"The Tao gives them life; their integrity nurtures them."**
- Ch 55 — *含德之厚* → **"One whose integrity runs deep…"**

### One tension, left honestly open

*Integrity* is not flawless. It has picked up a faint modern corporate echo — "business integrity," the poster on the break-room wall. We are betting that the older, structural sense — *intactness* — is strong enough to carry the weight, and that set against the deadening piety of "virtue" it will strike a modern ear as both truer and more alive. But this is finally the ear's decision, not the dictionary's. A living translation keeps testing its own keywords; if some later chapter makes *integrity* buckle, we will hear it, and we will come back to this page. For now it stands — **the Way, made whole, in a single thing.**

---

*Entry standard, going forward: begin with the live problem, not a definition; read the character as a picture and watch it change over time; let the cross-textual evidence argue the case; name what we set aside and why; and leave any real tension open rather than pretending it closed.*

## 帝 (Dì) — A God, and the One That Was Deposed

*Say "dee," falling. **One appearance in the whole book**, as the last word of Chapter 4 — and the most contested character in the history of translating Chinese into English.*

**Locked: 帝 → "god." 象帝之先 → "older than any god."** *(Settled 2026-08-31.)*

***Any*, not *the*, and the choice is load-bearing twice over.**

**It refuses to assert what the field has not settled.** Whether the Shang had a single high god is an open question in the scholarship, so *the high god* would smuggle a whole theological architecture in through the definite article — where nobody would notice it, because articles are not words readers weigh. **The definite article confers status exactly as a capital does** (standing rule 5): *the* high god reads as a title, *any* god reads as a category. It is the fault of *the Source* and *the One*, wearing a different part of speech.

**And it is the stronger claim, which the argument below needs.** If the Tao precedes only *the* high god, a claimant may answer *"my line descends from a different power."* If it precedes **any** god, the chain of descent has no floor anywhere. **The universal quantifier closes the escape the definite article leaves open.**

---

### The line is about where 帝 stands, not what 帝 is

Chapter 4 ends 象帝之先 — *"…before 帝."* The word names a god, and English has only ever done two things with it: **inflate it** into *God*, *the Lord*, *the Creator* — or **erase it** into an ancestor, a beginning, nothing at all.

Both destroy the line, and for the same reason. **They treat the sentence as a claim about what 帝 *is*, when it is a claim about where 帝 *stands*.** Inflate the word and the line becomes incoherent, because a God with something before him is not the Christian God. Erase it and the line becomes empty, because the whole point is *which* thing the Tao is said to precede.

**And the thing it precedes is not what it looks like.** 帝 is chosen for a reason that is neither purely theological nor purely political — because by the time this chapter was written, **those two things had become the same word.**

---

### The character: a calyx, a fire, or a pivot — but not a person

**說文解字 (c. 100 CE) is wrong here, and the reason it is wrong is the whole story in miniature.** Xu Shen gives 諦也，王天下之號也。从丄，朿聲 — *"帝 means 諦 (*dì* — to scrutinize); the title of one who rules the world. From 丄 (the archaic 上, 'above'), with 朿 (*cì* — a thorn) as sound."* Modern palaeography rejects that analysis. **By Xu Shen's day 帝 had meant *emperor* for three centuries, and he read the graph backwards from the word he knew.** The dictionary that preserves the oldest Chinese lexicography had already lost this one to the political meaning.

The oracle-bone graph is genuinely disputed. The three live readings:

- **A flower calyx** — the ring of sepals where blossom joins stem; the original form of 蒂 (*dì* — calyx, peduncle). **The part that holds the fruit and is not the fruit.**
- **A bundle of sacrificial firewood, or an altar** — linking the graph to 禘 (*dì*), the name of a great ancestral sacrifice.
- **A circumpolar asterism** at the north celestial pole *(Pankenier)* — the still point the sky turns around.

**None of the three is a person.** A calyx, a fire, a pivot: a joint, a rite, a centre of rotation. Whatever 帝 was, the graph is not a man on a throne and not a maker of worlds.

**And whether the Shang had a single high god is contested in the field**, not settled — *"Was There a High God Ti in Shang Religion?"* is a live question. 帝 in the oracle bones may name a supreme power over rain, harvest, war and the king's illnesses; it may be a collective term for the pantheon; it may be an honorific for the royal father. **The English must not settle what the scholarship has not.**

---

### 帝 was already a deposed god, and that is why it is the right word

This is the part the standard renderings lose, and it is chronology, not interpretation.

**Shang (to c. 1046 BCE):** 帝 / 上帝 is the high power. The living king does not sacrifice to 帝 directly — his **ancestors** do the petitioning, from the 宗 (*zōng*), the ancestral temple. Authority runs *king → ancestors → 帝*.

**Zhou conquest (c. 1046 BCE):** the Zhou **displace 帝 with 天 (*tiān*)** and invent 天命 (*tiān mìng* — the Mandate of Heaven) to justify having overthrown the Shang. This is documented as a legitimation device, effectively state propaganda: one legitimate ruler at a time, holding a mandate a god can withdraw. The Zhou king styles himself **天子 (*tiān zǐ*) — the child of 天.**

**So 帝 does not come to Laozi as the reigning god. It comes as the god a dynasty took down and replaced — the *previous* administration's highest power.**

**Warring States, 288 BCE:** King Min of Qi takes the title 東帝 (*dōng dì* — Di of the East) and King Zhao of Qin takes 西帝 (*xī dì* — Di of the West). **The first living human beings to claim the word.** It lasts months; both drop it on Su Dai's advice that two 帝 would only compete.

**221 BCE:** 秦始皇帝 (*Qín Shǐ Huáng Dì*) welds it permanently to the throne, and 帝 means *emperor* from then on.

**Chapter 4 is not attested at Guodian (~300 BCE); its earliest witness is Mawangdui, c. 200 BCE.** So the earliest readers we can actually document read 帝 **after** kings had grabbed it and after Qin had made it imperial. **They heard the god and the emperor in one word, and they heard a word that had already been deposed once.**

**"Empty theology" and "a critique of the emperor" are therefore not alternatives to choose between. In this character they are the same object**, and that is the answer to why Laozi reached for 帝 rather than for 天.

---

### What the line actually does: it takes the floor out of legitimation

Read the chapter's last two lines together, because they are one move:

> 吾不知**誰之子**，象**帝**之先。
> *I do not know **whose child** it is… before **帝**.*

**誰之子 — "whose child" — is not idle. 子 (*zǐ* — child) is the load-bearing word of Chinese political legitimacy, and this book uses it that way elsewhere.** Chapter 62 has **天子** (*tiān zǐ*) — the ruler, *the child of the sky*. Chapter 54 has 子孫以祭祀不輟 — *"descendants never break off the sacrifices,"* the ancestral cult running down the generations. Authority in both the Shang and the Zhou settlement is **inherited downward from a highest power**: the Shang king through his ancestors to 帝, the Zhou king directly as 天's child.

**Chapter 4 names both ends of that apparatus and pulls them apart.**

- Line 2 puts the Tao at the ancestral temple: 似萬物之**宗** — 說文 on 宗: **尊祖廟也。从宀从示**, *"the temple where ancestors are honoured; from 宀 (a roof) and 示 (the altar."* But it is hedged — 似, **it only *seems* to be the ancestor.**
- Line 6 denies it a parent: **吾不知誰之子**, *I do not know whose child it is.* **A thing with no parent cannot be inherited from, and cannot be claimed by descent.**
- Line 7 places it before 帝 itself: **帝之先.**

**Put those together and the genealogy of rule runs out of floor.** If something with **no parentage** stands **before any god**, then there is no ultimate ancestor at the bottom of the chain, and every claim of the form *"I rule because I descend from the highest"* is standing on nothing. **The Son of Heaven is a child; this has no parent and got there first.**

That is not a lament about a particular ruler. **It is a critique of legitimation by descent — which is the mechanism of dynasty itself.** And it is made without naming a single king, which is why it survived.

**It also explains the choice of 帝 over 天.** 天 is the *Zhou's* word, with the Mandate welded to it. To argue against the Zhou settlement in the Zhou's own vocabulary is to argue inside their frame. **Naming 帝 reaches behind that settlement to the god the Zhou themselves deposed, and says: even that one was not first.** The book does the same move to the Zhou's word in its own place — Chapter 25's ladder runs 人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然, sky modelling the Tao and the Tao modelling only being-so-of-itself. **Two chapters, two of the age's highest powers, each demoted using its own name.**

---

### The hardest question in the chapter: is 象 "seems," or is it *image*?

**Chapter 4 hedges five times in seven lines** — 似 twice, 或 twice, 吾不知 once. It is the most epistemically cautious chapter in the book. So a great deal turns on whether the final word 象 (*xiàng*) is a **sixth hedge** or the one thing the chapter is willing to assert.

**似 is this book's word for *seems*, and Chapter 4 uses it twice.** Its five occurrences are all comparative hedges: 似萬物之宗 and 似或存 here, 似鄙 at Chapter 20, 似不肖 twice at Chapter 67.

**象 is this book's word for *image*, and four of its five occurrences are unambiguously the noun** — and all four are central:

> 無物之**象** (14) — *the image of no-thing*
> 其中有**象** (21) — *within it there is an image*
> 執大**象**，天下往 (35) — *hold the great image, and the world comes*
> 大**象**無形 (41) — *the great image has no form*

**The fifth is this line.** If Laozi wanted a third *seems*, 似 was in his hand — he had just used it twice in the same seven lines. Switching to 象 for a third hedge is unmotivated; switching to 象 to name what the thing **is** is not.

**Both commentators read it as a hedge.** 王弼 paraphrases: 不亦**似**帝之先乎 — *"is it not as if before 帝?"* 河上公 simply asserts 道自在天帝之前. Their reading is old and it is defensible: 象 as "to resemble" is ordinary classical usage.

**But 王弼's own system argues against his paraphrase.** He built a hermeneutic on 言 / 象 / 意 (*words / image / meaning*), and in it 大象 — the great image — is **the essence itself**, the image that has no form. He treats 象 as a technical term everywhere else and flattens it here.

**And Laozi's chapters end on their strongest word, not their weakest.** 以此 (21) · 玄之又玄，眾妙之門 (1) · 道法自然 (25). A chapter that has hedged five times and then closes *"it also seems to…"* would be uniquely limp.

**So the reading this entry recommends: 象 is the noun.** The chapter refuses every assertion it might make about the Tao — and then, in its last three characters, names the one thing it will say: **an image, and older than the god.** Not a greater god behind the god. **A god-shaped place with an image of no-thing in it.** That is the empty theology, stated positively, and it is why 無物之象 at Chapter 14 reads as the same thought.
