*The traditional reading is not refuted, only outweighed. Anyone rendering* seems *here is in the company of both commentaries, and the line still works. What it loses is the landing.*

---

### Why this word above all others: the Term Question

**帝 is the word the missionaries fought over for two generations, and the man who won that fight built the English Tao Te Ching.**

The **Term Question** was the long dispute over which Chinese word would be conscripted to mean the Christian *God*: 神 (*shén*), 上帝 (*shàng dì* — "the 帝 above"), or 天主 (*tiān zhǔ*). It was never resolved by agreement. **The Chinese Union Bible was printed in two editions**, one using 上帝 and one using 神, because the parties could not be reconciled.

**James Legge (1815–1897) led the 上帝 party, and his side won** — by 1910 it had prevailed. Legge came to China with the London Missionary Society; his 1891 Tao Te Ching still underlies countless later versions. **The man who rendered 象帝之先 for the English-speaking world had spent decades arguing, in print and as doctrine, that 帝 means God.**

*(Traffic ran both ways, which is what makes the overlay so hard to see from inside English. The Chinese Union Bible renders John 1:1 as 太初有道，道與神同在，道就是神 — "In the beginning was the **Tao**; the Tao was with 神; the Tao **was** 神." Two of Laozi's central words were drafted to carry Logos and God before most English readers ever met either. See `process/overlay-audit.md`.)*

**The irony is exact.** Legge's God is an eternal creator with no antecedent. **Chapter 4's whole point is that 帝 has one.**

---

### What is set aside, and why

**"God"** — imports monotheism, creation from nothing, and a personal will, none of which 帝 carries in the oracle bones. Worse here than elsewhere: a God with something before him is not the Christian God, so the word makes the line unreadable in its own terms. It also takes Legge's side in a missionary controversy the Chinese text is not a party to.

**"the Lord"** — the same import in older clothes, plus a feudal relation (lordship, service, obedience) 帝 does not name.

**"the Creator"** — the worst, because the chapter argues the opposite. The Tao only 似 *seems* to be the ancestor of the countless things, and its own parentage is unknown. A chapter this careful about not asserting an origin cannot be handed a Creator in its final line.

**"Heaven"** — a double error: it imports the Christian afterlife **and** takes 天's English, already ruled on here (天 → *sky* / *nature*, never a realm). **And it destroys the argument**, because the whole force of 帝 is that it is *not* 天 — it is the god 天 replaced.

**"the Emperor"** — right for 221 BCE onward, and it collapses the line into politics alone. The reason to keep *god* is that the word carries both, and the reader should feel the second meaning arriving under the first.

**"the ancestor"** — what we had, borrowed from 宗 three lines up. It flattens a **god** into a **forebear** and makes the chapter say one thing twice, destroying the 宗 / 帝 bracket that holds it together.

**"the high god"** — this entry's own earlier recommendation, refused. It asserts a **singular supreme deity at the top of a hierarchy**, which is precisely what the scholarship on Shang religion has not settled, and it smuggles that assertion in through the definite article rather than through a word anyone would notice. *The* confers status the way a capital does.

**"the gods," "the pantheon"** — the opposite over-reach: they assert a plural set and a structure. 帝 is one word and the line makes one claim.

**Lowercase, always.** *any god*, never *any God* and never *the High God*. Capitals confer status (standing rule 5), and capitalizing here would re-import through typography exactly what the wording refuses.

---

### The working register

**帝 → "god," and at its one occurrence, *any god*.** No flexion, no sweep. The whole weight falls on three characters:

> 吾不知誰之子，象帝之先。
> *I do not know whose child it is. An image, older than any god.*

**Lowercase, always, and without the definite article.** The small *g* says: this **was** a god to the people who used the word — not a metaphor, not a personified force we are being polite about — and it was **not *the* God.** The bare *any* says the text is not describing the architecture of the divine. Between them they restore the god the English had deleted without installing a theology the Chinese does not hold.

---

### What stays open

**Whether to name him at all.** *"before Dì"* would treat 帝 as we treat 道 — an untranslated proper name, glossed once. It is honest about how much is contested, and it refuses to decide for the reader. It is also opaque, and it asks someone who has met one Chinese word to meet a second by Chapter 4. **Recommended against, without confidence.**

**Whether 象 is image or *seems*.** Argued above; the recommendation departs from both commentaries, which is not a thing to do lightly. **If Shalom keeps the traditional reading, the political argument above survives intact** — it rests on 誰之子, 宗 and 帝, not on 象.

**And a genuine strain, left standing: 帝 is a *name*, and *any god* is a *category*.** Laozi wrote one specific word — a power with a cult, a history, a deposition and a theft — and the rendering answers with a class. That loss is real, and it is accepted on the division of labour this repository runs on: **the line has to be true and to land; the entry carries the deep meaning.** A reader who wants the bronze-age god the Zhou deposed and the Qin stole has to come here, which is what entries are for.

**Locked 2026-08-31.** The `forbidden:` list is safe to enforce because **帝 occurs in one chapter and nothing else in Chapter 4 can legitimately claim any of those words** — there is no 天 (*tiān*) in this chapter, no ruler, and no maker. *God*, *the Lord* and *Creator* are capitalised in the list, so the capital is the violation and the lowercase *god* we use stays legal; *heaven*, *emperor* and *the high god* are lowercase and catch any casing.

**What is still open is 象 (*xiàng*), and it is settled against this entry's first instinct.** An earlier draft argued 象 here is the noun *image* — the book's term at 無物之象 (14), 其中有象 (21), 執大象 (35), 大象無形 (41) — on the grounds that 似 is the dedicated hedge and is already used twice in this chapter. **The grammar defeats it.** In all four places where 象 is unambiguously a noun it is *marked* as one, by 之, by 有, or by 大. **At 象帝之先 it stands bare before a noun phrase, which is the shape of verb plus object** — and both commentaries read it as a comparison. Chapter 4 is also 象's first appearance in the book, so an English *image* would land where no reader can yet hear the thread. The line reads *"It seems older than any god."*
entries.render: god — *any god* at its one occurrence

entries.body:
## 復命 (Fù Mìng) — Returning What You Were Sent With

*Say "foo ming," both syllables falling. Two lines, both in Chapter 16, and it names the third rung of the chain that ends in clear-seeing.*

**Locked: 復命 → "returning to what is given."** *(Never "returning to destiny," never "restoring destiny," never anything built on "the mandate" — and not the past tense, "what **was** given.")*

**The present tense carries the decision.** *Was given* puts the giving behind us, in a naming chain whose other members — 靜 (*jìng* — stillness) and 常 (*cháng* — the ever-present) — are timeless. *Is given* is ongoing: what any thing is given, always. And the passive keeps the giver **present but unnamed**, which is what the Chinese does: 命's graph has a mouth in it and never says whose.

### It is a name, not a new thing

This is the single most useful fact about the term, and it is easy to miss. Chapter 16 describes **one event** and then names it four times over, each name becoming the subject of the next line:

| Chinese | What it does |
|---|---|
| 各復歸其根 | the event: **each returns again to its root** |
| 歸根**曰**靜 | that return **is called** 靜 (*jìng* — stillness) |
| 是謂**復命** | it **is called** 復命 |
| 復命**曰**常 | 復命 **is called** 常 (*cháng* — the ever-present) |
| 知常**曰**明 | knowing 常 **is called** 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing) |

曰 (*yuē*) is *"is called"*; 是謂 (*shì wèi*) is *"this is called."* **Nothing new enters at 復命.** The chapter is handing a second name to the returning it has just shown you, and then a third, so that a motion you can watch in a field becomes a thing you can know.

So the question is never *what else happens at 復命* — it is **what the returning looks like when you call it by this name.**

### The two characters, down to the radicals

**復 (*fù*) — a foot on a road it has walked before**

Our vendored 說文解字: **往來也。从彳复聲** — *"going and coming. From 彳 (chì), with 复 (fù) for sound."*

彳 is one half of a walking graph, and the 說文 says so where it defines 行 (*xíng* — to walk): **人之步趨也。从彳从亍** — *"a person's stepping and hurrying. From 彳 and 亍 (chù)."* 行 is a crossroads; 彳 is its left-hand stride.

And 复, the half Xu Shen calls phonetic, is not phonetic only — he glosses it **行故道也**, *"to travel the old road."* Its oracle-bone form sets a **foot beneath a dwelling**: going out from where you live and coming back to it. *(复 is not among the 711 characters the Laozi uses, so the repository's 說文 does not carry it; that gloss comes from outside this repo.)*

**So 復 holds two feet** — one inside 复, and 彳 wrapped around it when the bronze script built the fuller graph. It is the most pedestrian word in the chapter, and **the road it walks is one it knows**.

**命 (*mìng*) — a voice over someone kneeling**

Our 說文: **使也。从口从令** — *"to send. From 口 (kǒu) and from 令 (lìng)."* 使 (*shǐ*) in classical Chinese is both *to send* and *the one sent* — an envoy.

Each part, one level down:

- **口 (*kǒu*)** — 說文: **人所以言食也。象形** — *"what a person speaks and eats with. A pictograph."* A mouth.
- **令 (*lìng*)** — 說文: **發號也。从亼、卪** — *"to issue a call. From 亼 (jí) and 卪 (jié)."*
- **亼 (*jí*)** — the assembling sign: three strokes converging. Read either as an inverted 口, or as a **hand-bell rung to call people in**.
- **卪 (*jié*, also written 卩)** — **a kneeling figure.** *(說文 itself reads it as 瑞信也, "an auspicious tally"; the kneeling-person reading is modern palaeography, and neither component is among the Laozi's 711.)*

**And the two characters were one.** In the oracle-bone script **命 and 令 are the same graph** — the gathering-sign above, the kneeling figure below. A chief sounds a bell to call people in; whoever receives the order kneels to take it. **口 was added during the Western Zhou bronze period**, and by the small seal script the two had separated into 命 and 令.

So the scene inside 命 is complete: a summons, a gathering, someone on their knees, and **a mouth** — the utterance made explicit, which is the whole of what 命 adds to 令.

**Which is why the compound is not a redundancy.** 復 walks a road it already knows. 命 is what was said, out loud, over the one who was sent down it.

**A note on how physical the chapter's returning is.** Two lines above 是謂復命 stands 各復歸其根, and 歸 (*guī*) is 說文 **女嫁也。从止，从婦省** — *"a woman marrying. From 止 (zhǐ — a foot), from an abbreviated 婦 (fù — woman)."* **復歸 carries three feet between them**, and it arrives at 根 (*gēn*), which is 說文 木株也 — a **stump**. Nothing in this passage is abstract until the chapter names it: the returning is walked, and the place walked to is a piece of wood in the ground.

### What the commentators make of it

Both read it as coming back to what one was allotted to be, and both reach for the same compound:

> **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE):** 歸根則靜，故曰靜。靜則復命，故曰復命也。復命則得**性命**之常，故曰常也
> *"Returning to the root is stillness, hence 'stillness.' Stillness is 復命, hence '復命.' 復命 is attaining the constancy of 性命 (xìng mìng — inborn nature and allotted span), hence 'the ever-present.'"*

> **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han):** 言安靜者是為復還**性命**使不死也
> *"The still one is returning to their 性命, so as not to die."*

**Both link 復命 to 常 through constancy** — which is what the next line does too, so the commentary and the text agree on the joint.

**But 性 (*xìng* — inborn nature) has zero occurrences in the Tao Te Ching.** 性命 is the vocabulary of a later philosophical settlement, read back onto a text that does not use it. The reading may be right; the word is theirs. An English that says *nature* here would be translating the commentary. *(`CLAUDE.md`: a commentator's gloss is not the text.)*

### The reading the commentators do not take

**復命 is also standard classical Chinese for an envoy reporting back after completing a commission** — and 說文 glosses 命 with 使, the envoy word itself.

Under that reading the chapter's shape is exact. Things 作 (*zuò* — 說文 起也, *"to rise"*): they are sent out. They come to their fullest. They 復: they return, and what they hand back is the charge they went out with.

Neither commentator takes it. The graph and the idiom do, and the chapter's own 作 → 復 architecture fits it without strain. **This edition records both rather than choosing**, because nothing in the Chinese forces the choice and the difference is real: one is *resuming what you always were*, the other is *discharging what you were given to do*.

### What is set aside

**destiny, fate** — both make 命 a script settled before the actor arrives. 命 is spoken *to* someone, at a moment, and it can be reported back on. *Fate* additionally carries the Greek Moirai and Christian providence into a text with neither.

**mandate** — 天命 (*tiān mìng* — the Mandate of Heaven)'s word, the Zhou warrant-to-rule. **天命 has zero occurrences in this book.** Using it here imports a 天 that grants and withdraws, which is the overlay `tian-天.md` exists to strip.

**"restoring destiny," "the system's command"** — the Source table's literal glosses, and the second is mechanistic in exactly the way `CLAUDE.md` names as this edition's own besetting temptation.

**"returning to the source," "returning to the origin"** — 復命 is not 歸根 restated in cosmic terms. 根 (*gēn*) is 說文 木株也, a **stump**; the chapter has already given the return its concrete name and is now giving it a different one. Collapsing the two throws away the reason there are two.

### The working register

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 是謂復命 | 16 | This is called *(the chosen phrase)* |
| 復命曰常 | 16 | *(the same phrase)*, repeated verbatim as the subject |

**The phrase must survive repetition**, because 是謂復命。復命曰常 is the chapter's tail-head device (頂真 *dǐng zhēn*): the last word of one line opens the next. Whatever is chosen is said twice, adjacently, and a phrase that reads well once may not read well immediately again.

### What was set aside, and why it took four tries

***returning to the allotted course*** — a *course* is a path you run, and the chapter's event is a thing **finishing** one, not rejoining it. 命 is not a path: everything the graph gives is a moment — a bell, a gathering, someone kneeling, a mouth. The phrase also sat comfortably in a sermon, which is the hymn test failing.

***returning the charge* · *returning the message*** — both take 復命 **transitively**, handing the commission back, which is the envoy idiom and is genuinely available. But **neither commentator reads it that way**, and `CLAUDE.md`'s tie-breaking order puts the classical commentaries above this edition's ethos and above poetic intuition. Both also need an antecedent the chapter never supplies — *which* charge, *which* message — and *the message* additionally carries the English sense of *the moral*.

***returning to what is*** — the worst of the four, and the reverse check catches it in an unusual form. *What it is* is already **自然 (*zì rán* — of itself)**'s English at ch 25 (道法自然 → *"the Tao models itself on being what it is"*), and 自然 is not merely another term: **chapter 51 sets it against 命 in a single clause** — 夫莫之命而常自然, *"no one 命s it, and it is always 自然."* Rendering 命 with its own antonym's English would collapse the book's antithesis from the inside.

### The tension, left open

**命's verb is unsettled one chapter over.** Ch 51's 夫莫之命而常自然 reads *"no one commands it"* — but *command* is 令 (*lìng*)'s English at ch 32, in the identical 莫之X而 frame, and the two characters were **one graph** before the Western Zhou split them. See `ming-命.md` and `WORKLIST.md` T2-29.

**And the commentators' reading is not the only one the book supports.** 復命 is standard classical Chinese for an envoy reporting back from a commission, and 說文 glosses 命 with 使 — the envoy word. The chapter's 作 → 復 architecture fits that without strain. This edition follows the commentators and records the other reading rather than burying it: one is *resuming what you always were*, the other is *discharging what you were given to do*, and nothing in the Chinese forces the choice.

## 敢 (Gǎn) — The Forward Press to Take

*Say "gahn," dipping. Ten lines across seven chapters, and 不敢 (bù gǎn) is the third of the book's three treasures.*

**Locked: 敢 → "push / venture" — the forward press to take.** *(Never "dare," "dares," "dared," "daring.")*

Every English Tao Te Ching renders 不敢 (*bù gǎn*) as **dare not**. It is the natural English, and it inverts the book.

In modern English, *he did not dare* means **he was afraid**. Chapter 73 says the opposite in six characters:

> 勇於**敢**則殺，勇於**不敢**則活
> *"Courage in 敢 kills. Courage in **not**-敢 lives."*

There is a **courage of not-敢**. Whatever English carries the word must be able to be brave. *Not daring* cannot: it makes the third of Chapter 67's three treasures sound like timidity, in a chapter that two lines earlier says 慈故能勇 — *"tenderness, and so you can be brave."*

### The character: a hand, a weapon, and a boar

The oracle-bone accounts read 敢 as **a hand holding a hunting implement, going after a wild boar** (豕, *shǐ*). Its oldest sense is *to hunt, to pursue*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* keeps that and abstracts it slightly: 敢，**進取**也 — *"敢 is to advance and take."*

**So 敢 is appetite, not bravery.** It is the forward motion of someone going after a thing in order to have it. Courage may accompany that; it is not what the word means.

**And it may be 爭's cousin.** On one account the bronze-script form of 敢 is built on **爭** (*zhēng* — two hands pulling at a single object), with 甘 supplying only the sound. If that holds, the two characters are relatives — and so are the book's two great refusals. 不爭 declines to pull at a thing two hands already hold. 不敢 declines to go after a thing no hand holds yet. Between them they cover the whole of wanting. *(Scholars differ on the graph; recorded as a resonance, not a proof. See `zheng-爭.md`.)*

### 不敢 is a politeness formula, not a confession

Classical Chinese uses 不敢 the way English once used *I should not presume*:

- 不敢高攀 — *"I could not presume upon your attention."*
- 愧不敢當 — *"I am ashamed, and do not deserve it."*

This is the language of **declining to help yourself to something**. Nobody in these phrases is frightened; they are being well-mannered about appetite.

### The book supplies its own gloss

Chapter 67 names the third treasure as 不敢為天下先, then four lines later says what abandoning it looks like: 舍後且先. 王弼 glosses the particle 且 in three characters — 且猶**取**也, *"且 is like 取, **to grab**."*

So what 敢 does to 先 (*xiān* — the front) is **grab at it**. 不敢 is not-grabbing. The verdict on the person who does grab is 死矣 — *that is death* — which is not a sentence anyone passes on the merely timid.

### Where it stands

| Chapter | Chinese | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 使夫智者**不敢**為也 | so the guileful will not push to act |
| 30 | **不敢**以取強 | never pushes on to seize dominance |
| 64 | 而**不敢**為 | and never pushes them |
| 67 | **不敢**為天下先 ×2 | never pushing to be first in the world |
| 69 | 吾**不敢**為主，而為客 · **不敢**進寸，而退尺 | does not venture to act as host · does not venture an inch forward |
| 73 | 勇於**敢**則殺，勇於**不敢**則活 | the load-bearing line |
| 74 | 孰**敢** | who would venture? |

**Seven chapters, and only Chapter 73 uses 敢 affirmatively.** Everywhere else it appears under negation, which it shares with 爭 — see that entry, where all nine occurrences are negated.

### Chapter 69 shows the register

> 吾不敢為主，而為客；不敢進寸，而退尺
> *"I do not venture to act as host, but act as guest; do not venture an inch forward, but retreat a foot."*

Host against guest is a question of **propriety** — who presides, who defers — and it has nothing to do with courage. An inch forward against a foot back is a question of **position**. Both are the vocabulary of someone choosing not to take precedence, which is what 敢 is for.

### What is set aside

**dare, daring** — the fear reading, which reverses Chapter 73 and makes Chapter 67's third treasure a confession of nerves. Forbidden outright. *(If a drafted chapter ever needs it — Chapter 73 is the only candidate, since 勇 stands beside 敢 there and blocks the timid reading — that is a `lock-ok` waiver with its reason stated, not a loosening of the lock.)*

**presume** — the exact word for 不敢, and unavailable: 恃 (*shì*) holds it at Chapters 2, 10 and 51, where 為而不恃 reads *"acts but does not presume."* **That rendering is itself loose** — 恃 means *to rely on, to lean on*, as our own source tables gloss it every time and as Chapter 34's 萬物恃之以生 (*"the countless things rely on it to live"*) requires. If 恃 is ever corrected to *rely*, *presume* comes free and should be reconsidered here. Logged in `WORKLIST.md`.

**fear, afraid, shrink, flinch, hesitate** — all import the timidity the lock exists to remove.

**bold, boldness** — right for affirmative 敢 but positive in English, where the book treats 敢 as the fault.

### Working register

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 不敢為, bare | 64 | never pushes them |
| 不敢為 + role or position | 67, 69 | never pushing to be first · does not venture to act as host |
| 不敢 + verb | 30, 69 | never pushes on to seize · does not venture an inch |
| 敢, affirmative | 73, 74 | venture |

**不敢為 is rendered as a unit at Chapter 64.** *"And never pushes them"* carries 敢為 in one verb rather than splitting it, because English *push to handle* will not stand. The chapter's contrast survives intact and is sharper for it: 輔 (*fǔ*) is the spare timber lashed alongside a cart-wheel to brace it, and a brace holds from the side where a push moves from behind. **Support them; do not push them.**

### What stays open

**Whether Chapter 73's one affirmative 敢 wants a different word.** Nine of the ten occurrences are negated; the exception is 勇於**敢**則殺，勇於不敢則活 — *"courage in 敢 kills; courage in not-敢 lives."*

There, 敢 is **nominalised** after 於, so it wants a noun and the modal problem disappears — which reopens a candidate the lock otherwise excludes. **Pursue.** *"Courage in pursuit kills; courage in not pursuing lives"* reads better than *courage in pushing*, and it returns the word to its own picture: a hand with a hunting weapon, going after a boar.

Everywhere else *pursue* fails, and for two reasons worth keeping written down. **The grammar:** 敢 is an auxiliary taking a verb — 敢**為**, 敢**進**, 敢**以取** — and English *pursue* is transitive and cannot fill that slot; *"never pursuing to be first"* is not a sentence. **The semantics:** what 敢 reaches for in this book never runs away. The front of the line, the host's seat, an inch of ground, dominance. Pursuit implies quarry; 敢 is helping yourself to what is already there, which is why 不敢 became a formula of manners rather than a term of the chase.

So the boar belongs in this entry and not in the verse — the etymology justifies the reading, it does not supply the English. **The one line where it might supply the English is Chapter 73's, and that is left open until the chapter is drafted.**

**Laozi drives a wedge through a word the language keeps whole.** 勇 (*yǒng* — courage) and 敢 sit together in Chapters 67 and 73, and in ordinary Chinese they join into one compound, 勇敢 (*yǒng gǎn*), which is simply the word for *brave*. This book splits the halves and assigns them opposite values — 慈故能**勇**, *tenderness and so courage*, against 不**敢**為天下先. Chapter 73 states the split as a paradox: 勇於不敢, **courage in not-venturing**.

Whether that distinction was live in Laozi's period or is his own coinage, nothing in this book settles.

**And the sage arrives at the front regardless.** Chapter 7: 後其身而身**先** — *"placing themselves last, the sage is first."* Chapter 66: the world 樂推, gladly pushes them forward. So 不敢為天下先 forbids the **reaching**, not the **arriving** — and whether a refusal that reliably delivers the thing refused is an ethic or a technique is the same question left open at the foot of `zheng-爭.md`. The two entries end in the same place, which is probably not an accident.
entries.render: push / venture — the forward press to take

entries.body:
## 公 (Gōng) — Impartiality

*Say "gong," first tone, level and held. A word English splits into two that have nothing to do with each other: a virtue and a peerage.*

**Locked: 公 → "impartiality" where it names the quality; "lord" or "minister" where it names the office.** *(Never "duke." Reasoning below.)*

Open almost any English Tao Te Ching at Chapter 42 and you will find *dukes*. Open it at Chapter 16 and you will find *fairness*, or *equanimity*, or *the impartial*. Nothing tells the reader these are one word. So the fact the Chinese states plainly — **the office is named after the virtue** — disappears, and with it the quiet judgment the text passes every time it uses the title.

### The character is a negation, and that is the whole of it

公 is two pieces:

- **八** (*bā*) — two strokes turning away from each other. It is the numeral eight by sound-loan, but the picture is *dividing*, and by extension **turning one's back on**.
- **厶** (*sī*) — a small self-enclosing curl. It is the original form of **私** (*sī* — private, one's own).

So the graph is *turning your back on the self-enclosing*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) glosses it 公，平分也 — **"公 is fair division"** — and then, unusually, names a source: 韓非曰：背厶爲公, *"Han Feizi says: turning your back on 厶 is 公."*

Han Feizi's own sentence, from 五蠹 (*Wǔ dù* — "The Five Vermin"), gives the full form:

> 古者蒼頡之作書也，自環者謂之**私**，背私謂之**公**。
> *"When Cangjie made writing in ancient times, what encircles itself he called **私**, the private; what turns its back on 私 he called **公**."*

**That 公 is a negation and not a positive quality is the finding.** English *impartiality*, *fairness*, *justice* all sound like attainments — things you build up. 公 is what is left when the curl uncurls. You do not acquire it; you stop doing the other thing.

### Why that matters at Chapter 16

Ch 16 puts 公 on a chain where each line begins with the word the last one ended on:

> 知常**容**，**容**乃**公**，**公**乃**王**，**王**乃**天**，**天**乃**道**，**道**乃久
> *knowing the ever-present is capaciousness; capaciousness is impartiality; impartiality is sovereignty; sovereignty is the open sky; the open sky is the Tao; the Tao endures.*

Every rung widens the circle beyond the self, and **公 is where the widening leaves the person.** 容 (*róng* — capaciousness) is still an inner quality, something you have. 公 is the first rung that is not about you at all, because it is defined as facing away from you. Read as *equanimity*, rung two collapses back inside the person and the ascent stalls — which is exactly why that rendering was set aside.

### The counter-term is in the book, twice

Laozi does not use 公 and 私 in one line, but he uses 私 where it counts, and it is the same negation running the other way.

> Ch 7 · 天地所以能長且久者，以其不自生 … 非以其**無私**邪？故能成其**私**。
> *"Sky and earth endure because they do not live for themselves … Is it not because they have no private self? And so they can fulfil their own."*

That is 公 stated as a paradox: the self is completed by facing away from it. And Ch 19 gives the instruction in four characters — 少**私**寡欲, *"reduce the private, diminish desire"* — where 私 sits beside 欲 (*yù* — desire) as one of the two things to thin out.

### The office, and the judgment hidden in it

Chinese titles are often meaning-transparent in a way English peerage is not. English has one good parallel: *justice* is both the virtue and the person who holds the office — Justice Roberts. Nobody hears *fair division* in **duke**.

That transparency does work in Chapter 42:

> 人之所惡，唯孤、寡、不穀，而**王公**以為稱。
> *"What people most hate is to be called orphaned, meagre, unworthy — yet kings and lords take these very words as their titles."*

The chapter is about rulers naming themselves with words of **lack**. A title that means *turned away from the private* belongs in that sentence, and the joke is sharper for it: the rank itself already says *not for yourself*, and the chapter is telling rulers to live up to their own letterhead.

And in Chapter 62 the manuscripts hand us an argument. Where the received text reads 三**公**, the Mawangdui silks write 三**鄉**, which editors read as a loan for 三**卿** (*sān qīng* — the three high ministers). **The oldest witness names the office with the plain word for a minister of state** — not with a rank. *Minister* is therefore not a modernization; it is the older reading's own word.

### What is set aside

**"Duke."** Rejected outright. It imports the European feudal ladder — duke, marquess, earl — an entire social order the Zhou did not have and did not resemble, and it severs the office from its meaning. A reader who meets *duke* in 42 and *impartiality* in 16 has no way to know they read the same character.

**"Equanimity."** Inner calm. It puts rung two of Ch 16's ladder back inside the person, halting a climb whose whole motion is outward. 公 is a direction of facing, not a state of nerves.

**"Justice."** A legal and moral frame, concerned with **desert** — what a person is owed. 公 is concerned with **whose interest** — it asks who you are facing, not who deserves what. The distinction is the difference between a courtroom and a horizon.

**"The public"** as a noun. A modern civic abstraction with a nineteenth-century shape, and it makes 公 a body of people rather than a way of standing.

*"Fairness"* is not forbidden, and it is not wrong — only thinner. Fairness is a **procedure**; 公 is a **direction**. You can execute a fair procedure while facing entirely inward.

### Working register

| The grammar | Where | Render |
|---|---|---|
| the quality, as a noun in the ladder | 16 (容乃公) | **impartiality** |
| the quality, as an adjective | — | **impartial** |
| the office, compounded with 王 | 42 (王公) | **lords** |
| the office, the three highest of state | 62 (三公) | **the three ministers** |

### What stays open

**The two senses cannot take one English word, and this entry does not force them to.** Every available rendering for the office severs it from the root, so a reader of Chapter 62 will not hear what a reader of Chapter 16 hears. That is a real loss, and the glossary can only partly repair it: the entry can say *the office is named after the virtue*, but the verse cannot.

Whether that is worth a translator's note in the finished edition, or whether the loss should simply be borne, is not settled here.

**And 私 has its own drift.** It reads *"selfish"* at Ch 7 and *"the self"* at Ch 19 — and Chapter 7's paradox, 故能成其私, *"and so they can fulfil their own,"* has vanished from the English altogether, which takes the sting out of a line built to sting. 私 may want an entry of its own rather than shelter under this one.
entries.render: impartiality / impartial (the quality) · lord / minister (the office)

entries.body:
## 貨 (Huò) — Goods

*Say "hwaw," falling. Five appearances across five chapters — 3, 12, 44, 53, 64. Three of them are the same four-character phrase, and that phrase carries one of the book's sharpest political arguments.*

**Locked: 貨 → "goods." · 難得之貨 → "rare goods."** *(Not "treasure," not "the precious," not "wealth.")*

---

### Scarcity is a fact; the value is conferred

Chapter 3 says 不貴難得之貨，使民不為盜 — *"do not prize 難得之貨, and the people do not become thieves."* The line is a causal claim about **what a ruler does**, and the standard English quietly destroys it:

> *"By not valuing **the precious**, no one becomes a thief."*

If the goods are *already precious*, the advice is circular. **Do not prize the prized.** It shrinks to a shrug about austerity, and the ruler drops out of the sentence — which is the one place the sentence is pointing.

The Chinese does not say the goods are precious. It says they are **難得** (*nán dé* — hard to obtain), which is a fact about **acquisition**, not a verdict about **worth**. The argument runs:

> **the goods are hard to get → the ruler prizes them → people steal.**

The scarcity is a fact about the world. **The value is conferred by the prizing.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE) states the causation in four characters and then follows it to its end: 貴貨過用，貪者競趣，穿窬探篋，沒命而盜 — *"prize goods **beyond their usefulness**, and the greedy race for them: they tunnel through walls, rifle chests, and steal at the cost of their lives."* 貴貨過用 (*guì huò guò yòng*) is the cause, and its subject is the ruler.

河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han) supplies the image, on chapter 64: 聖人不眩為服，不賤石而貴玉 — *"the sage is not dazzled into adorning themselves; does not despise stone and prize jade."* **賤 (*jiàn* — to hold cheap) and 貴 (*guì* — to prize) are both things a person does.** Stone and jade differ in what someone does about them.

---

### The character: a shell that changes hands

貨 is 貝 (*bèi* — a cowrie shell) with 化 (*huà*) above it. 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE): **財也。从貝化聲** — *"property. It follows 貝, with 化 as the sound."*

**貝 is a drawing of a cowrie shell**, and it is not a metaphor. Cowries were currency in the Shang and early Zhou, strung and counted, and they are why the whole vocabulary of value in Chinese is built on this one radical.

**化 is two people, one of them upside down.** 說文: 教行也。从𠤎从人 — *"teaching put into practice. It follows 𠤎 and 人."* 人 (*rén*) is a person standing; 𠤎 is the same figure inverted. The graph is **a body turning over** — transformation, one state becoming another. It is the 化 of 自化 (*zì huà* — "transform of themselves"), which chapter 37 and chapter 57 make the whole point of good government.

So even taken as a pure sound-element, 化 sits over the shell in a word for **things that circulate**. 貨 is money in motion. Goods that change hands.

### The three 貝 characters, and why English has three words for them

The book uses three characters built on the cowrie, and our English had been shuffling them.

| | 說文 | what it is | our word |
|---|---|---|---|
| **貨** (*huò*) | 財也 — *"property"* | 貝 + 化: a shell that **changes hands** | **goods** |
| **寶** (*bǎo*) | 珍也 — *"a precious thing"* | 宀 (*mián* — a roof) over 王 (jade) and 貝 (cowrie): **a hoard that does not move** | **treasure** |
| **貴** (*guì*) | 物不賤也 — *"a thing that is not cheap"* | a **position on a price scale**, paired against 賤 (*jiàn* — cheap; 說文 賈少也, *"small in price"*) | **precious · prize** |

**貨 moves, 寶 sits still, 貴 is a rating someone assigns.** They are not three words for the same idea, and the differences are exactly what chapter 3 is arguing about. Giving 貨 the word for a hoard (*treasure*) or the word for a rating (*precious*) collapses the very distinction the line depends on.

---

### Where it appears

**Three of the five are one stock phrase**, 難得之貨, always under a verb of prizing or in a list of what corrupts:

> 不貴**難得之貨**，使民不為盜 (3) — *not prizing rare goods, the people do not become thieves.*
> **難得之貨**，令人行妨 (12) — *rare goods make conduct go wrong.*
> 是以聖人欲不欲，不貴**難得之貨** (64) — *so the sage wants the not-wanting, and does not prize rare goods.*

**The other two are ordinary and concrete.** Chapter 44 sets it against the body: 身與貨孰多 — *"the self or goods, which is worth more?"* Chapter 53 puts it at the end of a list of a ruler's excesses: 財貨有餘 — *"wealth and goods in surplus"*, where 財 (*cái* — property) and 貨 form a bound compound and each keeps its own English.

**What the goods actually are** is not left to guessing. 河上公 names them on chapter 3: 好珎寶，黃金棄於山，珠玉捐於淵 — *"fine treasures; gold left in the mountain, pearls and jade abandoned in the deep."* Gold, pearls, jade. **Nobody needs jade.** That single fact decides several of the rejected renderings below.

### The thief was drooling

說文 on 盜 (*dào* — thief), the word chapter 3 says the ruler creates: **私利物也。从㳄，㳄欲皿者** — *"to take private profit from a thing. It follows 㳄 (*xián* — drool), the drooling of one who wants the dish."*

A thief, in the oldest analysis of the graph, is **someone salivating over a vessel.** The theft begins in the wanting, and chapter 3's third line says where the wanting begins: 不見可欲，使民心不亂 — *"do not display what can be desired, and the people's hearts are not thrown into disorder."* Display, then appetite, then theft. The chapter blames the first link, and the character agrees with it.

---

### What is set aside, and why

**"precious" — it is 貴's word, and it makes the line circular.** 貴 renders *precious* at chapters 70, 72 and 75, and *prize* as a verb at 20 and 64. In chapters 3 and 64 貴 is the verb standing directly over 貨, so *"do not prize precious goods"* puts one character's English on top of another and argues in a circle. **Forbidding it here is safe**: 貴 occurs in chapters 3 and 64 *only* inside 不貴, verbal both times, so no legitimate claimant for *precious* exists in either chapter.

**"treasure" / "treasures" — it is 寶's word.** 寶 has chapters 62, 67 and 69 and never shares a chapter with 貨, so the words can be kept apart cleanly. And the senses genuinely differ: 寶 is a hoard under a roof, the three 寶 of chapter 67 that one 持而保之 (*chí ér bǎo zhī* — "holds and keeps safe"). 貨 is the opposite motion.

**"scarce" — it imports a shortage the chapter denies.** *Scarce* is relational: not enough of a thing for what is wanted. But nobody needs jade. Call the goods scarce and the people's wanting becomes **natural, a real shortfall honestly felt** — and then the ruler cannot be blamed for it, which unmakes the whole stanza. Chapter 12 says the same from the other end: 腹 (*fù* — belly), the organ that **can** be satisfied, against 目 (*mù* — eye), the one that cannot. Scarcity is a fact about bellies. These chapters are about eyes. *(Secondarily: scarcity is the founding term of modern economics and drags that apparatus into a Warring States line.)*

**"wealth" — it belongs to 富 (*fù*), and to 財 in the one chapter they share.** 富 carries *wealth · wealthy · enrich* at chapters 9, 33 and 57. Chapter 44 had 貨 wearing that word and it has been swept to *goods*.

**"hard to get" / "hard to come by" — blocked, and instructively.** These are the literal sense of 難得, and they cannot be used: **"hard" is 堅 (*jiān* — rigid)'s word**, settled across chapters 36, 43, 76 and 78, where 堅強 (*jiān qiáng*) is what a corpse is. And 難's own English elsewhere is *difficult* (chapters 2, 63, 73), which will not go attributive in verse without grinding. Both routes close.

**"luxuries," "rarities," "coveted," "costly" — each puts the verdict back in the noun.** *Luxury* is Latin *luxuria*, excess, and it does the chapter's work for it: Laozi's claim is that these are ordinary goods that prizing turns into objects of theft, not that they are inherently excessive. *Coveted* collides directly with 可欲 (*kě yù* — what can be desired), which is *the desirable* two lines below in chapter 3's own triad. *Costly* is a price, and a price is conferred value.

---

### The working register

**貨 → "goods," in all five places, with no flexions** — and that, not *rare goods*, is what the frontmatter locks. **"Rare" is not 貨's rendering**; it renders 難得 (*nán dé* — hard to obtain), which as the closing section says renders no character at all. Putting *rare goods* in the `render:` field would overstate the lock and would push an unglossed Chinese phrase into the generated CSVs. Chapter 53's 財貨 is a bound compound and reads *"wealth and goods,"* 財 keeping its own word.

**難得之貨 → "rare goods," as a unit.** The phrase is lexical in classical Chinese — a **category of thing**, not a fresh description — so it takes a category name in English rather than a relative clause. That also restores something chapter 3 had lost: its three objects are 賢 (*xián* — the talented, one character), 難得之貨 (four), and 可欲 (two), so **the middle line is deliberately the heaviest**, and an English triad of neat two-word abstractions had flattened it.

**貴 keeps *prize* as its verb here.** Chapters 3 and 64 both open the phrase with 不貴, and both now read *does not prize*, matching 貴食母 (*guì shí mǔ* — "prize feeding from the mother") at chapter 20.

---

### What stays open

**"Rare" renders no character.** This is the honest cost of the lock and it should not be smoothed over. 難 (*nán* — difficult) simply goes unspoken in these three lines: *rare* is a fact about **quantity**, 難得 is a fact about **acquisition**. The causal chain still runs — rare, therefore hard to obtain honestly, therefore stolen — but it runs as an inference the reader makes, not as something the line says. 王弼's thieves 穿窬探篋，沒命而盜, tunnelling through walls at the cost of their lives, are no longer visible in the English. Their labour mirrored the trader's, and that mirror is gone.

**It is gone because English will not carry it.** There is **no one-word English adjective meaning "difficult to obtain" that is not also a value word** — because in English, difficulty of acquisition is simply *how we say* a thing is valuable. That gravitational pull is what dragged three separate renderings of one phrase toward *the precious*, *rare treasures* and *precious goods*, independently, in three different chapters. **Rare** is the last word on that slope that stops before the verdict. It is not the whole of 難得, and no available word is.

**The book uses the scarcity-makes-value inference elsewhere, and does not disown it.** Chapter 70 puts the two characters in one couplet: 知我者**希**，則我者**貴** (*zhī wǒ zhě xī, zé wǒ zhě guì* — "those who know me are few; those who pattern themselves on me are precious"). 河上公 draws the link explicitly: 希，少也…惟達道者乃能知我，故為貴也 — *"希 means few… only those who have reached the Tao can know me, and therefore it is precious."*

So **the same commentator who has the sage refuse to let rarity confer value on jade (64) lets rarity confer value on understanding (70).** That is not obviously a contradiction — one is a ruler setting a price that other people will steal to meet, the other is a plain observation about how few readers there are — but the machinery is identical, and the book never says where the line falls. Anyone reading 貨 as a straightforward critique of valuing scarce things has to account for chapter 70. *(See `希` in `glossary/TRIAGE.md`, still owed an entry; whatever English it takes must not be *rare*, which is spent here.)*

**And one word here is doing a job the book does elsewhere with a whole chapter.** 貨 is goods **in circulation** — the shell that changes hands. Chapter 80 imagines a state where 有舟輿，無所乘之 (*yǒu zhōu yú, wú suǒ chéng zhī* — "there are boats and carts, and no occasion to ride them") and neighbours grow old without visiting. That is a world with no 貨 in it, because nothing is moving. Whether the book is against **prizing** goods or against **circulating** them is not settled by this character, and the two readings pull the political chapters in different directions.

## 極 (Jí) — The Far End

*Say "jee," rising. Six lines across five chapters, and the graph beneath it is a standing body.*

**Recommended: 極 → "the far end" — the point at which a thing runs out.** *(Not "limitless," not "the Absolute," not "the Ultimate," not "infinite," not "extreme," not "utmost." The compound 無極 → "the endless.")* *Two lines remain unsettled; see the close.*

極 is the late graph. The original is **亟 (*jí*)**, and in the oracle-bone script 亟 is a standing person with one horizontal stroke above the head and one below the feet — traditionally read 極于頂 (*jí yú dǐng* — "the pole at the crown") and 極于踵 (*jí yú zhǒng* — "the pole at the heel"). A figure drawn between the two things a body can touch: what is over it, and what it stands on. Bronze forms add 口 (*kǒu* — a mouth) and 又 (*yòu* — a hand).

There is no fence in the graph. There is a person at full extension, and the two places their reach runs out.

Then 木 (*mù* — wood) was added, and the same idea became a building. 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE) on 極: **棟也。从木亟聲** — *"the ridgepole. From 木, with 亟 for sound."* The 棟 (*dòng*) is the topmost beam of a roof, the timber the rafters lean into from both slopes. Not an ornament set on top of the house: **the last structural member, the one past which there is no more house.**

A body at full stretch; a roof at its topmost beam. Both are terminal points of something extended. Both are finite, because the thing that reached them is. And neither is a boundary imposed from outside — which is what separates 極 from every English word for a limit.

### The commentators gloss it with one word, seven times

Wherever 極 appears, 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE) and 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han) reach for **窮 (*qióng* — to exhaust, to use up)**:

| Chapter | Line | The gloss |
|---|---|---|
| 28 | 復歸於無極 | 王弼: 不可窮也 — *"it cannot be exhausted"* |
| 28 | 復歸於無極 | 河上公: 歸身於無窮極也 — *"return the body to what has no exhausting 極"* |
| 58 | 孰知其極 | 河上公: 禍福更相生，誰能知其窮極時 — *"disaster and fortune give birth to each other in turn; who can know the time of their exhausting 極?"* |
| 59 | 莫知其極 | 王弼: 道無窮也 — *"the Tao is inexhaustible"* |
| 59 | 莫知其極 | 河上公: 莫有知己德之窮極也 — *"no one knows the exhausting 極 of their own integrity"* |
| 25 | on 自然 | 王弼: 窮極之辭也 — *"an expression of the exhausted 極"* |
| 36 | on 柔弱 | 王弼: 柔弱同通，不可窮極 — *"the soft and the yielding alike run through; they cannot be run out to the 極"* |

Seven instances, one word. **極 is not how far a thing extends. It is where a thing runs out** — a claim about supply, not about size.

That is also what 無極 (*wú jí*) says at chapter 28. Not a thing of unbounded extent: a thing you cannot use up. A roof with no topmost beam.

### The hardest line: 致虛極

致 (*zhì* — to send all the way there) 虛 (*xū* — empty) 極 (*jí*) invites an objection that turns out to be instructive. If emptiness has no measure, then reaching its 極 is reaching the limit of the limitless.

**The objection dissolves, because 虛 in this book is never boundless.** Every occurrence is a container with its contents gone — a heart at chapter 3, a bellows at 5, hollow words at 22, a granary at 53. 說文 makes 虛 a settlement-mound, a unit of surveyed land. *(See `xu-虛.md`.)*

**And the graph closes the question. The 極 in 致虛極 does not belong to emptiness. It belongs to the person doing the emptying** — the standing body, crown to heel, at the end of its reach. The line does not measure the hollow. It measures how far you go into it.

What is left is a better difficulty, and a real one. **The verb is a travelling and the method is a subtraction.** 致 is 夊 (*suī* — a dragging foot) beneath 至 (*zhì* — to arrive); 說文: 送詣也, *"to send all the way there."* You go on foot. But 河上公 says how you go: 得道之人捐情去欲，五內清淨，至於虛極 — *"one who has gained the Tao sheds feeling and casts off desire; the five viscera are clear and still; and so arrives at 虛極."* Chapter 48 gives the same movement in the same grammar: 損之又損，以至於無為 — *"reduce, and reduce again, until arriving at non-doing."*

**You travel by taking away.** The only way to reach the far end of a hollow is to keep removing until there is nothing left to remove.

### What is set aside

**limit** — the word English reaches for first, and the reason the rest of the list is needed. A limit is a fence: a stop set from outside, marking where you are not allowed to go. 極 is the far point of a reach, measured by the reacher. The two are opposite kinds of word, and only one of them has a person in it.

**limitless** — the wrong axis. It answers *how big*, where every commentator answers *how much is left*.

**the Absolute, the Ultimate** — 極 is the load-bearing beam of a specific roof. Both import a metaphysical absolute the graph does not hold, and *the Ultimate* additionally drags in 太極 (*tài jí* — "the supreme ridgepole"), Song-dynasty cosmology reading its own system back into a Warring States word. The failure has the same shape as 一 (*yī* — one) rendered *the One*.

**infinite** — a ridgepole is finite, a body's reach is finite, and 說文 offers no other picture.

**extreme** — belongs to 甚 (*shèn* — excessive), which carries it at chapters 29 and 44. English *extreme* also means immoderation, a verdict 極 does not pass.

**utmost** — belongs to 至 (*zhì* — to arrive at), which carries it twice in chapter 55: 精之至也 and 和之至也, *"vital essence at its utmost," "harmony at its utmost."*

### The working register

**極 flexes by grammar, and the flexions are not interchangeable.**

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 無極, the compound | 28 | the endless |
| 知其極, the far point of a process | 58, 59 | where it ends |
| 極 after a verb and its object | 16 | the terminal degree of the verb, not a noun |
| 古之極, the far point of a practice | 68 | *(unsettled — see below)* |

**The line-final position at chapter 16 is grammatical, not decorative.** 致虛極 and 守靜篤 (*shǒu jìng dǔ* — "hold to stillness, 篤") are the same three-beat shape twice: verb, object, terminal degree word. 篤 (*dǔ* — steady; 說文 馬行頓遟, *"a horse's gait, halting and slow"*) cannot be a noun head — nobody arrives at the thickness of stillness — so 極 in the matching slot is doing the same adverbial work. 王弼 confirms it from the other side by binding the two into a single compound across both lines: 言致虛，物之極篤 — *"reaching emptiness is things' 極篤"* — and again 是物之極篤也. He can only pair them if they are the same kind of word.

### The tension, left open

**Chapter 68's 古之極 is the one appearance this entry cannot place.** 是謂配天，古之極 — *"this is called being 配 (pèi — matched, as one of a pair) with 天 (tiān — sky), the 極 of the ancients."* It is not a process whose end is unknowable, and it is not adverbial. It reads as *the far point the ancients reached*, which is exactly the graph — but that line is already contested at 配天, and settling one half would settle both. *(See `tian-天.md`.)*

**And the book reaches a 極 exactly once.** Chapter 16 is the only imperative: go there. Everywhere else the word is denied — unknowable at 58 and at 59 twice, negated outright at 28. Four refusals and one instruction, and the instruction is the one addressed to a person rather than to a process. Whether that is the text distinguishing what a body can do from what a world does, or a word used loosely across a compiled book, the six lines do not say.

flexions.why: the compound 無極, where the negation turns the limit into its absence

entries.render: the far end — where a thing runs out

entries.body:
## 精 (Jīng) — Vital Essence

*Say "jing," level and light. Only three appearances, in two chapters — and one of the smallest footprints in this glossary hides one of its clearest inversions.*

**Locked: 精 → "vital essence" / "essence."** *(Not "primordial mass," not "soul," not "spirit," not "energy.")*

Chapter 21 rendered 其中有精 as *"within its dark depths lies the primordial mass of creation."* That is not a loose translation; it is the **precise opposite** of the character. 精 is what remains when the mass is taken **away**.

### The character, read slowly — hulled rice

精 is 米 (*mǐ* — rice) beside 青 (*qīng*), which supplies the sound and lends a sense of *fresh, pure*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) glosses it in a single word: **擇也** — *to select, to sift.*

The picture is **grain that has been hulled and winnowed**: the husk beaten off, the chaff blown away, the broken and the empty discarded, and what is left is the small heavy edible heart of the thing. 精 is the *result of subtraction*. Everything bulky has been removed.

That is why "primordial mass" fails so completely. **Mass is exactly what 精 is not** — mass is the husk and the chaff, the undifferentiated bulk that sifting removes. The rendering also imports Big Bang cosmology, a different overlay from the mechanistic one but the same family of anachronism, and it fails the pointing test flatly: Laozi could point at a bowl of polished rice. He could not point at a primordial mass.

Every good English sense of the word follows from the winnowing: *refined*, *concentrated*, *choice*, *precise*, *potent*. In modern Chinese 精 still carries all of them, and 精米 is still polished rice.

### The evidence — both chapters are about undiminished potency

**Chapter 55, the newborn.** 未知牝牡之合而朘作，精之至也 — *not yet knowing the union of female and male, yet quickening with life; this is 精 at its utmost.* The infant has the most 精 of anyone in the book, and has spent none of it. Nothing has been dissipated, nothing performed, nothing sought. The concentration *is* the vitality.

The same chapter then draws the line that keeps 精 from meaning merely "energy": 心使氣曰強 — *when the heart drives the 氣, that is forcing.* **氣** (*qì*) is breath-energy in motion, and it can be driven, pushed, mismanaged. 精 cannot be driven; it can only be kept or squandered. One is a current, the other a reserve. A translation that renders both as "energy" loses the whole distinction Chapter 55 is built on — and it is the distinction that makes 益生曰祥 (*to force life to increase is an ill omen*) legible.

**Chapter 21, the source.** 窈兮冥兮，其中有精；其精甚真，其中有信 — *deep and dim, and within it there is 精; its 精 is utterly real, and within it there is trust.* Here the sifting image does its cosmological work: at the bottom of the indistinct there is not a mass but a **concentrate** — the small dense real thing left when everything vague has been winnowed off. The chapter's whole descent is a sifting: through 象 (*xiàng* — image), 物 (*wù* — thing), 精, 信 (*xìn* — trust), each finer than the last.

### The lock: what is set aside, and why

**"Primordial mass"** inverts the character, as above, and dates the text to the twentieth century.

**"Soul"** is on the overlay watchlist for exactly this word. Chinese has a vocabulary for souls — 魂 (*hún*, the ethereal soul) and 魄 (*pò*, the corporeal one) — and Laozi never uses 魂 and uses 魄 once, at chapter 10, for the body's own **aliveness** (`po-魄.md`). Rendering 精 as "soul" imports a separable immortal self into a book with no such thing, and makes Chapter 55's newborn a vessel for something rather than simply a creature brimming.

**"Spirit"** carries the same freight and collides with 神 (*shén* — numinous potency), a different character that the text does use (6, 29, 39, 60).

**"Energy"** collapses 精 into 氣, as Chapter 55 forbids. It is also the vaguest word available in English for the most precise word in the family.

> **Why "energy" is not on the `forbidden` list.** It cannot be. Chapter 55 contains **both** 精 and 氣, and 氣 legitimately takes *vital energy* in 心使氣曰強 (*when the heart drives the vital energy, that is forcing*) — so forbidding the word for 精 fires a false error on a correct line. `tools/check_locks.py` gates on whether a character is present in the chapter, which cannot express *right for that character, wrong for this one, same chapter.* The rule this implies is general: **a forbidden rendering must be a word no other character in those same chapters can legitimately claim.** The same limit applies to 德 and 信 (see `glossary/xin-信.md`), and this distinction is held by the reader of the entry rather than by the tool.

**"Semen"** deserves naming, because it is a real reading and not a foolish one: in later Daoist and medical literature 精 unambiguously means seminal essence, and Chapter 55's line about the infant's arousal invites it. We decline it for two reasons. The specialized sense is **later** than this text, and taking it here would make the passage a claim about one organ in one sex, where the point is a whole small body full of unspent life. The male-default is the text's, not the argument's. *(See the Chapter 55 manuscript note on 朘 / 全, where the same question arises in the source text itself.)*

### The working register

精 barely flexes — three occurrences, two grammatical positions:

- as the thing present in something → **vital essence** (其中有精 → "within it there is vital essence")
- when already named and referred back to → **essence** (其精甚真 → "its essence is utterly real")
- at its extreme → **vital essence at its utmost** (精之至也)

**Never** "primordial mass," "soul," "spirit," "energy," "life force."

### The tension, left open

**Is it one word here, or two senses?** Chapter 55's 精 is unmistakably **bodily** — an infant's undissipated vitality, sitting in a line about genitals and grip strength. Chapter 21's 精 is **cosmological** — what is found at the bottom of the indistinct, before anything has a name. English "vital essence" covers both, which is convenient and may be a cheat.

The winnowing image is what argues they are one word: in both places 精 is *the concentrate left after everything loose is removed*, whether the sifting is done to grain, to a body, or to the visible world. But it is worth admitting that Laozi may simply be using a household word for *the good part* in two unrelated ways, and that our unified reading is tidier than his usage.

We leave it single, and note the seam here rather than smoothing it in the verse.

## 可 (Kě) — Can Be

*Say "kuh," dipping and then rising. Thirty-six appearances across twenty chapters, two of them in the book's first six characters.*

**Locked: 可 → "can be"** (before a verb, the subject is what the verb is done to) **/ "can"** (as 可以, the subject does the verb) **/ "cannot"** (不可, for what the situation does not allow). *(Not "must not" or "should not" for a plain 不可; see* Cannot, not must not *below. No check can hold that ruling; see* What no rule can enforce.*)*

可 says what a situation allows. It is not a person's strength or skill; that is 能 (*néng*), its partner, treated below. 可 is the gap in the world through which a thing can happen, and 不可 is a world with no such gap. The book uses it most often in the negative, and almost always about the Tao or about the world, saying what cannot be done to them.

### The graph: a mouth, and a breath getting out

**Our vendored 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*): 𦘫也。从口丂，丂亦聲** — *"to consent. From 口 (kǒu — mouth) and 丂 (kǎo), and 丂 also gives the sound."*

- **口 (*kǒu*)** is a mouth. 說文: 人所以言食也, *"what a person speaks and eats with."*
- **丂 (*kǎo*)** is drawn as a breath pushing up against a line. 說文 describes it as breath that wants to come out and is held back from above. In 可 it does two jobs: it is the sound, and it is the breath leaving the mouth.

**The oldest sense is permission, not possibility.** 𦘫 is the old form of 肯 (*kěn* — to be willing, to agree). So for Xu Shen 可 is the mouth saying *yes*: *all right, it may be done.* Some modern scholars propose an even older sense, *to sing*, since 可 written twice is 哥, and 歌 (*gē* — song) is built on it. That is a tentative proposal. What is certain is that the word began as someone **allowing** something, and *possible* is that permission read off the world instead of a person. 可 is in the Shang oracle bones, already in this shape.

That sense never left. 朝聞道，夕死**可**矣 (論語 4.8) is *"hear the way in the morning, and in the evening you **may** die."* And modern Chinese still answers *yes, fine* with 可以.

### Two constructions, two voices

This is the grammar the English must keep, and the first line depends on it.

**可 + verb: the subject receives the action.** 道可道 is *"the Tao that **can be** made into a way."* 名可名 is *"the name that **can be** named."* The Tao is not doing the *dào*-ing. It is what would be *dào*-ed. The same construction gives 可欲 (3), *"what can be desired,"* which English has as one word: **the desirable.**

**可以 + verb: the subject acts.** 可以 is 可 with 以 (*yǐ* — by means of), *"has the means to."* 可以長久 (44, 59) — *"you **can** last long."* 可以有國 (59) — *"you **can** have the state."* 美言**可以**市尊 (62) — *"fine words **can** buy honor."*

**With an intransitive verb, 可 is simply *can*.** 大道汎兮，其可左右 (34) — *"the great Tao overflows. It can go left or right."* 左右 (*zuǒ yòu*) is used as a verb with nothing to act on, so there is no one to receive the action and the subject just *can*.

**One 可以 in our base is a copying error.** 知止可以不殆 (32) stands alone against every other witness, which read 所以 (*suǒ yǐ* — that by which): knowing when to stop *is how* you come to no danger. We follow 所以 (`notes/manuscript.md`, Ch 32), so the line carries no *can*.

The line can be checked by swapping the forms: 道可以道 would mean *the Tao can make a way*. The book does not say that.

| Construction | Voice | English | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 可 + verb | the subject receives | **can be** | 道可道 (1), 可名為大 (34) → *"it can be called great"* |
| 不可 + verb | the subject receives | **cannot be** | 不可名 (14) → *"it cannot be named"*; 不可為也 (29) → *"it cannot be handled"* |
| 可以 + verb | the subject acts | **can** | 可以長久 (44) → *"you can last long"* |
| 可欲 | a fixed noun | **the desirable** | 不見可欲 (3) → *"by not displaying the desirable"* |
| 不可不 + verb | cannot-not | **must** | 不可不畏 (20) → *"what people fear must be feared"* |

### Cannot, not must not

不可 has two readings, and English has to choose between them every time:

- **cannot**: the situation does not allow it, so trying fails.
- **must not**: you are forbidden to.

The book means the first. The pattern is clearest at chapter 29, the line that matters most:

> 天下神器，不可為也，不可執也。為者敗之，執者失之。
> *"The world is a sacred vessel. It cannot be handled. It cannot be grasped. Those who handle it ruin it. Those who grasp it lose it."*

The next sentence gives the reason, and the reason is a result, not a rule: handle it and it breaks. **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*)** reads it exactly that way: 萬物以自然為性，故可因而不可為也，可通而不可執也。物有常性而造為之，故必敗也 — *"the countless things take being so of themselves as their nature. So they can be followed and cannot be handled, can be passed through and cannot be grasped. Things have their own nature, and to manufacture them is to ruin them, surely."* 必 (*bì* — surely, without fail) is a prediction. **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*)** agrees: 以有為治之則敗其質性, *"govern it by handling, and you ruin its nature."* *Must not* would turn a description of how the world works into a commandment. That is a verdict the line does not carry (`process/principles/no-verdict-the-chinese-lacks.md`).

The other lines run the same way. 不可致詰 (14), *it cannot be questioned through to the end*. 善閉無關楗而不可開 (27), *masterful security uses no locks, yet cannot be breached*. 不可得而親 (56), *you cannot draw them near*. 王弼's gloss on 56 is a logic, not a law: 可得而親，則可得而疏也, *"if they could be drawn near, they could be held off."*

**不可不 is the one place *must* belongs.** 人之所畏，不可不畏 (20) is *cannot not fear*, and English says that as **must**: *"What people fear must be feared."* This *must* is still necessity rather than a command. 王弼 reads it in the first person: 人之所畏，吾亦畏焉, *"what people fear, I fear too."*

### 能, the partner: a bear

**能 (*néng*)** is the other English *can*: ability, what an agent is able to do. It appears thirty-three times across seventeen chapters, often as 孰能 (*who can…?*) and 莫能 (*no one can*).

Our 說文: 熊屬。足似鹿。从肉㠯聲。能獸堅中，故稱賢能；而彊壯，稱能傑也 — *"a kind of bear, with feet like a deer's. From 肉 (ròu — flesh), with 㠯 (yǐ) for sound. The 能 beast is solid at its core, and so the able are called 賢能; and it is strong, and so the outstanding are called 能傑."* The graph is a **bear**: two paws, and a head with an open mouth. The word for the animal later took 火 (fire, here four dots for the feet) and became 熊 (*xióng*). Xu Shen's account of how a bear came to mean *able* is a commentator's story, but the picture is right for the word: 能 is strength in a body.

**The voice keeps them apart in English.** 可 is *can be*, the situation's allowance. 能 is *can* or *is able to*, someone's power. 莫之能守 (9) — *"no one can guard them"* — is a failure of ability. 不可長保 in the same chapter — *"it will not keep for long"* — is the world not allowing it. Where both stand together, the book is saying something about each. At 70: 吾言甚易知，甚易行…天下莫能知，莫能行 — *"my words are very easy to know, very easy to follow. In all the world, no one can know them. No one can follow them."* The words *can be* known. People *cannot* know them. The fault is in the agents, not the words.

### What we set aside

- ***must not / should not*** for a plain 不可 — puts a commandment where the book describes a consequence (above). Chapter 36 is the case where it came closest to fitting, and *cannot* holds there too (below).
- ***may*** — the oldest sense, and fine in 論語, but in modern English *may* means *perhaps* as often as *is permitted*. *"The Tao that may be made into a way"* would read as a guess.
- ***is possible to / is able to be*** — accurate and wooden. 可 is a small word and wants a small English word.
- ***-able*** suffixes (*nameable*, *graspable*) — compact, but they turn a statement about the world into a property of the thing. *"It is ungraspable"* says what the Tao is like. *"It cannot be grasped"* says what happens when you try. The book means the second. *The desirable* (3) is the one exception, because 可欲 is a fixed noun and English has the noun.

### Chapter 36, the hardest line

> 魚不可脫於淵，國之利器不可以示人。
> *"A fish cannot leave deep water. / A state's tools of advantage cannot be shown."*

**The two clauses are one parallel, and the English keeps it.** Both read *cannot* (Shalom's call, 2026-10-14).

**Why *cannot* for both:**

- **王弼 reads both halves as one consequence:** 魚脫於淵則必見失矣。利國器而立刑以示人，亦必失也 — *"a fish that leaves the deep is surely lost. To set up punishments as the state's tools and show them to people, that too is surely lost."* 亦 (*yì* — also) ties the two clauses together, and 必 makes both predictions.
- **The fish line is plainly not advice.** A fish is not forbidden to leave the water. It dies. The second line borrows the first's logic.
- **The chapter keeps its *musts* for the four 必固 lines** (*"you must first stretch it out…"*), where 必 (*bì*) prints them.

**What it costs:** 河上公 hears advice: 治國權者不可以示執事之臣也, *"the authority that governs the state must not be shown to the ministers who run affairs."* 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*) reads the whole chapter as counsel to a ruler: rewards and punishments, the state's 利器, 在君則制臣，在臣則勝君, *"held by the lord they control the ministers; held by the ministers they overcome the lord."* And 可以 rather than 可 marks the second clause slightly differently from the first. On their reading the line is a warning to rulers, and *must never* would be honest to it. That reading is set aside, not refuted.

### What no rule can enforce

***Must not* and *should not* are ruled out for a plain 不可, and they cannot go on `forbidden:`.** *Must* is 不可不's English at 20, and chapter 36 prints *must* four times for 必 (*bì*), in the same chapter as two 不可. The checker keys on chapter presence, so forbidding *must* would flag correct lines. The reader holds this one: **不可 is *cannot*; *must* belongs to 必 and to 不可不.**

### Left open

**Chapter 35's *never* is softer than the Chinese.** 用之不可既 is *"use it, and it cannot be used up."* *"It never runs out"* reports a record, where 不可 says the world doesn't allow it. The *never* is declared as a flexion because the line sounds right, but it is a small loss.

**English *can* serves both characters.** The voice usually keeps them apart (*can be* against *can*), but where 可以 makes the subject act, 可以 and 能 land on the same English. 可以有國 (59), *"you can have the state,"* and 能守之 (32), *"able to hold to this,"* are different claims, an opening and a capacity. English barely shows it.

flexions.why: 可欲 is a fixed phrase, what can be desired, and English has the word
不可不 is cannot-not, which English says as must
不可既, cannot be used up, said as it never runs out

entries.render: can be (可 + verb) / can (可以 + verb) / cannot (不可)
