entries.body:
## 亂 (Luàn) — Disorder

*Say "lwahn," falling. Four lines across four chapters, and the dictionary defines it as its own opposite.*

**Locked: 亂 → "disorder."** *(Never "chaos," never "chaotic.")*

### The graph: a tangle with hands in it

> 亂，**治**也。从乙，**乙，治之也**；从𤔔。
> *"亂 is to bring to order. From 乙 (yǐ), and **乙 is what orders it**; and from 𤔔 (luàn)."* — 說文解字

Read that twice, because it says the opposite of what the character is used to mean. **說文's headword gloss for 亂 is 治 — to govern, to put in order** — and it then singles out one component and names it *the thing that does the ordering*. The tool is inside the graph.

𤔔 is the rest of it: a hank of **silk** with a hand above and a hand below. 說文 draws both hands in our own corpus — 爪, **覆手曰爪**, *"a covering hand,"* reaching down; 又, **手也**, a hand, reaching up. The bronze forms show the threads on a frame, one hand holding, one working a shuttle through.

**And the hands are untangling, not tangling.** This is the fact that reorders the whole entry, and the dictionary states it twice. Besides 亂，治也, 說文 defines the 𤔔 element outright — in the entry for a character **this book uses**:

> 辭，訟也。从𤔔，**𤔔猶理辜也。𤔔，理也。**
> *"辭 (cí) is pleading a case. From 𤔔, because 𤔔 is like **putting right** (理) a wrong. **𤔔 means 理 — to put in order.**"*

辭 stands at chapter 34 — 萬物恃之以生而不**辭**, *"the countless things rely on it to live, yet it refuses none."* So the Laozi already contains one 𤔔-character, and the dictionary explains it as sorting out a dispute.

*A divergence, recorded rather than settled: a minority reading takes the bronze graph as silk on a loom that* cannot *be sorted — the hands present but defeated. Either way the hands are at work on the tangle, not making it.*

**So 亂 does not name a mess. It names a mess somebody has their hands in.** That is why chapter 64 can say 治之於未亂 at all: the tangle is addressable, and the counsel is to get to it early.

### Where it stands, and what it is set against

| ch | line | set against |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 不見可欲，使民心不**亂** | 聖人之**治** three lines later, and 無不**治** at the close |
| 18 | 國家昏**亂**，有忠臣 | 昏 (*hūn* — clouded) beside it; loyal ministers as the symptom |
| 38 | 忠信之薄，而**亂**之首 | 忠信 (*zhōng xìn* — loyalty and trust), worn thin |
| 64 | 為之於未有，**治**之於未**亂** | **治 itself, in the same clause** |

**Chapter 3 shows what it does to a person.** 亂 there is something done **to** the heart from outside, not a state it generates: 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) glosses the line 心無所亂也, *"the heart has nothing to be disordered by"* — remove the display and the disordering has no purchase. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) pairs it with 惑 (*huò* — led astray): 不惑亂也. Both read it as agitation rather than as misunderstanding, which is why *confused* is wrong for it: that word puts the damage in the knowing, and this chapter has just spent two lines separating knowing from the heart. *(This was established during the ch 3 rebuild of 2026-08-31 and is recorded in `notes/translation.md` → Ch 3.)*

**Chapter 64 prints the pair the dictionary describes** — *"Order it before it falls into disorder."* Two of the four chapters set 亂 directly against 治, and the English keeps them visibly related, which *chaos* could not do.

**王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads 64 as a matter of scale, not of kind**: 治之於未亂 gets the gloss 謂㣲脆也, *"this refers to what is faint and brittle."* The disorder is not a different condition arriving from outside. It is the same thing, further along — a thread or two before it is a knot.

### The 反訓, and why the verse does not show it

A character that faces both ways is called a 反訓 (*fǎnxùn*), and 亂 is the standard example: the tangle and the untangling in one graph. It is the most interesting thing about the word. **It is also not what this book does with it.**

All four of Laozi's lines sit on the disorder side — a heart stirred by what it was shown (3), a state come apart (18), where the rot starts (38), the thing to catch early (64). **The 治 sense is the dictionary's, not the text's**, and an English that reached for it would be rendering a fact about the character over a fact about the sentence. The graph belongs in this entry; the verse says what the verse says. Same arrangement as 萬 (*wàn*), which is a scorpion here and *the countless things* on the page.

### What is set aside

**"chaos"** was the rendering at chapter 18, and it is the one to refuse.

It is a **cosmological** word in English — Hesiod's Χάος, the void before creation, *chaos and old night* — and it points at the wrong end of this book's cosmology. Where Laozi does describe an undifferentiated beginning he uses 混成 (*hùn chéng*, ch 25), rendered *"something formed in the undifferentiated."* 亂 is not that. It is **political and domestic**: a state coming apart, a household out of harmony, a heart stirred up.

And it is the wrong shape for the graph. **Chaos is a condition with nobody in it.** 亂 has two hands in it. You cannot catch chaos early; you can catch a tangle early, which is the whole of chapter 64.

**"unravelled"** is the near miss, and it is worth the paragraph.

It **performs the graph** — silk coming undone — and in English it faces both ways exactly as 亂 does, since one unravels a mystery and a plan unravels. It would carry the 反訓 natively, with no help from this entry. *"Order it before it unravels"* (64) and *"the people's hearts do not unravel"* (3) are both better lines than the locked ones.

It fails at **chapter 38**, and the failure is structural rather than a matter of taste. 亂之**首** is *the head of* 亂, and *"the head of the unravelling"* is not English. The obvious repair — *"where the unravelling begins"* — spends 首 (*shǒu*) on *begins*, and **首 and 始 (*shǐ*) were separated in that exact couplet during Pass D**, 而亂之首 against 而愚之始, because they had been sharing one English. Restoring that collision to gain a better line elsewhere is a bad trade. One chapter should not decide four, but a rendering that breaks in one of four is not a lock.

**"untangled"** is the opposite error, and naming it is the point. *Untangle* is the **治 half** of the 反訓 — the hands succeeding — and that is the half this book never uses. Put it in any of the four lines and the meaning inverts: chapter 18 would have nations becoming *untangled* as loyal ministers appear, which reverses the chapter's whole argument. It is the rendering the **graph** supports and the **text** forbids, which is a useful thing for a reader to see stated rather than left as a puzzle.

**"turmoil"** is better than *chaos* and still wrong: a word about agitation and feeling, so it carries the heart at ch 3 and drops the constitutional sense at 18 and 38. It has no relation to *order*.

### The working register

- as the state a thing falls into → **disorder** (亂之首 → "the head of disorder")
- as what a thing is kept out of → **thrown into disorder** (使民心不亂 → "the people's hearts are not thrown into disorder")
- beside 治 → keep the two English words visibly related (治之於未亂 → "order it before it falls into disorder")

**Never** "chaos," "chaotic," "untangled."

### Settled alongside

**治 (*zhì*) was locked on 2026-09-23** — *govern*, with a declared flexion to *order* at chapters 8 and 64 — so the pairing this entry rests on is now held at both ends. `zhi-治.md`. 說文 files 治 as **a river**, which is the other half of this entry's picture: 亂 is the tangle, 治 is what you do to a watercourse, and 王弼 says what that consists of at ch 60 — **不擾也**, *"it is not to disturb."*

**正 (*zhèng* — upright) stays out of it.** *Order* is also worn by 正 at chapter 45 — 清靜為天下正, *"clear stillness brings order to the world"* — and 正 is one of the calls Shalom has deferred (`WORKLIST.md` T4-2, 正/奇). It is named here so that a reader who notices the third claimant knows it was seen and left alone.

## 民 (Mín) — The People

*Say "meen," rising. Thirty-two appearances across thirteen chapters, nearly all of them in the book's political half.*

**Locked: 民 → "the people,"** always with the article, **and "the people" belongs to 民 alone.** *(Not "the masses," "the multitude," "the populace," "subjects," "citizens," "commoners," "peasants," or "the governed." That 人 (*rén* — a person) must not wear "the people" is a ruling no check can hold; see* What no rule can enforce *below. 百姓 (*bǎi xìng*), the other word for the population, is locked to "everyone": `baixing-百姓.md`.)*

民 is the people **as seen from the seat of government**: the population a ruler governs, taxes, frightens, loves, or leaves alone. The word is never neutral about who is looking. In every line but one, someone stands across from 民: a sage, a ruler, a state, those over them. Laozi's whole political teaching is addressed to that someone, and 民 is the name for the ones on the other side of the address.

### The graph: sprouts, or a blinded eye, and nobody knows

**Our vendored 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE): 眾萌也。从古文之象** — *"the many sprouts. From the shape of its ancient form."*

萌 (*méng*) is a shoot breaking the soil. Xu Shen defines the people as **a field coming up**: numerous, low, alive, and not yet anything in particular. 段玉裁 (*Duàn Yùcái*, 1815) defends the reading against editions that print 氓 (*méng* — the common folk) in its place. 萌 is the original, he says, and the ancients called the people 萌, with many examples in Han writing. 林義光 (*Lín Yìguāng*, 1920) arrived at the same picture from the bronze graphs, which he read as a plant pushing up out of the ground.

**The other reading is the one that circulates, and it is a theory.** 郭沫若 (*Guō Mòruò*, 1930s) read the bronze graph as **an eye pierced by a blade**: captives blinded in one eye and set to work, so that 民 began as a word for slaves. 白川靜 (*Shirakawa Shizuka*) and 藤堂明保 (*Tōdō Akiyasu*) took it up. Its critics, 永澤要二 (*Nagasawa Yōji*) and 加納喜光 (*Kanō Yoshimitsu*), point out that nothing supports it beyond the shape. The oracle-bone graphs once claimed for 民 are themselves disputed, and the form securely identified as 民 begins with the bronzes. Guo was building a Marxist history of ancient China, and a blinded slave fit the slave society that history required. The reading may be right. But it is one scholar's argument, made inside a framework, and it should not be quoted as the meaning of the graph.

**What the two readings share is position.** A sprouting field and a captive labourer are both **low, numerous, and acted upon**. Whichever picture is true, the graph does not draw a person standing upright, as 人 does. It draws a mass seen from above.

### The evidence: 民 always has someone across from it

The pattern is the argument, and it is complete enough to read as a table.

| Ch | Line | Who stands across |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 使民不爭 · 使民不為盜 · 使民心不亂 · 常使民無知無欲 | the sage who governs (聖人之治) |
| 10 | 愛民治國 | the one asked *can you* |
| 19 | 民利百倍 · 民復孝慈 | the ruler told to cut off and abandon |
| 32 | 民莫之令而自均 | the rulers who could hold to the Tao (侯王) |
| 57 | 民彌貧 · 民自化 · 民自正 · 民自富 · 民自樸 | 我 (*wǒ* — I), the sage speaking |
| 58 | 其民淳淳 · 其民缺缺 | 其政 (*qí zhèng* — its government) |
| 65 | 非以明民 · 民之難治 | the ancients who were masterful at the Tao |
| 66 | 欲上民 · 欲先民 · 民不重 · 民不害 | the one who would rise above them |
| 72 | 民不畏威 | the authority they stop fearing |
| 74 | 民不畏死 · 若使民常畏死 | the one who would kill to frighten them |
| 75 | 民之飢 · 民之難治 · 民之輕死 | 其上 (*qí shàng* — those over them), three times |
| 80 | 小國寡民 · 使民重死 · 使民復結繩 · 民至老死 | the small state that *lets* them |

**Chapter 57 shows the relation working.** The sage speaks four times in the first person, and each time 民 answers in the reflexive: *I do not do, and the people transform themselves.* 民 is defined by being on the receiving end of rule. The teaching is that the best rule gives them nothing to receive.

**Chapter 75 names the direction outright.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) comments on the whole chapter in one sentence: 言民之所以僻，治之所以亂，皆由上，不由其下也，民從上也 — *"this says that the reason the people go astray, and the reason order falls into disorder, all comes from above and not from below. The people follow those above."* Hunger, unruliness, and the cheapness of life are all traced upward. 民 is the word for the people as the ones it happens to.

### The witnesses draw the line too

The copying tradition let 民 and 人 change places three times, and each change falls where the distinction is being drawn.

| Ch | Our base | The older reading | A ruler in the line? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 57 | 人多利器 | **民**多利器: Guodian, and the lemmas of both 王弼 and 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) | yes: *the state grows benighted* |
| 60 | 聖人亦不傷人 | 聖人亦不傷**民**: 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*) | yes: the chapter is governing a large state |
| 64 | 民之從事 | **人**之敗也: Guodian, bundle C | no: anyone's affairs |

**In every case the oldest reading puts 民 where a ruler is present and 人 where none is.** Three cases is a pattern worth noticing and too few to rest on alone, but it agrees with the thirty-two lines above. And chapter 57 at Guodian sets the two side by side, a line apart: **民**多利器，而邦滋昏；**人**多智，而奇物滋起. The people's weapons trouble the state; *someone's* cleverness breeds strange contrivances. 河上公 makes that second 人 the rulers themselves, 人謂人君百里諸侯也 (*"人 here means the rulers, the lords of a hundred li"*), while 王弼 glosses it as the people's cleverness. They disagree about who 人 is. Neither treats it as 民.

### What is set aside, and why

**"The masses."** Nineteenth-century class politics, and it is the word the blinded-slave etymology was built to support. It makes 民 a bloc, a demographic, an object of history. Chapter 80's villagers who *find their food sweet, their clothes fine* are not the masses. `zhong-眾.md` rejects the word for the same reason.

**"The multitude."** King James English. It fails the hymn test outright, and it belongs, if anywhere, to 眾 (*zhòng* — the crowd), which is a plurality and not a relation.

**"The governed."** The most accurate label, and the most tempting. It says exactly what the table above shows. That is the problem: it states as a definition what the lines *show* by putting a ruler across from 民 every time. *"I do not do, and the governed transform themselves"* turns a line about people into a line about administration, and *"the governed go hungry"* takes the hunger away. The Chinese performs the relation. It does not name it. `process/principles/perform-dont-label.md`.

**"Subjects," "citizens."** Each brings a constitution with it. *Subjects* have a sovereign, *citizens* have rights, and 民 has neither in this sense. Both carry a theory of the state the book does not share.

**"The populace," "the population."** Census words. They count where 民 is a relation.

**"Commoners," "peasants."** They name a rank and an occupation. Some 民 were peasants. The word does not say so, and chapter 80's people keep records, own boats, and wear fine clothes.

### The working register

- the default, with the article → **the people** (愛民 → "loving the people"; 民之難治 → "the people are hard to govern")
- possessive → **the people's** (使民心不亂 → "the people's hearts are not thrown into disorder")
- under a number word, the article drops by English grammar → **people** (小國寡民 → "a small state, few people")
- **ch 64 alone → people**, bare: 民之從事 → *"people always ruin their affairs."* It is the one 民 in the book with no ruler in sight, and Guodian reads 人 there. The flexion records the line as it reads and why.

### Its neighbours

| | Graph | What it names | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| **民** | sprouts, or a disputed eye | the people across from a ruler | *the people* |
| **人** (*rén*) | a person standing, in profile | a human being, anyone | *people · a person · others* |
| **眾** (*zhòng*) | figures under the sun or an eye | the many, the crowd | *the crowd · the many* (locked) |
| **百姓** (*bǎi xìng*) | 百 a hundred, 姓 a clan name, from 女 (*nǚ* — woman) and 生 (*shēng* — birth) | the whole population, named from among themselves | *everyone* (locked, `baixing-百姓.md`) |

### What no rule can enforce

**人 must not render as "the people," and the checker cannot say so.** A `forbidden:` entry works by chapter presence, and chapter 57 holds both characters: 民 five times, legitimately *the people*, and 人 twice. Any ban on *the people* would flag 民's own lines. The ruling is for the reader: **in a chapter with 民, *the people* is 民's, and 人 takes *people*, *a person*, or *others*.** Chapter 57's *"the more sharp weapons the people have"* is not a breach: it renders the 民 that every witness but our base prints, a fork recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`.

**百姓 is held by its own entry.** It is locked to *everyone*, and it forbids *the people*, which the checker can enforce because none of its chapters (5, 17, 49) holds 民.

### Left open

**Chapter 60 fits the pattern, and we keep our base against it.** 韓非 reads 聖人亦不傷**民**, which is exactly where the pattern above would put 民. But both transmitted commentators read 人 in both clauses, and 王弼 builds the next line on the symmetry: 神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人…故曰兩不相傷也, *"the numinous does not harm people, the sage also does not harm people… therefore it says the two do not harm each other."* The couplet needs the same object twice. 韓非 is explaining the line in his own terms, and an explanation can sharpen a distinction the text left flat.

**"The people" has its own echoes.** *We the People*, *a people's republic*, *let my people go*. English hears popular sovereignty, revolution, or a covenant in the phrase, and 民 carries none of them. It is the plainest English the word has, and it fails the hymn test less badly than anything else. But it is warmer and prouder than 民 is, and the reader who hears *the people* as the sovereign hears the opposite of chapter 75, where the people are the ones a sovereign eats.

flexions.why: the one 民 with no ruler in the line, and the oldest witness reads 人 there

entries.body:
## 命 (Mìng) — What You Were Sent With

*Say "ming," falling. Three lines in two chapters, and one of them is the hinge of Chapter 16's chain toward clear-seeing.*

**Recommended, not yet locked: 命 → the allotted course — what is spoken over a thing and sent with it.** *(Never "mandate," never "destiny," never "fate," never "decree." Chapter 16's line and Chapter 51's verb are both still open; see the close.)*

說文解字 (c. 100 CE): **使也。从口从令** — *"命 is 使 (shǐ — to send; also, an envoy). From 口 (kǒu — a mouth) and 令 (lìng)."*

Each part, one level down:

- **口 (*kǒu*)** — 說文: **人所以言食也。象形** — *"what a person speaks and eats with. A pictograph."* A mouth.
- **令 (*lìng*)** — 說文: **發號也。从亼、卪** — *"to issue a call. From 亼 (jí) and 卪 (jié)."*
- **亼 (*jí*)** — the assembling sign, three strokes converging. Read either as an inverted 口, or as a **hand-bell rung to call people in**.
- **卪 (*jié*, also written 卩)** — **a kneeling figure.** *(說文 itself reads it as 瑞信也, "an auspicious tally"; the kneeling-person reading is modern palaeography. Neither component is among the Laozi's 711 characters, so the repository's 說文 does not carry them.)*

**And 命 and 令 were one graph.** In the oracle-bone script they are the same character — the gathering-sign above, the kneeling figure below. A chief sounds a bell to call people in; whoever receives the order kneels to take it. **口 was added during the Western Zhou bronze period**, and by the small seal script the two had separated.

**So the graph stacks up into a scene**: a summons, a gathering, someone on their knees, and a mouth. 命 is 令 with the utterance made explicit — and the dictionary defines the whole with 使, the word for *sending* and for *the person sent*.

**命 is what is spoken over you, and then you go.** Not a plan, not a fate written in advance: an instruction handed to someone at the moment they are dispatched. Everything below follows from that being a **speech act with a destination**, rather than a decree of the universe.

### 天命 is not in this book

天命 (*tiān mìng* — the Mandate of Heaven) is the compound this character is famous for: the Zhou dynasty's founding political theology, in which a ruler holds power by warrant from 天 (*tiān* — sky) and forfeits it by misrule. It is the single most consequential thing 命 does in classical Chinese.

**It has zero occurrences in the Tao Te Ching.**

So *mandate* imports a warrant-to-rule the book never invokes, and *destiny* and *fate* import a Greek and a Christian freight on top of it. All three make 命 a plot written in advance. The character describes a thing said out loud to someone who then leaves the room.

### 令 is in the book, and the two collapse in English

令 runs eight lines across four chapters, and the book puts the two characters in the **same frame** one chapter apart:

> ch 32 — 民莫之**令**而自均 — *"the people, with no one 令-ing them, even out of themselves"*
> ch 51 — 夫莫之**命**而常自然 — *"with no one 命-ing it, it is always so of itself"*

Identical construction 莫之X而, different character — **and the two were one graph before the Western Zhou split them**, which is why they are so easy to collapse and so worth keeping apart. The graphs separate them cleanly: **令 is the order as issued** — impersonal, and the book uses it that way (ch 12's 五色令人目盲, *"the five colours make people's eyes blind"*; ch 57's 法令, *"laws and decrees"*). **命 is the order as given to someone who is then sent.** One is the decree; the other is the commission.

### The commentators agree, in a word the text does not have

**王弼 (*Wáng Bì*, d. 249 CE):** 歸根則靜，故曰靜。靜則復命，故曰復命也。復命則得**性命**之常，故曰常也 — *"returning to the root is stillness, hence 'stillness.' Stillness is 復命, hence '復命.' 復命 is attaining the constancy of 性命 (xìng mìng — inborn nature and allotted span), hence 'the ever-present.'"*

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*, Han):** 言安靜者是為復還**性命**使不死也 — *"the still one is returning to their 性命, so as not to die."*

Both reach for **性命**. And **性 (*xìng* — inborn nature) has zero occurrences in the Tao Te Ching.** It is the vocabulary of a later settlement — 性 becomes a central term after this text, and both commentators are reading it back.

Their reading may still be right. But it is not the book's own word, and an English that says *nature* at Chapter 16 would be translating the commentary rather than the line. *(`CLAUDE.md`: a commentator's gloss is not the text.)*

### 復命 has its own entry

The compound at Chapter 16 — 是謂復命，復命曰常 — is treated in **`fuming-復命.md`**, including the two readings the book supports (the commentators' *return to what one was allotted*, and the idiom's *an envoy reporting back*), and the three candidate renderings with their costs.

### What is set aside

**mandate** — 天命's word, and 天命 is absent from this book. It imports the Zhou warrant-to-rule, and with it a 天 that grants and withdraws, which is precisely the overlay this edition strips from 天 (see `tian-天.md`).

**destiny, fate** — both make 命 a script settled before the actor arrives. 命 is spoken *to* someone, at a moment, and it can be reported back on. *Fate* additionally carries the Greek Moirai and the Christian providence in a text that has neither.

**decree, law** — 令's territory, and the book uses 法令 (*fǎ lìng*) for exactly that at ch 57.

**command** — 令 already carries it at ch 32, in the identical 莫之X而 frame. If 命 takes it too at ch 51, the pair the book distinguishes collapses into one English word. *(This is the open question below, not a settled prohibition — ch 51 currently reads* commands*.)*

**"the system's command"** — the Source table's literal gloss, and mechanistic in the way `CLAUDE.md` names as this edition's besetting temptation.

### The working register

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 命 as a negated verb | 51 (莫之命) | *(unsettled — must not be* command*, which is 令's at ch 32)* |
| 復命, the compound | 16 ×2 | *(unsettled — see below)* |

### The tension, left open

**Chapter 16's line is settled.** 是謂復命，復命曰常 → *"returning to what is given"* — present tense, giver present but unnamed. The four candidates it beat, and why, are in `fuming-復命.md`.

**Chapter 51's verb**, 夫莫之命而常自然, reads *"no one commands it"* — 令's English, in 令's own construction.

**And Chapter 51 has a variant.** Our vendored 王弼 carries 命並作爵 — *"命 is written 爵 (jué — to confer a noble rank) [in other editions]"* — under a collation note flagging the line as probably an editorial gloss mistaken for Wang Bi's own comment: 〔案此句疑係命字下原校注語誤作弼注〕. If 爵, the line reads *"no one ennobles it."* That is the conferral sense of 命 showing through in a second character, and it argues that whatever is happening at ch 51 is a **granting**, not an ordering.

**令 is owed an entry of its own.** Eight lines, four chapters, and at least three Englishes — *makes* (12), *command* (32), *laws* (57).
