entries.body:
## 明 (Míng) — Clear-Seeing

*Say "ming," rising like a question. Thirteen appearances across twelve chapters. Conventionally "enlightenment" — a word that points the reader in exactly the wrong direction.*

**Locked: 明 → "clear-seeing" / "clarity" / "sees clearly."** *(Not "enlightenment," not "illumination," not "brilliance.")*

Render 明 as *enlightenment* and you hand the reader a whole cosmology they did not ask for: transcendence, ascent, a higher state attained, light breaking in from somewhere else. Every one of those is foreign to what Laozi does with this word. 明 is not a state you rise into. It is what is left when you stop obstructing your own sight.

The early draft of this glossary put it better than most translations manage: **"You don't ascend; you just stop being blind."** That instinct was right, and the evidence supports it overwhelmingly.

### The character, read slowly — moonlight through a window

In its modern form 明 is 日 (*rì* — sun) beside 月 (*yuè* — moon): the two lights of the world, together. A satisfying image, and not wrong.

But it is not the oldest one. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) heads this entry not with 明 but with the older form **朙** — and that form is 月 (moon) beside **囧** (*jiǒng*), a **window**: a lattice or opening in a wall. The picture is **moonlight coming through a window into a dark room.**

Hold that against "enlightenment" and the difference is the whole entry. This is not the sun blazing at noon. It is not revelation, or radiance, or a light that transfigures. It is the **modest, sufficient light by which you can finally make out what is actually in the room with you.** Nothing has been added; nothing is transformed. You can simply see.

### The proof — Chapter 52 uses two different words

The decisive evidence sits in a single line:

> 用其光，復歸其明
> *Use its light; return to its clarity.*

**光** (*guāng*) is outward light — radiance, glare, the light a thing **emits**. It is what the sage is told to soften in Chapters 4 and 56 (和其光 — *dim your light*) and to hold without dazzling in Chapter 58 (光而不耀 — *bright but not dazzling*). **明** is what you **return** to.

If 明 meant "illumination," this line reads *"use its light, return to its light"* — a tautology. The chapter is drawing a distinction and the translation must keep it: 光 is **emission**, 明 is **reception**. One is the light you shine; the other is the seeing you come home to. "Illumination" names the wrong half.

### What 明 actually attaches to

Follow it through the text and it is perceptual every time — and strikingly modest in what it perceives.

**It sees small things.** 見小曰明 (52) — *seeing the small is called clarity.* Not the infinite, not the divine. The small. Enlightenment does not help you notice what is minute and near; clear sight does.

**It sees the self.** 知人者智，自知者明 (33) — *knowing others is cleverness; knowing yourself is clear-seeing.* The pairing is exact: 智 (*zhì*) is the outward-facing smartness that sizes up other people; 明 is turned around, and Laozi ranks it higher.

**It is blocked by self-display.** Here Laozi puns, because 見 means both *to see* and *to show oneself*:

> 不自見，故明 (22) — *they do not display themselves, therefore they see clearly.*
> 自見者不明 (24) — *one who displays themselves does not see clearly.*

The one who is busy being seen cannot see. Clarity is not something acquired; it is what returns when the performing self gets out of the light.

**It sees what does not change.** 知常曰明 — *knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing* — appears verbatim in **16** and **55**. This is a repeated formula and must read identically in both places.

**And it is quiet, not brilliant.** 是謂微明 (36) — *this is called subtle clarity.* 明道若昧 (41) — *the clear Tao seems murky.* The word for the highest seeing is repeatedly qualified as faint, subtle, easily mistaken for dullness. No tradition that meant "brilliance" would keep saying so.

### The lock: why not "enlightenment" or "illumination"

**"Enlightenment"** imports a Buddhist and New Age structure — *awakening*, ascent, a threshold crossed, a self transformed into a higher kind. Laozi has no such architecture. There is no attainment, no realized state, no before-and-after. There is a person who has stopped displaying themselves and can therefore see the small thing in front of them. The word also carries the European Enlightenment as a second ghost — reason, progress, the dispelling of superstition — which is if anything further off.

**"Illumination"** fails on the evidence: Chapter 52 sets 光 and 明 side by side, and "illumination" collapses them. It also names emission where the text names reception.

**"Brilliance," "brightness," "radiance"** — all three describe how a thing *appears to others*, which is precisely the 光 that Laozi keeps telling us to dim. And they contradict 微明 (subtle clarity) and 明道若昧 (the clear Tao seems murky) directly.

**"Wisdom"** belongs to a different character — 智 (*zhì*), which Chapter 33 explicitly ranks *below* 明.

### The working register

明 flexes by grammar; keep it inside one image — *sight that is unobstructed*:

- as the named state → **clear-seeing** (知常曰明 → "knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing")
- as a noun → **clarity** (用其光，復歸其明 → "use its light, return to its clarity"; 微明 → "the hidden clarity"; 襲明 → "clarity worn covered")
- as predicate or verb → **sees clearly / does not see clearly** (不自見，故明; 自見者不明)
- as a modifier → **clear** (明道 at 41 → "the clear Tao")
- 明白四達 (10) → **"clarity reaching the four quarters"**

**Never** "enlightened," "illuminated," "brilliant."

*Why this stays prose in `render:` and is not a `flexions:` entry.* The variation here is **grammatical, not chapter-scoped** — 明 takes the predicate form wherever it predicates, which happens at 22, 24 and 33 (47 left 明 for the received 名 on 2026-09-24), and would take it in a chapter nobody has written yet. `flexions:` exists for a licence tied to a named place, and its `flexion-chapter` rule checks exactly that; pinning a grammatical form to a chapter list would assert a condition the language does not have. See `CLAUDE.md` → *the frontmatter contract*.


### The tension, left open

One chapter uses 明 against everything above, and honesty requires flagging it rather than smoothing it.

**Chapter 65**: 古之善為道者，非以明民，將以愚之 — *those anciently good at the Tao did not use it to make the people 明, but to keep them 愚 (simple, uncarved).* Here 明 is not a virtue to be sought but something done **to** a populace, and the text is against it — the opposite pole from 愚 (*yú*), the useful simplicity Laozi elsewhere praises in himself (20).

Two readings are available. Either 明 here means something different — *clever, sophisticated, knowing-too-much*, the acquired brightness that makes people hard to govern and quick to scheme — or Laozi is being deliberately provocative, using the same word for a good thing (seeing clearly for yourself) and a bad one (being made bright by someone else). The second reading is sharper, and consistent with a book that says *the straight turns crooked* (58): even clarity curdles when it is administered rather than arrived at.

**We chose the first, and ch 65 reads *clever*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-24. `WORKLIST.md` T1-17.)* This entry used to say *"we do not choose between them"* while the verse had already chosen, and nothing recorded that. It is now the one declared exception to this lock, a `flexions:` entry scoped to ch 65, so `concordance.py --english` reports it as licensed instead of passing it in silence. **Three reasons.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) glosses the line outright: 明謂多見巧詐蔽其樸也, *"明 here means seeing too much, craft and deceit, which covers over their simplicity."* The chapter's own next lines put it among 智 (*zhì* — knowing, guile) as what makes a people 難治 (*nán zhì* — hard to govern). And the lock's English fails a test this project keeps: *"did not use it to make the people clear-seeing"* would say, in English, that the sages kept people from seeing clearly. That contradicts ch 16, 33, 52 and 55, where seeing clearly is the goal. A reading the Chinese permits but that lands as a different claim in English has not been translated. **The cost:** the provocation is gone from the verse, so this paragraph is where a reader finds it. *Clever* also sits close to 智's *cleverness* at ch 18 and 19, which `WORKLIST.md` T2-2 must weigh when 智 is settled.

Either way the entry's core holds. 明 is what you see with when nothing is in the way — including, in Chapter 65, the well-meaning hand of someone trying to enlighten you.

flexions.why: 明 done TO a populace by its rulers — 王弼: seeing too much, craft and deceit, covering their simplicity; the lock's English would make the sages keep people from seeing clearly

entries.render: clear-seeing / clarity — *see clearly* in predicate position, *clear* as a modifier

entries.body:
## 母 (Mǔ) — The Mother

*Say "moo," the third tone — it dips and then lifts. One of the Tao's truest names, and the one translators most often flinch from.*

Here, for once, the plain English word is exactly right. 母 is *mother*, and no cleverness improves on it. So the danger in this entry is not mistranslation — it is **abstraction**. For centuries, uneasy with a cosmos that has breasts and nurses its young, translators have quietly cooled 母 into "the Source," "the Origin," "the Matrix," "the Ground of Being" — each of them a way of holding the warmth and the body at arm's length. The work of this entry is the opposite of clever. It is to refuse the flinch and let her stay what she is: a mother. Bodily, generative, nursing — and, this is the hardest part, utterly unsentimental.

### The character, read slowly

Set the character beside its neighbor. 女 (nǚ) is *woman* — the old graph draws a figure kneeling, arms folded across the body. 母 is that very same figure, with **two dots added at the breast**. That is the entire difference. The mark that turns *woman* into *mother* is the breasts: 母 is specifically the one who has borne a child and *feeds it from her own body*. The character will not let you forget the body. Before "mother" is an idea, it is milk. Whatever cosmology we raise on this word, it rests on a nursing woman.

### What 母 does in the Daodejing

The Tao's oldest and warmest name is not "the Way." It is **the mother**. She is 萬物之母, the mother of the countless things (1); 天下母, the mother of the world (25) — "formed in the undifferentiated, born before heaven and earth," and able to bear it all. In Chapter 20 the sage marks themselves off from everyone precisely by *how they feed*: while the crowd gorges on the world's spectacle, 我獨異於人，而貴食母 — "I alone am different, and I prize **nursing from the mother**." The image is exact and unembarrassed — the sage as an infant at the breast, drawing sustenance straight from the source, while the world feasts on noise. And in Chapter 59 she is the **root**: 有國之母，可以長久 — hold the mother and you endure, "deep roots and a firm base, the way of long life."

### The return — womb and refuge (52)

Her deepest chapter is the fifty-second, and it is the most consoling movement in the whole book. 天下有始，以為天下母 — the world has a beginning, and that beginning is the mother. 既得其母，以知其子；既知其子，復守其母，沒身不殆 — *having found the mother, you know her children; and knowing the children, you return and hold fast to the mother — and to the end of your days, no harm.* Here she is not only where you came *from*; she is where you go *back to*. The countless things are her children (子), the whole manifest world her brood — and the movement of wisdom is to turn from the children back toward the one who bore them: to return, and hold, and rest. Womb and refuge at once — origin and destination, the source you were born from and the source you can always come home to. No harm, to the end.

### What we set aside

So we keep every warm and bodily thing the tradition has tried to abstract away. We do not render 母 as "the Source" (a word with no body), "the Origin" (a word with no arms), or "the Ground of Being" (a phrase that has never nursed anything). We keep the breasts the character draws. We keep the milk of 食母. We keep the womb of 玄牝 (the mysterious female, 6) and the children of 子. The Tao is not an impersonal principle a translator has dressed, for warmth, in a mother's robe. Laozi says the reverse: reach for the truest name you have for a source that bears all things and clings to none — and the word that comes is *mother*.

### Fierce, not fond

And now the hard honesty, without which this entry becomes a greeting card. **The cosmic mother is not sentimental.** The same book that calls her the mother of the world also says 天地不仁 — heaven and earth are *not kind*, not doting; they treat the countless things as straw dogs (5). Her love, if we call it that, is not the hovering fondness we pour into the word "mother." It is 生而不有 — she gives birth and does not possess; she bears you, nurses you, and *lets you go*. She does not cling, does not coddle, does not shield you from the weather. Her tenderness is the fierce, impartial, inexhaustible giving of a source that pours out life to all and keeps none of it. That is a deeper tenderness than sentiment — the love that can release what it made. To nurse from *this* mother is to be fed, and then set free.

### The open question

**On the capital, which she does not take.** *(Decided 2026-08-11, after argument; this entry had capitalized her for months without a ruling.)* She is rendered **mother**, lowercase, throughout. Chapter 25 offers her as a role — 可以為天下母, *"it can serve as the mother of the world"* — and then says in the next breath 吾不知其名, *"I do not know its name,"* before coining 道 under protest. All seven occurrences are genitive, possessive, or governed by 為 (*serve as*); she is never addressed and never stands as a bare subject. Heshang Gong makes it a simile outright — 如母之養子, *"like a mother nourishing her child."* And the capital would work against her: in English it confers institutional status rather than intimacy, lifting her out of the nursing body that the graph's two dots exist to draw. 道 keeps its capital because *"Tao"* is transliterated, not translated; every English word here is lowercase. *(Full reasoning in `notes/translation.md` → Typography.)*

Is she a metaphor, or the thing itself? Laozi hedges on purpose. The Tao *can be called* the mother of the world (可以為天下母) — and in nearly the same breath (1) he warns that no name holds it. So the mother is a name that points *truly* without *caging*: the most maternal thing we know, aimed at what has no name. We hold her the way Chapter 52 says to — not gripping the idea, but returning to the reality, and resting there. Her name is not the Tao. But of all the names, it may be the one that loves it best.

## 魄 (Pò) — Aliveness

*Say "paw," falling. One appearance in the whole book, in the first line of chapter 10.*

**Locked: 魄 → "aliveness."** *(Never "soul," never "spirit," never "life force." Not "breath," "energy" or "life" either, but those three are rulings no check can hold. See the last section but one.)*

*The line is* 載營魄抱一，能無離乎 *: "Housing your aliveness and embracing the one, can you keep these from parting?" 營 (yíng — a walled dwelling), the character beside it, is covered here as "housing."*

### The graph: a ghost, and the moon's pale light

> 魄，**陰神**也。从鬼白聲。
> *"魄 is the yin spirit. From 鬼 (guǐ — a ghost), with 白 (bái — white) for the sound."* — 說文解字

**鬼** is the same character chapter 60 renders *ghosts*. In the oracle bones it is a figure with an outsized head, usually read as a mask: the dead, or someone standing in for them. **白**'s original picture is unknown. A thumb (郭沫若, *Guō Mòruò*), a container and a human head have all been proposed, and none has won. 說文 counts it as sound alone.

**The graph is young, and the word is old.** 魄 has no oracle-bone or bronze form. The word does: Western Zhou bronzes date events by the moon's phases, and they write *pò* as **霸**, a moon (月) with a sound part. 既生霸 is *"after the light is born,"* 既死霸 *"after the light has died."* 說文 under 霸: 月始生，霸然也, *"the moon first coming to life, pale and bright."* 段玉裁 (*Duàn Yùcái*) notes the hand-over, 後代魄行而霸廢矣, *"in later ages 魄 took over and 霸 fell out of use"*. The moon sense survived inside it: 李軌 (*Lǐ Guǐ*), on the 法言, has 魄，光也, *"魄 is light,"* and 孟康 (*Mèng Kāng*) has 魄，月質也, *"魄 is the moon's body."*

**So 白 may be more than a sound.** A Han apocryphal text quoted by 孔穎達 (*Kǒng Yǐngdá*) puns the two outright: 魄，白也…白，明白也, *"魄 is white… white is brightness."* 說文 does not say 白亦聲 (*"白 also gives the sound"*), its usual mark for a part that carries meaning and sound at once, and the atlas reports 說文. This entry records that Han readers heard more.

*A calibration: we do not claim Laozi heard the moon in this word. By his time 魄 was a word for a part of a living person, and the evidence for that is what decides the English.*

### What 魄 is: the life that clings to the form

The locus classicus is 子產 (*Zǐ Chǎn*) in the 左傳 (*Zuǒ Zhuàn*), explaining how a man eight years dead could walk as a ghost:

> 人生始化曰魄，既生魄，陽曰魂。用物精多，則魂魄強。
> *"When a person first comes into being, that is called 魄. Once the 魄 is born, its yang side is called 魂 (hún). Draw on much 精 (jīng — vital essence) and the 魂 and 魄 grow strong."*

The commentators read it as plainly bodily, and the readings agree:

| source | says | in English |
|---|---|---|
| 杜預 (*Dù Yù*), on the 左傳 | 魄，**形**也 | *"魄 is the form"* |
| 孔穎達, on the same line | **附形之靈**為魄，附氣之神為魂 | *"the life clinging to the form is the 魄; the spirit clinging to the breath is the 魂"* |
| 孔穎達, continuing | 初生之時，**耳目心識，手足運動，啼呼為聲**，此則魄之靈也 | *"at birth, the ears, eyes and heart taking things in, the hands and feet moving, the crying that is its voice: this is the life of the 魄"* |
| 鄭玄 (*Zhèng Xuán*), on the 禮記 | **耳目之聰明**為魄 | *"the sharpness of ear and eye is the 魄"* |
| 白虎通 (*Báihǔ Tōng*) | 魄者迫也，猶迫迫然**箸於人**也 | *"魄 means pressed close: it clings tightly to a person"* |
| 禮記, 郊特牲 | 魂氣歸于天，**形魄歸于地** | *"the 魂 and the breath return to the sky; the form and the 魄 return to the earth"* |

Five things follow. 魄 is **first**, the life a person has before anything else. It is **bodily**, attached to the form and not to the breath. It is **sensing and moving**, and 孔穎達's example is a newborn. It **clings**. And it comes **in degrees**, strong or weak, as the 左傳 says.

王弼 (*Wáng Bì*), whose commentary this edition reads beside the text, puts 魄 on the same side in his own vocabulary. At chapter 4 the earth is 形魄, *"form and 魄,"* against the sky's 精象, *"essence and image"*: 地雖形魄不法於天則不能全其寧, *"the earth, though it is form and 魄, cannot keep its rest unless it models itself on the sky."* At chapter 25: 形魄不及精象, *"form and 魄 do not reach essence and image."*

### Chapter 10: the breath beside it

> 載營魄抱一，能無離乎
> 專氣致柔，能如嬰兒乎
> *"Housing your aliveness and embracing the one, can you keep these from parting?*
> *Gathering the breath to softness, can you be like an infant?"*

**The couplet names the two halves of a living person that the 禮記 pairs.** 祭義: 氣也者，神之盛也；魄也者，鬼之盛也, *"breath is the fullness of spirit; the 魄 is the fullness of ghost."* Aliveness stands in the first line and breath in the second. The infant the second line asks for is 孔穎達's picture of the 魄 itself.

**魂 (*hún*), the 魄's usual partner, never appears in the book.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) supplies it anyway: 營魄，魂魄也…魂在肝，魄在肺, *"營魄 is the 魂 and the 魄… the 魂 in the liver, the 魄 in the lungs."* The pairing is older than he is. It is in the 左傳 above, and in 韓非子 (*Hán Fēizǐ*)'s own commentary on chapter 60, 魂魄去而精神亂, *"when the 魂 and 魄 leave, essence and spirit fall into disorder."* What is Han is the **organ map**. In five-phase medicine the lungs are metal, autumn and white, and that is the second road by which whiteness reaches 魄. It runs through a system this text does not use. Michael Brashier has argued that even the two-soul scheme was a scholars' model, and that Han grave inscriptions set the 魂 and 魄 together at the tomb against the 神 (*shén* — spirit) at the shrine.

**Who houses whom.** 王弼: 載猶處也。營魄，人之常居處也…言人能處常居之宅, *"載 is like 'to dwell.' 營魄 is a person's constant dwelling… a person who can dwell in the house where they always live."* For him the 營魄 is the house and the person lives in it. ***Housing* takes the other direction**: the person holds the 魄. That is 王逸 (*Wáng Yì*)'s reading of the same phrase in the 楚辭 (*Chǔ Cí*), 載營魄而登霞兮, *"bearing my 營魄 I climb the rosy clouds,"* glossed 抱我魂靈而上升也, *"embracing my soul I rise."* It is also 河上公's, 當愛養之, *"you must cherish and nourish it."* The verb stands on 營's graph, 說文 營，市居也, *"a walled residence."*

**The witnesses.** The Mawangdui silk B text reads 戴營魄抱一，能毌離乎, with 戴 (*dài* — to carry on the head) for 載. The Peking University Han slips read 載**熒**魄, with 熒 (*yíng* — a glimmer) for 營. That is one witness, and it is a reason to look rather than a reading, but it puts the moon's pale light back into the line. Guodian has no chapter 10.

### Why "aliveness"

- **It is the body's own.** Nothing in it leaves the body or lives elsewhere, and *housing* already says where it is kept.
- **It carries the senses.** English *alive to* means sensitive to, which is 鄭玄's sharp ear and eye. *Vigor* had motion only.
- **It comes in degrees.** You can be more or less alive, as the 左傳's 魄 grows strong.
- **It is the infant.** 孔穎達's newborn, eyes open, limbs moving, crying, is aliveness you could point at, and chapter 10 asks for the infant one line later.
- **It brings nothing in.** No theology, no breath, no energy and no sex.

### What is set aside, and why

**"soul"** is what every English translation prints: Waley *the physical-soul*, Lau *the bodily soul*, Lynn *the earthbound soul*, Legge *the animal soul*, and plain *soul* in Henricks, Mair and Ivanhoe. Each qualifier is an attempt to take back what the noun imports, a separable, immaterial self, and the qualifiers are the evidence that it does. Already refused for 精 (*jīng*) and 身 (*shēn*) on the same grounds.

**"the corporeal soul"** is the accurate label, and it is right in a note. In the verse it is a technical term for the overlay; see `process/principles/perform-dont-label.md`.

**"spirit"** is 神's (6, 39, 60), and 神 is the half the 禮記 sets against the 魄.

**"life force"** and **"life-energy"** are the popular English for 氣 (*qì* — breath), which is the other half. *Energy* is 氣's own word at chapter 55.

**"vitality"** shares its root with two locked phrases: 精 is *vital essence* (21, 55) and 氣 is *vital breath* (42) and *vital energy* (55). The 左傳's definition would then read *"draw on much vital essence and the vitality grows strong,"* and the distinction it draws is lost.

**"vigor"** leans toward virility, and the sexual vitality in this book is 精's, at chapter 55's 朘作.

**"the animating part"** sends 魄 the wrong way. *Anima* is breath, and breath is 氣's, in the next line.

**"the quick"** is the creed's *the quick and the dead*, and chapter 55 already *quickens*.

**"body"** and **"flesh"**: *body* is 身's (13, 54, 76), and *flesh* is Pauline, Romans 8, the hymn test.

### The working register

One occurrence, a noun, the object of 載 (*zài* — to carry, to ride, to dwell in). The two characters before it are rendered together by one verb:

| Chinese | English | renders |
|---|---|---|
| 載營 | *housing* | 營's graph, a walled dwelling, with 載's carrying |
| 魄 | *your aliveness* | 魄. *Your* is supplied, as English needs a possessor |

### What no rule can enforce

**"breath," "energy" and "life" are ruled out for 魄 and are not on the `forbidden:` list, because they cannot be.** 氣 stands in chapter 10 and prints *breath* there. *Energy* is its English at chapter 55, and a future reading of chapter 10 could use it. 生 (*shēng*) stands in chapter 10 too (生之畜之), and *life* is its word elsewhere. `check_locks.py` gates on whether a character is present in the chapter, and all three characters are. So *soul*, *spirit*, *life force* and *vigor* are held by the build; *breath*, *energy* and *life* are held by this entry and by the reader. See `process/principles/ruling-and-enforcement-are-two-facts.md`.

### Left open

**The ghost.** Aliveness ends at death; the 魄 does not. 子產's whole point is that a strong 魄 can outlast the person: the 禮記 sends it into the ground with the body, and it is what lingers at the tomb. The English keeps the living half of the word and drops the half that goes into the earth, and it has to, because the only English that keeps both is *soul*. Laozi's line is about a living person keeping two things from parting, so the ghost is offstage. It is not gone.

**Whether 白 carries meaning.** 說文 says sound. The 霸 word family and a Han pun say more. 明白 (*míng bái* — clarity) stands four lines below in this chapter, and `WORKLIST` T2-23 already asks whether that compound is bound. Whether the chapter hears 魄 and 明白 together is a reason to look and not a reading (`process/principles/distribution-locates.md`).

**The direction of 載.** 王弼 has the person inside the 營魄; 王逸 and 河上公 have the person holding it. The verse follows the second. 王弼 is the commentator this edition most often follows, and here it does not.
entries.shuowen: The yin spirit. From 鬼 (guǐ — a ghost), with 白 (bái — white) for sound.

entries.body:
## 樸 (Pǔ) — Uncarved Wood

*Say "poo," dipping and lifting. Eight appearances across six chapters — 15, 19, 28, 32, 37, 57. Perhaps the most concrete image in the book, and the one most often turned into an abstraction.*

**Locked: 樸 → "uncarved wood" / "the uncarved."** *(Lowercase. Not "simplicity," not "the Uncarved Block" as a capitalized proper noun.)*

樸 is a piece of timber that has not yet been made into anything. That is the whole word, and its power is that it stays a piece of wood. The temptation — and most translations succumb — is to lift it into a virtue: *simplicity, purity, primal innocence*. But an abstraction cannot be **split**, and splitting is precisely what Chapter 28 does to it. Keep the wood, and the argument survives.

### The character, read slowly

樸 is built on **木** (*mù*) — a tree, the oldest and plainest graph for wood — with a phonetic element beside it. The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it 木素也: *wood in its 素 state*, where **素** (*sù*) is **undyed silk** — cloth still the color it was when it came off the worm.

So the character's own definition reaches for its twin. And Laozi puts them side by side, once, in **Chapter 19**:

> 見素抱樸
> *See the undyed; embrace the uncarved.*

Two materials, one condition: **before human working.** Silk before the dye-vat, timber before the chisel. Not innocent, not sacred — just not yet turned into something for us.

### Chapter 28 — the block and the vessels

The central passage, and the reason the wood must stay wood:

> 樸散則為器
> *When the uncarved is split up, it becomes vessels.*

**器** (*qì*) is a vessel, a tool, an implement — a thing with a **function**. And here is the whole idea in one motion: the block has no function. Carve it, and you get a bowl, a wheel, a handle — each useful, each *named*, each now only one thing. What the block loses in becoming useful is **everything it might otherwise have been.**

Note where this lands in the chapter's architecture. Chapter 28 is built of three parallel triads, each closing on 復歸於 — *return again to*: return to **the infant** (嬰兒), return to **the limitless** (無極), return to **the uncarved** (樸). All three name the same direction: back toward what has not yet been made particular.

And 器 in Chinese is not only pottery. It is also what a **person** amounts to — 成器 means *to become someone useful, to amount to something*. So 樸散則為器 reads, without strain, as a sentence about people: society takes the whole raw human and carves them into a function. A role. A job title. Useful, named, and no longer able to be anything else.

### Why the uncarved is nameless

Two chapters bind 樸 to 無名 (*wúmíng* — namelessness), and the link is exact rather than poetic:

> 道常無名，樸。(32) — *The Tao is ever nameless, uncarved.*
> 吾將鎮之以無名之樸。(37) — *I will settle them with the nameless uncarved.*

**Carving is naming.** A shaped thing can be named because it is now one determinate thing — *this is a bowl*. The block resists naming for the same reason it resists use: it is not yet any particular thing. Chapter 1's nameless (無名) and Chapter 28's uncarved (樸) are one condition described in two materials — one in language, one in wood.

Which explains the strangest line of the group:

> 樸雖小，天下莫能臣也。(32)
> *Though the uncarved is small, nothing in the world can make it a subject.*

**臣** (*chén*) is a vassal, a servant, one who serves under. You cannot subordinate the uncarved — because to subordinate is to assign a function, and to assign a function is to carve. What has no use cannot be put to use. Its smallness is not weakness; it is the reason nothing can get a grip on it.

### The resolution — 大制不割

Chapter 28 does not leave us with a prohibition on all shaping, which would be unlivable. It closes:

> 聖人用之，則為官長，故大制不割。
> *The sage uses them, and so becomes chief of officials — therefore the greatest shaping does no cutting.*

**制** (*zhì*) is to tailor, cut out, regulate, govern. **割** (*gē*) is to sever. So: *the great carving does not sever.* The sage does not refuse to govern, and does not pretend the world contains no vessels. What they refuse is the **cut** — the severing that turns a whole person into an instrument. Shape without severing; use without reducing. That is the practical form of 無為 (*wúwéi* — non-doing) applied to people.

### The far echo — Chapter 41

One more line belongs to this cluster, and its manuscript fork makes it sharper: 大器晚成 (41), which the older witnesses read as 大器**免**成 — *the great vessel is **never** completed.* This edition follows the manuscript reading.

Set it beside Chapter 28 and it snaps into place. If a vessel is made by cutting, then the **greatest** vessel is the one never finished being cut — which is to say, the block itself. The great vessel is never completed because completion is exactly what would ruin it.

### What we set aside

**"Simplicity."** The most common rendering and the most costly. It is abstract, it sounds like a lifestyle preference, and it cannot be split into vessels. Chapter 28's argument becomes unreadable.

**"Purity," "innocence," "primal wholeness."** These import moral and spiritual value the wood does not carry. An uncut log is not virtuous. It is simply uncut — which is a fact about its history, not its character.

**"The Uncarved Block," capitalized.** The initial capitals turn a log into a doctrine, and this is exactly the devotional typography the overlay audit warns against: in English, capitals confer deity. Laozi's word is small and homely — 樸雖小, *the uncarved is small*. Keep it lowercase.

**"Raw material," "unprocessed material."** Correct in denotation, industrial in feel, and they imply the thing is *awaiting* processing — which inverts the value.

**Leaving it untranslated as *pu*.** The image is fully available in English. Transliterating would mystify a piece of wood.

### The working register

- as noun → **uncarved wood**, or **the uncarved** where the sentence needs it to act as a subject (樸散則為器 → "when the uncarved is split up, it becomes vessels")
- in simile → **like uncarved wood** (敦兮其若樸 → "solid, like uncarved wood")
- bound to namelessness → **the nameless uncarved** (無名之樸)
- predicative, of people → **plain** — a licensed flexion, see below
- **器** as its counter-term → **vessel** where the thing is a container, **tool** or **instrument** where the point is function

**On "plain" at Chapter 57.** 我無欲，而民自樸 is rendered *"I am desireless, and the people become plain of themselves"* — and it should stay. The line sits in a four-part refrain (transform / right / enrich / ——), each member a short predicate ending in 自 (*of themselves*); "become uncarved of themselves" would stall it, and "plain" carries 樸's core sense exactly. This is a deliberate flexion, not a drift: the plain people of Chapter 57 and the uncut wood of Chapter 28 are the same image at two scales.


### Is there a paradox inside the word? — the "block" question

A tempting reading holds that 樸 is *self-contradictory by construction*: to have a **block**, someone must already have felled, squared, and sawn the timber — so the "uncarved block" is always already carved. It is an elegant thought. It does not survive the evidence, and it is worth showing why, because what replaces it is better.

**The lexicography.** The *Shuowen* defines 樸 as 木素 — *plain wood, unworked lumber.* Not a block. Not a blank. A **state**, not a shape.

**The word-family.** 樸 is 木 (wood) + the phonetic 菐. Change the material radical and you get **璞** (*pú*) — 玉 (jade) + the same 菐 — meaning **uncut jade still in the rock**, the stone as it comes out of the mountain. The shared phonetic carries the sense *raw, pre-worked*, and jade-in-the-matrix is unambiguously a natural object that no hand has touched. Whatever 菐 means, it is not "prepared stock."

**The company it keeps.** Chapter 28's architecture is decisive. Three parallel triads, each closing on 復歸於 — *return again to*:

> 復歸於**嬰兒** — return again to the **infant**
> 復歸於**無極** — return again to the **limitless**
> 復歸於**樸** — return again to the **uncarved**

Three slots, one grammar, one category. An infant is not a prepared material; neither is the limitless. 樸 sits among *original natural conditions*, not processed intermediates.

**The syntax.** Chapter 32 reads 道常無名。樸雖小 — *the Tao is ever nameless; though [it is] uncarved and small…* Here 樸 attaches to **the Tao itself**. The Tao is not a piece of squared timber awaiting a chisel.

So the "block" is **English**, not Chinese — a noun supplied by translators to give an adjective a body. Scholars have said so directly: Pas and Leung note that the addition of "block" is an *interpretation* rather than a translation of the original sense of plain wood. This is a further argument for our lock: **"uncarved wood," never "uncarved block."** The block imports a paradox Laozi did not write — and worse, by satisfying the appetite for paradox, it hides the three real ones.

### The paradoxes that are actually there

**1. You are told to return to a state that cannot be recovered.** 復歸於樸 (28). Wood does not un-carve. Once the block is vessels, no craft on earth makes it a block again. Yet the instruction stands, three times over, in parallel with returning to infancy and to the limitless — both equally irreversible. Either the instruction is impossible, or *returning* means something other than reversal: not restoring a former shape but ceasing to identify with the shape you were cut into. The text does not explain. It simply keeps pointing backward along a road that only runs forward.

**2. The great carving does not cut.** 大制不割 (28) — Laozi's own explicit paradox, placed in the very passage where the block becomes vessels. 制 is to tailor, cut out, govern; 割 is to sever. The greatest shaping does no severing. Not a refusal to shape — a shaping that leaves nothing cut.

**3. The un-usable is used.** Chapter 32 insists that nothing in the world can make the uncarved a subject — 天下莫能臣也 — because it has no function to be pressed into. Then Chapter 37: 吾將鎮之以無名之樸 — *I will settle them with the nameless uncarved.* The ruler **deploys** it. The thing defined by having no use is picked up and used, and the paradox is exactly the point: what settles a grasping world is the one thing that cannot be grasped.

**And one more, structural.** Chapter 32 says 始制有名 — *when the carving begins, there are names.* Naming **is** carving. Which means every word in this book is a cut, including the word 樸 — Laozi is using chisels to point at the uncut log. He seems to know it: 道可道，非常道 (1), and 知者不言 (56). The book is a carving that argues against carving.

That is the honest shape of the thing. The paradox is not buried in the etymology; it is in what Laozi *does* with a perfectly ordinary word for raw timber. Which is more interesting, and more his.

### The tension, left open

The obvious objection: bowls are good. Wheels are good. A world of uncut logs is a world with nothing to eat from. Laozi knows this — Chapter 11 is a hymn to the usefulness of vessels, and Chapter 28 has the sage *using* the carved things and governing with them.

So this is not a counsel to remain unformed. It is closer to a warning about **which way the traffic runs.** Everything in the book moves toward the uncarved — return to the infant, return to the limitless, return to the block — while the world moves the other way, cutting and naming and assigning, until nothing whole is left. The instruction is directional, not absolute: know that you were a block before you were a tool, and that the tool is the smaller thing.

What the text will not say is how much carving a life requires. It offers only 大制不割 — *shape without severing* — which is less a rule than a discipline of the hand, and, like most of this book's central instructions, easier to recognize than to follow.

## 器 (Qì) — Vessel

*Say "chee," falling. Twelve appearances across nine chapters. A concrete object that abstraction keeps reaching for — and the one word in this glossary that the mechanistic overlay attacks directly.*

**Locked: 器 → "vessel" / "tool" / "implement."** *(Not "system," not "mechanism," not "machine.")*

Chapter 29 read 天下神器 as *"the world is a sacred system."* That single substitution costs the chapter its argument, because the next clause is 不可執也 — *it cannot be grasped* — and then 執者失之, *those who grasp it lose it.* **You can grasp at a vessel and break it. You cannot grasp a system.** The image and the warning are one gesture, and abstraction severs them.

The danger runs the other way too. Chapter 11's whole case depends on 器 staying a **pot**: 埏埴以為器 — *knead clay to make a vessel* — and the vessel is useful only because of the hollow. Let 器 drift toward "structure" or "function" and the argument evaporates, because a structure has no inside.

### The character, read slowly — a dog guarding the crockery

器 is four 口 (*kǒu* — mouth, opening) around 犬 (*quǎn* — dog). The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) is unusually plain about it:

> 皿也。象器之口，犬所以守之。
> *A vessel. It depicts the mouths of containers, with a dog to guard them.*

The picture is a **yard of open pots with a dog watching over them.** It is worth sitting with, because it says two things at once. 器 is a *made* thing — fired, shaped, owned. And it is a thing **worth guarding**: valuable enough that you set an animal on it.

That second half is what makes 神器 (*shén qì*) in Chapter 29 land. In the late Zhou a 神器 was concrete: the **ritual bronzes**, above all the 九鼎 (*jiǔ dǐng* — the nine cauldrons), whose possession was the visible warrant of the mandate to rule. The chapter opens on 將欲取天下 — *wishing to seize the world* — and answers that the world is a sacred vessel and cannot be grasped. To a contemporary ear that is not a metaphor. It is a sentence about reaching for the cauldrons. *(See the Reading Note at Chapter 29.)*

### The evidence — 器 is what wholeness becomes

**The fall from the uncarved.** Chapter 28: 樸散則為器 — *when the uncarved wood is broken up, it becomes 器.* This is the hinge of the whole 樸 argument. 器 is the **plural, specialized, useful** state on the far side of a loss: one log becomes many tools, each good for something and none good for everything. The word is not an insult, but it names a diminishment.

**And yet 器 is exemplary.** Chapter 11 makes a clay pot one of three proofs that emptiness is what works — 有器之用, *there is the use of the vessel* — alongside the wheel's hub and the room's windows. The vessel here is not fallen; it is the teacher.

**And weapons are 器.** Chapter 31 says it three times: 夫佳兵者，不祥之器 · 兵者不祥之器 · 非君子之器 — *fine weapons are implements of ill omen; weapons are implements of ill omen; they are not the implements of a person of quality.* Chapter 57's 人多利器，國家滋昏 (*the more sharp implements among the people, the darker the state grows*) and Chapter 36's 國之利器不可以示人 (*the sharp instruments of the state must not be displayed*) run the same way. Here "implement" or "instrument" serves better than "vessel," and the flexion is licensed.

**And a person can be one.** Chapter 41's 大器晚成 — in our base text *"the great vessel is completed late,"* and in the Mawangdui and Guodian witnesses 免成 / 曼成, *never completed*, which we follow. Classical Chinese applies 器 to people as **capacity** — the size of what someone can hold — and the idiom survives in modern Chinese as *a person of great capacity matures slowly*. Chapter 67's 故能成器長 (*and so can become the elder of the vessels*) uses the same personal sense.

### The lock: what is set aside, and why

**"System"** is the mechanistic overlay, and this project's own besetting temptation. It abstracts a fired clay pot into a set of relations, breaks Chapter 29's grasping image, and empties Chapter 11's hollow. It also fails the pointing test twice over: Laozi could point at the pot and at the dog.

**"Mechanism," "machine," "apparatus"** import moving parts and a designer. 器 has neither. A pot does nothing; that is the point of Chapter 11.

**"Utensil"** is not wrong so much as small and domestic — it makes 神器 (the world) and 不祥之器 (weapons of ill omen) faintly absurd. Keep it out of the register.

**"Organ"** is a real classical sense of 器 and is right to leave unused here: nothing in these nine chapters is anatomical.

**"Vessel" everywhere** would also be an error. Chapter 31's weapons are not vessels, and Chapter 28's carved tools are not vessels. The lock is a small family — *vessel, tool, implement* — held together by being **made, concrete, and usable**, and it flexes by what the chapter has in hand.

### The working register

- containers, and the world as one → **vessel** (有器之用 → "the use of the vessel"; 神器 → "a sacred vessel"; 大器 → "the great vessel")
- what the uncarved becomes → **tools** (樸散則為器 → "when the uncarved wood is carved, it is made into tools")
- weapons and sharp things → **implement / instrument** (不祥之器 → "implements of ill omen"; 利器 → "sharp instruments")
- of a person → **capacity** (器長 → the elder among them; 大器晚成 and its variants)

**Never** "system," "mechanism," "machine," "utensil."

### The tension, left open

**Is 器 fallen or exemplary?** The text will not say.

Chapter 28 makes 器 the **result of breaking wholeness**: the uncarved log scattered into specialized tools, and the chapter's whole movement is a call to 復歸於樸 — *return to the uncarved.* On that reading 器 is a diminishment, and the sage's task is to be the log and not the chisel.

Chapter 11 makes 器 the **model of how anything works at all**, and Chapter 29 makes it **sacred**. On that reading being a vessel is not a fall but the condition of usefulness, and the hollow at the centre is the same emptiness the Tao is praised for.

Both are in the book, unreconciled, and we do not reconcile them. The nearest thing to a resolution is that Chapter 28 objects to being **one** tool — 樸散, *scattered*, made plural and partial — while Chapter 11 admires the vessel for **what it lacks**. A pot is not a specialized blade. But that reading is ours, and the text does not state it.

## 強 (Qiáng) — Strong

*Say "chyahng," rising. Twenty-one lines across twelve chapters, and the book makes it both the disease and the cure.*

**Locked: 強 → "strong" — *strengthen* where it takes an object, *forcing* where it strains against a thing's nature.** *(Not "mighty," not "forceful," not "brute strength," not "perseverance." 力 (lì) → "force.")*

Chapter 78 forces four words apart — 柔 (*róu* — soft) · 剛 (*gāng* — unbending) · 弱 (*ruò* — yielding) · 強 — and 強 is the one that carries opposite verdicts inside a single frame.

The book's sharpest joke depends on it, and any English that resolves the word makes the joke invisible.

Two chapters use the identical three-character frame **X 曰強** (*yuē qiáng* — "is called 強"):

> 守柔曰強
> *ch 52 — "holding to the soft is called 強"*

> 心使氣曰強
> *ch 55 — "the heart driving the energy is called 強"*

The first is praise. The second is a warning, and the line after it is 物壯則老 (*wù zhuàng zé lǎo* — "things at their prime grow old"). **One word, one frame, opposite verdicts.** A translation that renders the first *strength* and the second *forcing* has answered a question the text deliberately leaves standing — and has spent two English words to hide the fact that Laozi used one.

### The graph, and it is the same instrument as 弱

The character now written 強 is not the original word for strength. Two graphs are involved and the *Shuowen Jiezi* (c. 100 CE) separates them cleanly.

**彊** (*qiáng*) — 弓有力也，从弓畺聲: *"a bow having force"*; 弓 (*gōng* — a bow) with 畺 as phonetic. The image is a stiff bow, one that takes strength to draw.

**強** (*qiáng*) — 蚚也，从虫弘聲: *"the 蚚"*, a weevil in stored grain; 虫 (*chóng* — insect) with 弘 (*hóng*) as phonetic. From the Qin onward this borrowed graph displaced 彊 in the sense of strength, and it is the form our recension carries throughout: 彊 appears nowhere in the base text.

So two things follow, and the second is the one that matters.

**The word we read is a grain weevil borrowed for its sound.** The strength is a phonetic accident, exactly as 萬 (*wàn* — a scorpion) is an accident inside 萬物. Two of this book's load-bearing terms are insects conscripted by rhyme.

**And the word underneath it is a bow.** 弱 is two 弓 (bows) under 彡 (fine strokes) — a bow that gives. 彊 is 弓 at the limit of what it will take. **They are not opposites in kind. They are one instrument in two states**, and every image the book builds on the pair is a bow image:

> 木強則折
> *ch 76 — "a tree that is 強 snaps"*

That is a bow drawn past its give. Ch 76's whole botany is the same figure: 王弼 glosses 強大處下 as 木之本也 (*"this is the trunk"*) and 柔弱處上 as 枝條是也 (*"these are the branches"*). The trunk cannot bend and is nearer the ground; the branches bend and are nearer the light.

### The commentators name the quartet outright

河上公, glossing ch 42's 人之所教，我亦教之 (*"what others teach, I also teach"*), states both curricula in fourteen characters:

> 謂衆人所以教去弱為強，去柔為剛
> *"what the crowd teaches: leave 弱 for 強, leave 柔 for 剛"*

> 言我教衆人使去強為弱，去剛為柔
> *"I teach them: leave 強 for 弱, leave 剛 for 柔"*

A Han commentator, using all four characters, in two matched lines, treating them as a fixed set. This is the strongest evidence in the repository that 柔 · 剛 · 弱 · 強 must take four distinct and stable English words.

**And 王弼 states the paradox directly.** On ch 52's 守柔曰強:

> 守強不強，守柔乃強也
> *"holding to 強 is not 強; holding to the soft is truly 強"*

強 twice in seven characters, with opposite valence, from the fourth-century commentator the recension is named for. Whatever English 強 takes has to survive being said twice in one breath and meaning something different each time. **Strong survives it. Forcing does not, and neither does true strength.**

### Where it flexes, and the flexions are grammatical

The split is marked in the Chinese, so it can be checked rather than argued.

**Transitive, with an object — *strengthen*.** Two lines, and they are the same two lines where 弱 is licensed to read *weaken*:

- **ch 3** 弱其志，強其骨 — *weaken their ambition, strengthen their bones*
- **ch 36** 將欲弱之，必固強之 — *wanting to weaken it, first strengthen it*

The symmetry is not a coincidence: it is one grammar, so it is one exception, taken twice. A stance word cannot take an object.

**Straining against a thing's nature — *forcing*.** Where 強 modifies a verb of naming or describing, it is the strain of the act, not a quality of anything:

- **ch 15** 強為之容 — *forcing a description of them*
- **ch 25** 強字之曰道，強為之名曰大 — *forcing a style on it, I call it the Tao; forcing a name, I call it the vast*

The tradition heard this as a separate word. 河上公's text at ch 25 carries the phonetic note 強其文反, a *fanqie* spelling giving the third-tone reading *qiǎng* — "to force, to compel" — rather than *qiáng*. (These phonetic notes are later editorial additions to the Heshang Gong text, not the Han commentary itself; they record how the line was read, not what its first reader wrote.)

**Coercing something that is not yours — *force / dominance*.** Ch 30 uses 強 three times against the world and against people, where *strengthen* would be simply wrong: you do not strengthen a country by invading it.

- 不以兵強天下 — *does not use arms to force the world*
- 不敢以取強 — 河上公: 不以果敢取強大之名也, *"does not use boldness to seize the name of 強大"*
- 果而勿強 — 河上公: 果敢勿以為強兵堅甲以侵凌人也, *"succeed, but do not make strong troops and hard armor to trample people"*

**Everywhere else — *strong*.** Chapters 29, 33, 36 (柔弱勝剛強), 42, 52, 55, 76, 78.

### 力 is the plain word, and ch 33 has the pair inverted

強 cannot be settled without 力 (*lì* — a plough or an arm, the ordinary word for physical force), because ch 33 sets them against each other:

> 勝人者有力，自勝者強
> *"those who overcome others have 力; those who overcome themselves are 強"*

王弼: 勝人者有力而已矣，未若自勝者無物以損其力 — *"one who overcomes others merely has 力; unlike one who overcomes themselves, whose force nothing can diminish."* 河上公: 能勝人者不過以威力也 — *"one who can overcome others does so by no more than 威力"* (awe and force).

The couplet is **plain force against achieved strength**, and it rhymes with the line above it, where 智 (*zhì* — cleverness) is the lesser term against 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing). 力 is what you have. 強 is what you become.

**力 takes *force*** — which ch 68 already does (用人之力, *"using people's force"*) — and 強 takes *strong*. Neither needs an adjective; the couplet supplies the comparison.

### Never

**mighty · forceful · brute strength.** All three pre-judge. 強 is the word the book uses for the state it warns against *and* the state it recommends, and an English that carries a verdict cannot do both.

**perseverance** for 強行 (ch 33). 王弼 glosses it 勤能行之，其志必獲 — *"diligently able to practise it, their will surely attains"* — so persistence is the sense. But *perseverance* is a virtue-word that leaves no trace of 強, and it hides the fact that the chapter has just spent two lines distinguishing 力 from 強. Whatever the line takes, the character has to be audible in it.

**And do not let *strong* or *strength* drift onto its neighbours.** Two characters have borrowed 強's English in chapters that contain 強 — 固 (*gù* — firm) at ch 55's 握固, and 壯 (*zhuàng* — in its prime) at 物壯則老 in ch 30 and ch 55. A lock is a claim in both directions, and no checker rule can catch these: 固 and 壯 sit in the same chapters as 強, so the evidence gate that makes the tool trustworthy is exactly what blinds it here. This is a reader's job.

### What stays open

**強 is both the disease and the cure, and nothing in the text resolves it.** It is rigor mortis at ch 76, an army that cannot win at ch 76 and ch 30, a roof-beam at ch 42, the heart bullying the breath at ch 55 — and it is also what you are when you overcome yourself at ch 33 and when you hold to the soft at ch 52.

The temptation is to read the good instances as a different word, or as irony. 王弼 refuses that escape: 守強不強，守柔乃強也 puts both on the page at once and lets them stand. The English should be able to say the same sentence.

What is genuinely unsettled is **ch 55's 心使氣曰強**, the one line where the reader most needs help and gets least. Rendered *"the heart driving the energy is called strong,"* it can be misheard as approval for exactly one beat — until 物壯則老 lands in the next line. Whether that beat is a flaw or the point is not a question the Chinese answers.
entries.render: strong — *strengthen* where it takes an object, *forcing* where it strains against a thing's nature

entries.body:
## 全 (Quán) — Whole

*Say "chwen," rising. Three occurrences in eighty-one chapters, all of them in Chapter 22, and the word English keeps reaching for is a repair verb.*

**Locked: 全 → "whole" — as an outcome, *stay whole*; as a transitive act, *keep whole*.** *(Never "complete," never "perfect," never "flawless," and never any verb of repair.)*

### The live problem: English wants to fix something

Chapter 22 opens 曲則全 (*qū zé quán* — "bend, then whole") and closes 誠全而歸之. Four drafts of that closing line, in this repository, reached for a verb of restoration — *makes you whole*, *restores your wholeness* — and every one of them smuggled in **a breakage the Chinese never concedes.**

The chapter is not about being mended. It is about **not getting broken in the first place.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) says so in five characters, glossing 曲則全:

> 曲己從眾，不自專，則**全其身**也
> *"Bend yourself and follow the crowd, do not act on your own authority, then you **keep your body whole**."*

全其身 — **全 as a transitive verb meaning *keep intact***. Not *make whole*. The sense is attested straight through the lexical tradition: *to preserve, to keep whole or intact*. Preservation, never repair.

To *restore* is to bring something back to a former condition, which presupposes the loss. It is *make whole* with better manners. Under this lock, neither can stand.

### The character, read slowly — a piece of jade brought in whole

全 is **入** (*rù* — to enter, to bring in) over **玉** (*yù* — jade), written 王 with its dot dropped. The picture is **a piece of jade carried in unbroken.**

The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) glosses it 完也 (*wán* — intact), and the tradition attached to the graph reads **純玉曰全** — *"pure jade is called 全."* Not jade that has been polished into perfection: jade that arrived without a crack in it.

That single image carries the whole lock. **You cannot repair jade.** A cracked piece is not restorable; it is a different, lesser object. Wholeness in jade is not an achievement, it is a survival — which is exactly the claim Chapter 22 is making about a person who bends.

> **A caution specific to this repository.** The component at the bottom of 全 is **玉 (*yù* — jade), not 王 (*wáng* — ruler)**, though the two are written alike once 玉 loses its dot. There is no king inside *whole*. Given how much work `DISCOVERIES.md` §4 does to get a throne out of 王, it is worth saying plainly that this graph never had one.

### The evidence — a closed system, and a quotation

**全 occurs three times, all in Chapter 22:** 曲則全, the verbatim quote-back 古之所謂「曲則全」者, and the closing 誠全而歸之. **曲** (*qū* — bent) does the same: twice, both in Chapter 22, both bound to 全. Neither character appears anywhere else in the book.

That seals the pair inside one chapter and makes it a self-contained argument. It also raises a question the chapter answers itself — see the open tension at the foot of this entry.

**The material vocabulary around it, none of which is 全's word.**

| Character | Picture | Where | Rendered |
|---|---|---|---|
| **瑕** (*xiá*) | a **flaw in jade** | 27 · 善言無瑕謫 | *flawless* — already spent |
| **缺** (*quē*) | a **chipped jar** (缶 *fǒu*, an earthen vessel) | 45 · 大成若缺 · 58 | *deficient* |
| **散** (*sàn*) | scattered, broken up | 28 · 樸散則為器 | *carved* |
| **成** (*chéng*) | brought to completion | 14 chapters | *complete* |

The book thinks about integrity in **objects** — jade, jars, timber. 全 belongs in that company and should be rendered from it.

### The lock: what is set aside, and why

**"Complete"** belongs to **成** (*chéng*), which runs through fourteen chapters, and the two are not synonyms. *Complete* means **finished**; 全 means **undamaged**. A thing can be whole and unfinished — Chapter 41 insists on it: 大器晚成 (*dà qì wǎn chéng* — *"the great vessel is never completed"*). The book is openly suspicious of completion. It is not suspicious of wholeness.

**"Perfect"** imports an ideal, and usually a moral one. 全 is physical integrity, not attainment. Fails the hymn test on contact: *"bend, and you shall be made perfect."*

**"Flawless"** is the right semantic field and **the wrong chapter** — it is already carrying 瑕 (*xiá* — a flaw in jade) at Chapter 27, 善言無瑕謫, *"masterful speaking is flawless."* Two jade words in one book, and English has one good adjective for them. 瑕 got there first, and *flawless* also drifts toward **appearance**, where 全 is about **condition**.

**"Restore," "make whole," "heal"** — the repair family, rejected above. They concede the damage the chapter denies.

**"Preserved,"** as in the familiar *"yield and you will be preserved,"* fails on **voice**. The English passive hands the preserving to an unnamed outside agent. 全其身 has the person doing it themselves — which is the point of a chapter about what your own bending accomplishes.

**"Unbroken"** is not wrong, and was this edition's first rendering (*"Yield and remain unbroken"*). It was set aside for defining by negation: the jade is not merely *not shattered*, it is **whole and worth something**. The positive value is in the stone.

**"Intact"** is the most exact one-word gloss of the sense and is not used in the verse, because it is clinical — a word for shipping crates and evidence bags. It is the right word for the *definition* and the wrong register for the *poem*, and that gap is worth knowing when reading this entry against the line.

### 曲 (*qū* — bend), treated here

曲 is a picture of something **bent** — the older graph is read as a curved or notched implement, a bamboo frame or bent vessel. It is the ordinary word for *crooked, curved, bent aside*.

**Render it *bend*, and never *yield*.** *Yielding* is the locked English for **弱** (*ruò*), whose graph is two 弓 (*gōng* — a bow) with 彡 (fine strokes) — a bow is useful because it bends. This edition's earlier Chapter 22 read *"Yield and remain unbroken,"* which borrowed 弱's locked word for a character that is not 弱 and does not appear in that chapter. The two ideas are cousins; the two words are not interchangeable.

*Bend* also keeps the physical gesture the chapter needs, because the four opening lines are all bodily: bent, wronged-and-straightened, hollowed, worn out.

### The working register

- as the outcome of the 則 (*zé* — then, thus) construction → **stay whole** (曲則全 → *"Bend, and stay whole"*)
- as a transitive act, chiefly in the commentaries → **keep whole** (全其身 → *"keep their body whole"*)
- as a bare predicate → **whole**
- 曲 → **bend** / **bent**, never *yield*

**Never** *complete*, *perfect*, *flawless*, or any verb that implies the thing was broken first.

### The tension, left open

**Why does a word this load-bearing appear in one chapter and nowhere else?**

全 is the whole argument of Chapter 22 — it opens the poem, it is quoted back, it closes the poem. And in the other eighty chapters, silence. So does 曲. A vocabulary that central ought to recur, and it does not.

**The chapter may be telling us why.** It marks the line as borrowed: 古之所謂「曲則全」者 — *"what the ancients called 'bend, then whole'."* If Chapter 22 is commentary on an older proverb, then **the 曲/全 vocabulary arrived with the quotation** and was never Laozi's own. That would explain the distribution exactly, and it would make this chapter a rare thing in the book: not a teaching, but a defence of somebody else's.

It also leaves a second question genuinely unanswered. **Whole *what*?** 河上公 supplies 身 (*shēn* — the body) and reads the closing line as returning that body to one's parents unharmed — the filial register of his self-cultivation reading, and a Han import this edition declines. The text itself never says. It writes 全, bare, three times, and lets the reader carry it.

We keep it bare too.

## 仁 (Rén) — Humaneness

*Say "run," rising, with the tongue curled back. Eight lines across five chapters, and it is the first thing chapter 5 says sky and earth are not.*

**Locked: 仁 → "humaneness."** *(Not "benevolence," not "charity," not "goodwill.")*

**Benevolence** is the word this character wears in nearly every English Tao Te Ching, and it is a translation of the Latin, not of the Chinese. *Bene-volens* is a **disposition of the will**: to wish well. It names something happening inside one person.

仁 names something happening **between two**. The graph says so, and so does the earliest dictionary.

The cost of the Latin word is not vagueness. It is that the book's argument stops making sense. Ch 5 says 天地不仁 — and if 仁 is well-wishing, the line reads as cosmic indifference, a universe that does not care. That is not what either classical commentator thought it said, and it is not what the chapter goes on to do.

### The graph

**仁 is 人 (*rén* — a person) beside 二 (*èr* — two).** Two people, and the relation between them. The *Shuowen Jiezi* (c. 100 CE) glosses it in one word:

> 仁，親也。从人从二
> *"仁 is 親 (qīn — kinship, closeness). From 人 and from 二."*

Not a feeling one person has. **A closeness that exists only in the space between two.** Bronze forms write it with 人 over 二 or with 千 over 心; the constant is the pair.

**Humaneness** keeps 人 audible in the English, which is exactly what the character does. That is the whole argument for it, and it is enough.

### What the commentators actually say, and it rescues ch 5

The hardest line in the book for this character is 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗 — *"sky and earth are not 仁; they treat the countless things as straw dogs."* A 芻狗 (*chú gǒu*) is a dog plaited out of straw for a sacrifice: dressed and honoured through the ceremony, thrown away after.

Read with *benevolence*, that is a cold universe. **Neither commentator reads it that way.**

王弼 says what 仁 would require:

> 仁者必造立施化，有恩有為
> *"the 仁 one must construct and impose transformation; there is 恩 (ēn — favour, obligation) and there is 為 (wéi — doing)."*

So 不仁 is not the absence of care. It is the absence of **management with a debt attached** — 恩, the favour that expects to be remembered.

河上公 is more explicit still, and says the quiet part:

> 天施地化，不以仁恩，任自然也
> *"sky bestows and earth transforms, not by 仁恩 (humane favour), but by leaving things to be of themselves."*

> 聖人愛養萬民，不以仁恩，法天地行自然
> *"the sage **loves and rears** the people — not by humane favour, but modelling sky and earth in acting so of themselves."*

**愛養 — loves and rears.** The sage in ch 5 is not indifferent. The straw dog is not contempt; it is 不貴望其報也, *"expecting no repayment."* 仁 is care that keeps accounts, and the chapter is refusing the accounts, not the care.

### Why the book attacks it, and how little that is about goodness

仁 is never attacked alone. It arrives bonded to 義 (*yì* — duty) as 仁義, the Confucian virtue-pair, and always at the moment something else has already failed:

> 大道廢，有仁義
> *ch 18 — "the great Tao is discarded, and there is humaneness and duty"*

> 失德而後仁，失仁而後義
> *ch 38 — "integrity lost, then humaneness; humaneness lost, then duty"*

河上公 draws the consequence exactly: 大道之時，家有孝子，戶有忠信，**仁義不見也** — *"in the time of the great Tao, every family had devoted children and every household loyalty and trust, and humaneness and duty **were not visible**."* Not absent. **Invisible**, because nothing had gone wrong that would make anyone name them.

**王弼 goes further and refuses to call them evils at all.** Glossing ch 19's three severed pairs:

> 聖智，才之善也；仁義，人之善也；巧利，用之善也
> *"sagehood and knowing are the best of talent; humaneness and duty are the best of persons; cunning and profit are the best of use."*

Three pairs of **goods**, said to be insufficient as 文 (*wén* — cultural form). The chapter is not an attack on kindness. It is a claim that the named virtues arrive too late.

**And the oldest witness does not make the attack at all.** At Guodian (~300 BCE) the passage corresponding to ch 19 carries neither 仁 nor 義 nor 聖; the pairs severed there are different ones. See `notes/manuscript.md` · Ch 19 and `sources/variants.yaml`.

### Never

**benevolence.** A Latin will-word for a Chinese relation-word, and the standard English carries a whole missionary lexicon behind it — Legge's Tao Te Ching came out of the London Missionary Society, and this is one of the words that came with him.

**charity · goodwill.** Both are almsgiving words: they run in one direction, from the one who has to the one who lacks. 仁 runs between two who are simply near each other.

**kindness and love are not forbidden here, because they are not free** — 慈 (*cí* — tenderness) holds that ground and shares two chapters with this character. See `glossary/ci-慈.md`.

### What stays open

**仁 is the only word in this book that the text attacks and the commentators defend.** 王弼 calls it 人之善也, the best of what a person can be, in the middle of glossing a chapter that says to cut it off. 河上公 says it becomes invisible when things go well, which is praise disguised as dismissal.

So the English has to be sayable in two tones — as the thing that arrives when the Tao has already been discarded, and as the thing a decent person is. *Humaneness* manages it, barely, and mostly because it is flat enough not to editorialise. **Whether flatness is the right answer to a word this warm is not settled**, and ch 8's 與善仁 is where it presses hardest: there 仁 is not a symptom of decline but one of seven things water is good at.

## 柔 (Róu) — Soft

*Say "roe," rising. Eleven lines across seven chapters.*

**Locked: 柔 → "soft."** *(Not "supple," "pliant," "flexible," "gentle" or "tender," which is 慈's. Not "yielding" either, which is 弱's, but that ruling no check can hold. See the last section but one.)*

*剛 (gāng — unbending), its opposite, stands only twice in the book and is covered here.*

The book never praises 柔 for being kind. It praises it for **winning**. The soft and yielding **overcome** the unbending and strong (36). The softest thing in the world **gallops through** the hardest (43). Holding to the soft is called **strong** (52). The soft and yielding are **followers of life** (76). Nothing is softer than water, and nothing does better against the hard (78). Every line is about what happens when soft meets hard, and in every line soft is still there at the end.

### The graph: wood that bends and comes back

> 柔，**木曲直也**。从木矛聲。
> *"柔 is wood bending and straightening. From 木 (mù — wood), with 矛 (máo — a spear) for the sound."* — 說文解字

段玉裁 (*Duàn Yùcái*) spells out what the four characters mean: 凡木曲者可直，直者可曲，曰柔, *"any wood that, when bent, can be made straight, and when straight, can be bent, is called 柔."* The spear on top gives only the sound, so the meaning is all in the 木 (*mù* — wood) beneath.

**The phrase is older than the dictionary.** The 尚書 (*Shàngshū*)'s 洪範 (*Hóng Fàn*), the oldest list of the five phases, gives each its nature. Water soaks down, fire flames up, and 木曰曲直, *"wood is called bending-and-straightening."* The commentary attributed to 孔安國 (*Kǒng Ānguó*) glosses it 木可以揉曲直, *"wood can be 揉 into bent or straight."* 揉 (*róu*) is the same word with a hand added, and it belongs to the woodworker. In the 周易 (*Zhōu Yì*)'s 繫辭 (*Xì Cí*), the ancient sages 揉木為耒, *"bent wood to make the plough handle."* In the 考工記 (*Kǎogōng Jì*), the wheelwright's 揉輻必齊, *"the spokes he bends must match,"* which 鄭玄 (*Zhèng Xuán*) explains as working the wood over fire.

So the picture behind 柔 is a carpenter's: a length of green or heated wood taking a curve without splitting. It passes the pointing test. Laozi could have pointed at a plough handle.

**The word is older than the graph.** The 柔-and-矛 form is not known from the oracle bones. The word is already in Western Zhou bronze, in the formula 柔遠能邇, *"to 柔 the far and make able the near"*, cast on the 大克鼎 (*Dà Kè dǐng*) and the 番生簋 (*Pān Shēng guǐ*) lid. The 詩經 (*Shījīng*) and the 尚書 repeat it, and the 毛 (*Máo*) commentary glosses it 柔，安也, *"柔 is to settle."* That is the word as a verb, *to make soft*: to settle a distant people the way a woodworker settles a curve into wood. Laozi never uses it that way. In this book 柔 is always a quality and never takes an object.

### What the book does with it

**Water.** 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者莫之能勝, *"In all the world nothing is softer and more yielding than water, yet at attacking the hard and the strong nothing overcomes it"* (78). On ch 43, 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) names the two ends of the scale: 至柔者水，至堅金石。水能貫堅入剛，无所不通, *"the softest is water, the hardest metal and stone. Water can pierce the hard and enter the unbending; there is nowhere it does not get through."*

**The tongue.** On ch 78's 柔之勝剛, *"the soft overcomes the unbending,"* 河上公 answers with the body: 舌柔齒剛，齒先舌亡, *"the tongue is soft, the teeth are unbending; the teeth go first."*

**The infant.** 骨弱筋柔而握固, *"their bones are yielding and their muscles soft, yet their grip is firm"* (55). 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) says the softness is the reason for the grip: 以柔弱之故，故握能周固, *"because it is soft and yielding, its grip can close all the way round and hold."* A hard hand cannot wrap around a thing. Ch 10 asks for the same body from inside: 專氣致柔，能如嬰兒乎, *"gathering the breath to softness, can you be like an infant?"* 王弼 there: 致至柔之和, *"reaching the harmony of the utmost softness."*

**What is alive.** 人之生也柔弱，其死也堅強。萬物草木之生也柔脆，其死也枯槁, *"In life a person is soft and yielding; in death, hard and strong. In life the countless things, the grasses and trees, are soft and fragile; in death, withered and dry"* (76). Rigor mortis and dry stalks are the argument. Softness is how you tell that something is alive.

**The paradox.** 守柔曰強, *"holding to the soft is called strong"* (52). 王弼 states it in two short clauses: 守強不強，守柔乃強也, *"holding to the strong is not strong; holding to the soft is truly strong."*

**Why it wins.** 王弼 on ch 43 gives the mechanism, and it is the 說文's wood again: 至柔不可折, *"the utmost soft cannot be snapped."* What bends does not break. Ch 76 states the other side, in our base text: 木強則折, *"a strong tree snaps."*

### 柔 and 剛: bending against not bending

剛 (*gāng*) appears twice, both times opposite 柔: 柔弱勝剛強 (36) and 柔之勝剛 (78).

> 剛，彊斷也。从刀岡聲。
> *"剛 is strong enough to cut. From 刀 (dāo — a knife), with 岡 (gāng — a ridge) for the sound."* — 說文解字

**剛 is *unbending*, not *hard*, and a third character is why.** 堅 (*jiān*) also wants *hard*: 至堅 (43), 堅強 (76, twice), 攻堅強 (78). Ch 78 holds both a few lines apart, *"attacking **the hard** and the strong"* for 堅 and *"the soft overcomes **the unbending**"* for 剛. 說文 defines each by the other's neighbour, 堅，剛也 (*"堅 is 剛"*). 堅 is solid hardness, and it keeps *hard*, in twice the lines. 剛 is the edge that will not give, and *unbending* is exactly what 說文's 柔 is not. **The book's contest is bending against not bending, and the pair holds the 說文's picture between them:** 柔 is the wood that bends, 剛 the blade that will not. *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-14.)*

**Ch 78 needs four English words, not two:** 弱之勝強，柔之勝剛, *"the yielding overcomes the strong; the soft overcomes the unbending."* 柔 **soft** · 剛 **unbending** · 弱 (*ruò*) **yielding** · 強 (*qiáng*) **strong**. Where 柔 and 弱 stand together, 柔 comes first every time (36, 76 three times, 78), and the English keeps the order: *the soft and yielding*. The argument for keeping the two apart is in the 弱 entry.

**The I Ching holds the same pair the other way.** Its commentaries, the Wings, make 剛柔 (*gāng róu*) their central pair, with 剛 nearly a hundred times and 柔 nearly seventy, and treat the two as equal: each is right in its own place, and a 剛 line where 剛 belongs is correct. Laozi has 剛 twice, never writes 剛柔 as a compound, and both times takes the side of 柔. The I Ching's 文言 (*Wényán*) has the same superlative as ch 43, 坤至柔而動也剛, *"坤 (kūn — earth, the carrying hexagram) is soft to the utmost, yet in moving it is unbending."* The I Ching's usual English for the pair is *firm / yielding*, and this book can use neither word: *firm* is 固's (55, 59, 67) and *yielding* is 弱's.

### Why "soft"

- **It is the book's own images.** Water, a tongue, an infant's grip, new grass are all soft. None of them is *supple*.
- **It is English's own opposite to hard.** Ch 43's 至柔 against 至堅 is *the softest thing* against *the hardest*, and no other English pair is that plain.
- **It describes and does not praise.** *Soft* is how a thing meets pressure, whether that is a virtue or not. The book supplies the verdict itself (勝, 強, 生之徒), so the word must not supply one first.
- **The bending is carried by the pair.** The 說文's wood that bends and straightens is held in the seam between *soft* and *unbending*, which is where the book puts it.

### What is set aside, and why

**"supple," "pliant," "pliable," "flexible"** are the 說文's picture taken literally, and the strongest rivals. They name a trained or worked capacity, a gymnast's spine or a cane under the woodworker's hand, and they fail on the book's central image: water is not supple. They also cost ch 43 its plain opposites, since *the most supple thing gallops through the hardest* sets two unrelated scales against each other.

**"gentle"** and **"gentleness"** turn a material quality into a manner of conduct, and a manner that English praises. 河上公 reads 柔 that way more than once: 和柔謙讓, *"harmonious, soft, humble, deferring"* (on ch 3), and 柔順, *"soft and compliant"* (on ch 10). That is a commentator's ethics, which is evidence for a reading and not a rendering. The verse lines are about water and bones.

**"weak"** names a lack. It was removed from 弱 for that reason, and it would bring the same deficiency back in through 柔.

**"yielding"** is 弱's. Ch 78 sets the two in separate clauses.

**"tender"** is 慈's (*cí*, *tenderness*, the first of ch 67's three treasures). 慈 shares no chapter with 柔, so the build can hold this one.

### The working register

柔 never takes an object in this book. It describes a state, or names the thing in that state.

| Chinese | English | form |
|---|---|---|
| 骨弱筋柔 (55) · 人之生也柔弱 (76) · 草木之生也柔脆 (76, *soft and fragile*) | *soft* | predicate |
| 守柔 (52) · 柔弱勝剛強 (36) · 柔之勝剛 (78) · 柔弱者生之徒 · 柔弱處上 (76) | *the soft* | a quality named as a thing |
| 天下之至柔 (43) | *the softest thing in the world* | 至 (zhì — utmost), superlative |
| 莫柔弱於水 (78) | *nothing softer and more yielding than water* | comparative |
| 專氣致柔 (10) | *gathering the breath to softness* | the end point of 致 (zhì — to bring to the utmost) |

### What no rule can enforce

**"yielding" is ruled out for 柔 and is not on its `forbidden:` list, because it cannot be.** 弱 stands beside 柔 in chapters 36, 55, 76 and 78 and prints *yielding* in every one of them.

**"hard" is ruled out for 剛 and cannot be forbidden either.** A `covers:` character carries a rendering but no `forbidden:` list, and 堅, whose English *hard* is, stands in ch 43, 76 and 78. The reader holds this one: in ch 78, *hard* is 堅's and *unbending* is 剛's. See `process/principles/ruling-and-enforcement-are-two-facts.md`.

### Left open

**English *soft* has idioms that point the wrong way.** *Gone soft*, *soft-headed*, *soft on crime*: as a judgement of a person, English *soft* means lacking, which is exactly why 弱 lost *weak*. *Soft* survives here because its first sense is material, to the touch, and the book's images keep it there: water, tongue, sinew, grass. But ch 78 turns from water to whoever takes on the filth of the state, and a reader who hears *soft* as a judgement of character will hear the deficiency there. No English word for 柔 avoids this. *Supple* and *gentle* avoid it only by losing the image.

**The return.** 說文's wood bends **and straightens**. Its 柔 is not only something that gives way under pressure but something that comes back afterwards, and English *soft* does not say that. Bending and coming back is the motion of 反 (*fǎn*) and 復 (*fù*), *return*, which ch 40 calls the movement of the Tao. Whether the book hears that in 柔 is a reason to look and not a reading (`process/principles/distribution-locates.md`).

**The verb.** The oldest use of the word is political: 柔遠, *to settle the far*, to bring distant peoples round the way wood is brought round. This book never uses 柔 as a verb, but ch 78 does turn from water to the ruler of the state in the same breath. The verse keeps 柔 a quality, and the political sense stays in the background.
entries.shuowen: Wood that bends and straightens. From 木 (mù — wood), with 矛 (máo — a spear) for sound.
