## 弱 (Ruò) — Yielding

*Say "rwaw," falling. Ten lines across six chapters, paired throughout with 柔 (róu — soft).*

**Locked: 弱 → "yielding" — and *weaken* only where it takes an object.** *(Not "frail," not "feeble," not "feebleness," not "powerless.")*

**Weak** is the dictionary's first word for 弱, and it is a deficiency word in English. It names an absence — of force, of health, of resolve. Put it in the Tao Te Ching and the book acquires a doctrine it does not hold: that the way to prevail is to *lack* something.

That is not what the character does, and it is not what any classical reader thought it did.

### The graph

弱 is **two 弓** (*gōng* — a bow) side by side, with **彡** (*shān* — three fine strokes, the mark of hair or fine detail). A bow is a thing defined by bending: it is useful *because* it gives, and a bow that will not bend is firewood. The doubling and the fine strokes mark the quality as characteristic rather than incidental.

Nothing in the graph is about lacking. It is about **behaviour under load**.

### What the commentators actually say

The three glosses in this repository are unanimous, and none of them reads deficiency.

**王弼 on ch 40** (弱者道之用 — *"弱 is the Tao's use"*):

> 柔弱同通不可窮極
> *"Soft and 弱 alike **pass through**; they cannot be exhausted."*

通 (*tōng*) is to penetrate, to get through, to be unobstructed. This is a gloss about **capacity**, and about inexhaustibility — the opposite of the thing "weak" names.

**河上公 on ch 78**, where the text splits the compound into two clauses and he answers each with an image:

> 弱之勝強 — 水能滅火
> *"The 弱 overcomes the strong — water can put out fire."*
> 柔之勝剛 — 舌柔齒剛，齒先舌亡
> *"The soft overcomes the hard — the tongue is soft, the teeth are hard; the teeth go first."*

**河上公 on ch 36** (柔弱勝剛強):

> 柔弱者久長，剛強者先亡也
> *"The 柔弱 endure long; the hard and strong perish first."*

Water and a tongue are not weak. They are things that do not resist, and therefore do not break, and therefore are still there afterwards. **Yielding** is the English for that.

### The one exception, and it is grammatical

Two of the ten lines use 弱 **transitively, with an object**, where it means *to make weak* — a causative:

- **ch 3** 弱其志，強其骨 — *weaken their ambition, strengthen their bones*
- **ch 36** 將欲弱之，必固強之 — *wanting to weaken it, first strengthen it*

*Yielding* is a stance and cannot take an object. These stay **weaken**. The split is not a matter of taste: it is marked in the Chinese by the presence of an object, so it can be checked. Everywhere 弱 describes a state or a quality — ch 40, 55, 76, 78, and 36's own 柔弱勝剛強 — it reads **yielding**.

### 柔 and 弱 are two words, and ch 78 proves it

The compound 柔弱 is so common that it is tempting to treat the halves as one idea. **Ch 78 refuses:**

> 弱之勝強，柔之勝剛
> *"The yielding overcomes the strong; the soft overcomes the unbending."*

Two clauses, two pairs, no overlap. That line is the constraint every rendering has to satisfy, and it needs four distinct English words:

| | |
|---|---|
| 柔 (*róu*) | **soft** |
| 剛 (*gāng*) | **unbending** |
| 弱 (*ruò*) | **yielding** |
| 強 (*qiáng*) | **strong** |

So 柔 keeps **soft** and does not get *yielding*, which it had borrowed in ch 52 (守柔曰強) before this entry existed.

**剛 (*gāng*) is *unbending*, not *hard*,** because 堅 (*jiān*) holds *hard* a few lines away in the same chapter. The case is made in the 柔 entry, `rou-柔.md`, with the rest of 柔's.

### Why this matters for ch 76

Chapter 76 works by spending the **admiring** word on a corpse: 堅強 (*jiān qiáng* — hard and strong) is rigor mortis, and four lines later it is an army. That ambush is on 強 alone. An earlier draft of this entry's reasoning claimed the chapter *also* provokes by calling the living state weak — it does not, and translating to protect that invented second provocation is what put **weak** into the verse. Caught by Shalom, 2026-08-26.

### Renders

- **yielding** — ch 36 (柔弱勝剛強), 40, 55, 76, 78
- **weaken** — ch 3, 36 (將欲弱之), where the character takes an object

### Never

**frail · feeble · powerless.** All three name a lack. 弱 names a response.

Also never let 柔 take *yielding* — see the four-word table above. That ruling is held by the reader, not the build; `rou-柔.md` says why.
entries.render: yielding — and *weaken* only where it takes an object

## 善 (Shàn) — Masterful

*Say "shahn," fourth tone, falling. Forty-five lines in eighteen chapters — one of the largest words in the book, and the one that decides whether Laozi reads as a moralist.*

**Locked: 善 → "masterful," or "masterful at," wherever it names skill. "Good" only where the text is naming *good* as a category — which it does in order to criticize it.**

Render 善 as *good* throughout, as the English tradition does, and you produce a Laozi who divides people into the good and the bad, prizes goodness, and counsels being nice to the wicked. Almost none of that is in the Chinese. **Roughly thirty of the forty-five occurrences mean skilled at something**, and where the word *is* used as a moral category, the book's move is to warn you against the category.

### The character is a sheep, and it has two siblings

The *Shuowen Jiezi* gives the old form 譱 and glosses it: 吉也。从誩，从羊。**此與義、美同意** — *"auspicious; from 誩 and 羊; this has the same sense as 義 and 美."*

- **羊** (*yáng*) — a sheep, seen head-on: the horns, the face. The sacrificial animal.
- **誩** (*jìng*) — two 言 (*yán* — speech): two people speaking in turn, weighing a matter.

And the Shuowen's own cross-reference is the finding: **善 belongs to a family of three, and all three wear the sheep.**

| | Built from | Became |
|---|---|---|
| **美** (*měi*) | 羊 over 大 (a big person) — a large sheep | **beauty** |
| **義** (*yì*) | 羊 over 我 (a weapon, then *I*) | **duty, right conduct** |
| **善** (*shàn*) | 羊 over speech | **good** |

Its oldest sense survives in the character 膳 (*shàn* — the prepared dish, the meat offering), which is 善 with the flesh radical added back. **So 善 begins as *fit for the altar*: well-made, sound, up to standard, good of its kind.** Not morally good — **good at being what it is.**

That is precisely the sense Laozi uses, over and over.

### What the text actually does with it

**Thirty occurrences are 善 + a verb — skilled at doing something**, and they are the book's most concrete lines:

> Ch 27 · 善行無轍跡，善言無瑕謫，善數不用籌策，善閉無關楗而不可開，善結無繩約而不可解
> *masterful travelling leaves no tracks · masterful speech is flawless · masterful reckoning uses no counting rods · masterful shutting uses no bolts, yet cannot be opened · masterful tying uses no rope, yet cannot be untied*

A traveller, a speaker, an accountant, a locksmith, a knot-tier. **Five trades in five lines.** **Chapter 8 is the showcase: nine occurrences in thirteen lines**, more concentrated than anywhere else in the book — 上善, 善利, then the seven couplets 善地, 善淵, 善仁, 善信, 善治, 善能, 善時: masterful at ground, at depth, at giving, at speech, at governing, at what can be done, at timing. Chapter 68 gives four: the masterful officer is not martial, the masterful fighter does not rage, the masterful conqueror does not engage, the masterful user of people puts themselves below. Chapter 73 gives three more of the Tao itself: 不爭而**善**勝，不言而**善**應 — *does not contend yet masterfully prevails; does not speak yet masterfully answers.*

**None of that is ethics. All of it is craft.**

### Where 善 *is* moral, the book is attacking the category

Six occurrences use 善 as an abstract quality — and in the most important of them, Laozi is not recommending it. He is pointing at what happens when it becomes a name.

> Ch 2 · 天下皆知**美**之為美，斯惡已；皆知**善**之為善，斯不善已。
> *"When all the world knows beauty as beauty, ugliness arises; when all know good as good, the not-good arises."*

**He puts the two sheep-words side by side** — 美 and 善, beauty and good, the pair the *Shuowen* says share a sense — and shows both curdling at the moment they are made into categories. The not-good is not a pre-existing evil the good opposes. It is **manufactured by the act of naming the good.**

Chapter 58 finishes the thought: 正復為奇，**善**復為妖 — *the straight turns crooked, the good turns monstrous.* And Chapter 20 sets 善 against 惡 (*è* — bad) only to ask 相去若何, *what is the distance between them?*

So the book's two uses of 善 are not in tension. **They are one argument: be good at things, and be wary of Goodness.**

### Why this decides three chapters

Chapters 27, 49 and 62 make one claim in three vocabularies — nobody gets thrown away (see the Thread in `notes/reading.md`) — and **the rendering of 善 decides what kind of claim it is.**

Held as *good* and *bad*, Chapter 62 becomes a doctrine of grace: the Tao shelters sinners, and 罪 (*zuì* — **crime**) three lines later completes the gospel. Held as **masterful** and **unmasterful**, it becomes an argument about **use**:

> Ch 27 · 故善人者，不善人之師；不善人者，善人之**資**。
> *"So the masterful are the teacher of the unmasterful, and the unmasterful are the masterful's **資** (zī — raw material, working stock)."*

That is not mercy. It is a claim that **nobody is discarded because nobody is waste** — which is why the chapter puts it beside a locksmith and a knot-tier, and why 不貴其師，不愛其資 (*failing to value the teacher or love the raw material*) is called 大迷, great confusion.

### What is set aside

**"Virtuous," "righteous," "saintly."** Each turns a sheep fit for the altar into a person fit for heaven. 義 (*yì* — duty) is a different character and gets its own treatment; **benevolent** belongs to 仁 (*rén* — humaneness), which Chapter 8's 與善仁 uses in the same line as 善 and must stay distinguishable from it.

**"Good" used everywhere.** Not forbidden — it is right in Chapters 2, 20 and 58, where the category is the subject. But applied to 善行 or 善結 it flattens a locksmith into a saint.

**"Skilful" and "expert."** Accurate and bloodless. *Masterful* holds the register the trades give it, and it is what makes 善人 / 不善人 read as **the adept and the inept** rather than the righteous and the wicked.

### Working register

| The grammar | Where | Render |
|---|---|---|
| 善 + verb — skilled at | 8, 15, 27, 30, 41, 50, 54, 65, 66, 68, 73 | **masterful at** |
| 善人 / 不善人 — the kind of person | 27, 49, 62 | **the masterful / the unmasterful** |
| 善 as the named category | 2, 20, 58 | **good** — because the category is the target |
| 上善 — the superlative | 8 | **the most masterful** (settled 2026-09-02, below) |
| 善 as a verb, "to reckon as 善" | 49 | **count as masterful** |

### Chapter 49 — decided, and it follows Wang Bi

*(settled 2026-08-14.)* 善者，吾善之；不善者，吾亦善之 uses 善 four times in two lines — twice for the kind of person, twice as a **verb**, *to reckon as 善*. It now reads **"The masterful, I count as masterful; the unmasterful, I count as masterful too."**

**Wang Bi reads the chapter in Chapter 27's own vocabulary**, which is what decided it. His gloss on the couplet is 各**因**其**用**，則善不失也 — *"go along with each according to their **use**, and then 善 is not lost."* His gloss on the tag 德善 is three characters — **無棄人也**, *"there are no discarded people"* — which is Chapter 27's own line, 故無棄人, quoted here. And he closes the chapter with 能者與之，**資**者取之, *"those with ability, go along with; those who are **raw material**, take them up"* — 資 (*zī*) being the exact character Chapter 27 gives the unmasterful.

**Heshang Gong reads it morally** and it stays on the record: 百姓雖有不善者，聖人化之使善也 — *"though some of the people are not good, the sage transforms them and makes them good."*

**The English cost, named.** *Count as masterful* is heavier in the mouth than *am good to*. What it buys is the actual claim: 善之 is **appraisal**, not kindness. The sage is not being nice to the incompetent — they are **refusing to run the grading**, which is the same move as 何棄之有 (62) and 無棄人 (27), and a sharper thing to say.

**What it commits.** Ch 79 (常與善人) and Ch 81 (善者不辯，辯者不善) are undrafted and now inherit this: *"the masterful do not argue; arguers are not masterful."* Stranger than *"the good do not argue,"* and consistent with the rest.

### Chapter 8 — decided 2026-09-02, and it settles the grammar for the whole entry

**上善若水 now reads "The most masterful are like water."** *(Shalom's call.)* 上 (*shàng* — highest) is settled at ch 38, where 上德 / 上仁 / 上義 / 上禮 all read *the highest*, so *"supreme"* was the outlier. **The category reading is unavailable here**: *good* is reserved for chapters 2, 20 and 58, where the book attacks the category, and using it at ch 8 would make this chapter endorse what ch 2 dismantles. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads 上善 as a **person** — 上善之人如水之性, *"the person of the highest 善 is like the nature of water"* — which is this entry's own 善人 (*shàn rén* — the masterful). **The cost:** the plural person decides something the Chinese leaves open, since 上善 could be the quality itself. ***The highest excellence*** was rejected as bloodless and as Legge's phrase; ***true mastery*** was rejected because 真 (*zhēn* — genuine) is a live character in this book (21, 41, 54) and 上 is a graded rank word whose middle rung is printed at ch 41 (上士/中士/下士).

**善 governs a verb — eighteen times out of eighteen, and this is the proof the entry has been asserting without evidence.** The *Working register* table above claims a "善 + verb" grammar. Ch 8 is the only place in the book where the claim could fail, because its seven couplets are the only 善 + X where X could pass for a noun, and X善Y admits both parses in classical Chinese: 善 as a verb taking Y (*masterful **at** Y*), or 善 as an adjective modifying Y (*masterful Y*).

Everywhere else, X is a verb:

> 善行 *travel* · 善言 *speak* · 善計 *reckon* · 善閉 *shut* · 善結 *tie* (27) · 善救 *rescue* ×2 (27) · 善為 *handle* (15, 65) · 善貸 *give* (41) · 善攝 *nurture* (50) · 善建 *establish* · 善抱 *embrace* (54) · 善下 *go below* (66) · 善戰 *fight* · 善勝 *overcome* ×2 (68, 73) · 善用 *use* (68) · 善應 *respond* · 善謀 *plan* (73)

**Eighteen verbs, zero nouns.** And ch 8 sets the pattern inside its own chapter, four lines above the stanza: 水善**利**萬物, where 利 (*lì* — to benefit) is unambiguously verbal. The adjectival parse fails on its own terms as well — it yields *masterful order*, *masterful ability*, *masterful timing*, which read, and *masterful ground*, *masterful depth*, *masterful humaneness*, *masterful trust*, which do not. **A reading that survives three of seven loses to one that survives all seven.**

The seven now run in one shape: *In settling, masterful at ground. In the heart, masterful at depth. In giving, masterful at humaneness. In speech, masterful at trust. In governing, masterful at order. In affairs, masterful at what can be done. In moving, masterful at timing.*

**能 (*néng* — able) took *what can be done* rather than *ability***, because 能 has 32 lines in the book and 31 are the plain modal *can*; ch 8's is the only noun. Building the English out of *can* keeps it in the book's own vocabulary and removes the abstract-noun stack beside *masterful*. The cost is a slight drift of the capacity from the agent to the situation.

### What stays open


**淵 (*yuān* — a deep pool), inside ch 8's stanza, is not yet settled** and reads three ways across the book: *fathomless* (4), *depth* (8), *the deep abyss* (36). 說文解字 makes it banked water — 回水也…左右，岸也, *"swirling water… left and right are the banks"* — so *limitless*, which stood at ch 8 until 2026-09-02, was precisely backwards. Tracked as `WORKLIST.md` T2-24; not this entry's term, but it sits inside this entry's showcase chapter.
entries.render: masterful / masterful at · the masterful & the unmasterful (of people) · good (only where the text names the category)

## 身 (Shēn) — The Body

*Say "shen," level and flat. Twenty lines across nine chapters — and it went without an entry longer than almost any word this size, because it looked too ordinary to need one.*

**Locked: 身 → "body."** *(Never "spirit," never "soul." Never "self" either — but that one is a ruling no check can hold, and it is the rendering this character actually attracts, so it has a section of its own below.)*

*In the two lifespan compounds 終身 and 没身 the character marks the span of a life — "to the end of your days."*

### The graph: a person with the belly marked

> 身，**躳**也。象人之身。从人𠂆聲。
> *"身 is 躬 (gōng — the trunk). It depicts a person's 身. From 人 (rén — a person), with 𠂆 as the sound."* — 說文解字

The oracle-bone graph is a person drawn in profile with **the abdomen swollen**, and that swelling is the entire difference between this character and 人, which is the same profile drawn plain. 說文's phonetic analysis is the part to set aside — 段玉裁 (*Duàn Yùcái*), whose 說文解字注 is the standard commentary on the dictionary, calls the 从人𠂆聲 reading an error. It is a pictograph. Nothing in it was borrowed for sound.

And the oldest sense the word is attested in is **pregnancy**. The 詩經 (*Shī Jīng* — the Book of Odes) has it in 大明, on the mother of the Zhou dynasty's founding king:

> 大任**有身**，生此文王
> *"Da Ren **had 身**, and bore this King Wen."*

有身 — *to have a 身* — was how you said a woman was carrying. The sense later migrated to 孕 (*yùn* — pregnant), a character coined to take it back, and 身 and 孕 are cognate.

*A calibration, so the entry stays honest: we do not claim Laozi heard pregnancy in the word. By the fourth century BCE 身 was the ordinary word for a body, and 孕 had long since taken the narrower job.*

What survives the migration is the shape of the thing. **身 is not a neutral word for a person. It is a person seen as something that carries, and can be burdened.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reaches for exactly that at chapter 9 — 財多**累身**, *"much wealth burdens the 身"* — and again at 44, 財利不**累身**. And chapter 13's 為吾**有身** is, character for character, the Odes' idiom: *because I have a 身*. The chapter's claim is that having one is how you come to be carrying 大患 (*dà huàn* — great trouble).

### The lived person, and why the word is still "body"

身 is the physical, finite person — but a physical person as this tradition understands one, which is not a body with a mind bolted on. Chapter 54's 修之於身 (*cultivate it in the 身*) does not ask whether the practice is somatic or psychological, because the question has not been invented yet. 河上公 glosses the line:

> 修道於身，**愛氣養神**，益壽延年
> *"Cultivate the Tao in the 身: cherish the 氣 (qì — breath), nourish the 神 (shén — spirit), increase longevity and extend the years."*

Read that carefully, because it is not a merger. The 身 is the **site**; 氣 and 神 are what is nourished **in** it. He runs the same structure as a political analogy right through the book — 治身 (*governing the body*) set beside 治國 (*governing the state*), at 9, 26 and 44 — and at 26 he makes the dependency explicit: **治身不重則失神**, *"govern the 身 without weight, and you lose the 神."*

This is why the English is a plain word rather than a careful one. *The lived person*, *the embodied self*, *the psychosomatic whole* — each of these describes 身 accurately and none of them can go in a verse line. They are labels for the concept, and a label is not a rendering. English *body* is also, of the two obvious candidates, **the less dualist**: modern *self* is almost entirely interior, the mind's side of the very split this tradition does not make, while *body* is at least the whole organism. Context carries the rest. No reader takes *"cultivate this in your body"* for calisthenics.

### What 身 is weighed against

Across the nine chapters, 身 is weighed against 名 (*míng* — reputation) and 貨 (*huò* — goods) at chapter 44, against 功 (*gōng* — merit and office) at chapter 9, and against 大患 (*dà huàn* — great trouble) at chapter 13. **The class is everything a person could acquire — and 天下 (*tiān xià* — all under the sky, the world) is simply the maximum of that class.**

| chapter | set against | the line |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | 功 — merit, and the post it earns | 功遂**身**退 — *the work done, the body withdraws* |
| 13 | 大患 — great trouble | 為吾有**身** — *because I have a body* |
| 13 | 天下 — the world, twice | 貴以**身**為天下 · 愛以**身**為天下 |
| 26 | 天下 — the world | 而以**身**輕天下 — *and make their body light in the world* |
| 44 | 名 — reputation | 名與**身**孰親 — *your name or your body, which is dearer* |
| 44 | 貨 — goods | **身**與貨孰多 — *your body or goods, which is worth more* |
| 54 | 天下 — the world, as the far end of a ladder | 修之於**身** … 修之於天下 |

The three chapters that put 身 and 天下 in **one line** — 13, 26 and 54 — are the axis at full scale, and the answer is the same every time: the body is the thing that is not worth trading, and the world is what you are offered for it. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) puts the exchange in one clause at 44: 得多利而**亡其身**，何者為病也 — *"to gain much profit and lose your body — which of these is the affliction?"*

Chapter 54 is the same axis stretched into a ladder — 身 → 家 (*jiā* — family) → 鄉 (*xiāng* — community) → 國 (*guó* — state) → 天下 — with the body as the first rung and the world as the last. The chapter's second stanza walks the ladder back down, and its first step, 以身觀身, is 河上公's most concrete gloss in the chapter: 以修道之身觀不修道之身，孰亡孰存也 — *"observe the body that has cultivated the Tao against the body that has not: which perishes and which survives?"*

### Chapter 7, where the body is the whole point

The clearest case for the plain word is the chapter that most tempts you away from it. Chapter 7 opens on 天長地久 — *the sky is long, the earth enduring* — and asks why:

> 以其不自生，故能**長生**。是以聖人後其**身**而**身**先，外其**身**而**身**存。
> *"Because they do not live for themselves, therefore they can **live long**. So the sage puts their **body** last, and their **body** comes first; puts their **body** outside, and their **body** survives."*

存 (*cún* — to remain in existence) answers 長生 (*cháng shēng* — long life) directly, and 身 stands four times in eleven characters. 河上公 reads it with no metaphor whatever: 百姓愛之如父母…故**身常存**, *"the people love them as parents… therefore their body constantly survives."* The chapter is an argument that the one who does not grab **outlasts**, on the model of sky and earth. A self does not survive. A body does.

### The homophones, and the near-neighbours

Four characters sit close enough to this one to cause real trouble, and two of them are near-homophones. This is the same hazard 保 (*bǎo* — keep safe) carries against 寶 (*bǎo* — treasure); see `bao-保.md`.

| | sound | is | not to be confused with 身 because |
|---|---|---|---|
| **神** | *shén*, rising | spirit, numinous potency (6, 29, 39, 60) | **one tone apart from 身, and its opposite number.** 神 is what is nourished *in* the 身 |
| **精** | *jīng*, level | vital essence (21, 55) | its entry already forbids *spirit* for the same collision — `jing-精.md` |
| **私** | *sī*, level | private interest, grain withheld for oneself (7, 19) | **stands with 身 in chapter 7**, and the two are the chapter's argument |
| **我 / 吾** | *wǒ / wú* | I, me — the self seen and the self seeing | *self* is theirs — `wo-wu-我吾.md`, which names 吾/身 as its cousin-pair |

**神 against 身 is the sharpest of these.** 河上公 sets them in one couplet at chapter 9 — 嗜欲**傷神**，財多**累身**, *"craving harms the spirit; much wealth burdens the body"* — and the distinction is doing work, not decorating. Rendered the same, his sentence says nothing twice.

### What is set aside

**"spirit"** is 神's, and 神 is the character 身 is defined against. It also inverts lines outright: 及吾無身 becomes *"if I had no spirit, what trouble would I have?"*, which reverses chapter 13, where the trouble comes precisely from being embodied and exposed.

**"soul"** imports a separable, immortal thing the text does not have anywhere. Already refused for 精 on the same grounds.

**"self"** is 我/吾's, and at chapter 7 it is also 私's. Put it on 身 and the four lines that make chapter 7's argument read *their selves endure… they have no private self… their private self is fulfilled* — three selves, two characters, and the distinction 王弼 spells out (無私者，**無為於身**也 — *"to have no 私 is to not-do with regard to the 身"*) becomes invisible. There is a second cost: *body* and *self* used by turns, physical line and interior line, performs in English exactly the division between the biological and the psychological that this tradition does not make. **Choosing between them chapter by chapter is not sensitivity to context. It is a dualism, imported and then attributed to the text.**

**"person"** is the right width and belongs to 人 (*rén*), which stands beside 身 in six of these nine chapters.

**"life"** is 生 (*shēng* — to live), across some twenty lines, and chapter 7 needs both words in adjacent clauses.

**"flesh"** is narrower than the character and the register is Pauline. It fails the hymn test on sight.

**"being"** turns a thing you can point at into an abstract noun, and abstraction is the direction every overlay in this book travels. It is also the wrong size: 身 is finite, particular, and yours.

### The one flexion, declared

In **終身** (*zhōng shēn* — to the finish of the 身) and **没身** (*mò shēn* — to the sinking of the 身), the character marks **the span of a life** rather than the flesh: chapter 16's 没身不殆 and chapter 52's 没身不殆, 終身不勤, 終身不救. Both compounds read *to the end of your days*. This is metonymy the Chinese performs, not a licence taken in the English — the body standing in for the time a body lasts — and it is stated here so that the four lines are visibly an exception rather than a drift.

### What no rule can enforce

***"self" is ruled out in the verse, and it is not on the `forbidden:` list, because it cannot be.*** Those are two different facts and the difference matters: the ruling holds, and the enforcement does not exist. `check_locks.py` gates on whether a character stands in that chapter's own Chinese, and 身 shares chapter 7 with 私 and chapters 13, 16 and 54 with 我/吾 — all of which may legitimately print *self*. A rule keyed to 身's presence would fire on their lines. So *spirit* and *soul* are held by the build; *self* is held only by this entry and by the reader.

*(The list does carry **"the separate self"** and **"the ego"**, which are narrower strings no other character can claim. They block the two specific overlays that have actually appeared — the Advaita reading at chapter 13, and the psychoanalytic one. They do not block the plain word.)*

**And the collision with 神 is invisible to every check in this repository**, for the opposite reason: 神 appears in chapters 6, 29, 39 and 60, and 身 in 7, 9, 13, 16, 26, 44, 52, 54 and 66. **They share no chapter at all**, so the evidence gate can never see them meet. Only `concordance.py --english "spirit"` finds it, run by hand. This is the same two-way blindness that hid 固 and 壯 inside chapters that contained 強.

### Left open

**私 (*sī*) has no entry**, and reads two ways — *private self* at chapter 7, *the self* at chapter 19. Chapter 7 cannot be finished until it is settled, because 身 and 私 share the stanza and the whole point is that they differ.

**Whether 終身 and 没身 should converge.** They are different compounds — 終 (*zhōng* — to finish) against 没 (*mò* — to sink under) — and the English currently treats them as one idiom. That may be right, and it may be flattening a distinction the text is making about *how* a life ends.

flexions.english: to the end of your days
flexions.why: the lifespan compounds 終身 and 没身, where 身 marks the span of a life

## 生 (Shēng) — To Give Birth / To Live

*Say "shung," high and level. The most alive word in the book — and the easiest to quietly kill in translation.*

生 is the verb of the Tao's deepest act. It is what the Tao *does* to the world — 道生一 (42), 道生之 (51) — and what the sage is asked to do while claiming nothing: 生而不有. Almost every translator reaches, sooner or later, for "generate," "produce," or "create," and each of those performs the same quiet violence: it turns a *birth* into a *manufacture*. The stakes are larger than a word. To render 生 as *making* rather than *bearing* is to lose the feminine-generative essence at the very heart of the Tao — the mother the whole book is built around. This entry exists to keep her.

### The character, read slowly

生 is a sprout. The oldest forms draw a young plant (屮) pushing up through the line of the earth (一) — new growth breaking the surface. That one image is the whole word: to come up, to come forth, to be born, to live. And it is so fertile that it seeds the language itself. 性, one's inborn nature, is 心 + 生 — the heart's own growth. 星, a star, hides 生 inside it. And — this is the one to hold onto — **姓, the word for a family name, is 女 + 生: *woman* and *birth*, "born-of-woman."** In archaic China the oldest surnames were reckoned through the mother, and many still carry the 女 radical in their bones (姜, 姬, 姒). So at the very root of 生 sits the plainest fact of the feminine: life comes forth from her. Lineage itself was once counted from the one who gives birth.

### What 生 does in the Daodejing — the mother

Follow 生 through the text and you are following the mother. Laozi's cosmos is not built, forged, or commanded into being; it is *born*. The Tao is **萬物之母**, the mother of the countless things (1); **天下母**, the mother of the world (25, 52). Its generative source is **玄牝** — the *mysterious female*, whose gate is called the root of heaven and earth (6): a cosmic womb, "continuous, barely there, inexhaustible." The sage is told to *keep to the female* (守其雌, 28), to *play the female* at the gate of heaven (為雌, 10), to become the **valley** (谷) — low, empty, receptive, and therefore endlessly giving. And the fruit of all this bearing is the **newborn** (嬰兒, 赤子), Laozi's image of intact and undissipated life (10, 20, 28, 55). 母, 牝, 雌, 谷, 嬰兒 — the whole web is feminine, and 生 is its verb. When the Tao 生s the world, it is *gestating* it, not engineering it.

### The releasing — 生而不有

And here is the deepest thing 生 carries, the thing no "create" can hold. **The mother gives birth and lets go.** 生而不有 — she brings forth, but does not possess; 長而不宰 — she fosters, but does not rule. The child was never hers to keep. This is why 生 and 玄德 (Profound Integrity) are one teaching seen twice: to bear truly *is* to release. A maker owns what they make — *my creation*. A mother knows the life came *through* her, not *from* her, and belongs to itself. That releasing is the entire ethic of the book pressed into a single verb — and it evaporates the instant 生 becomes "produce."

### What we set aside

So we set aside **"generate"** — it hums with the mechanical and the electrical, turbines rather than wombs. And we set aside **"create,"** gently, because a *creator* is an author, and an author's shadow is ownership — the very possession 不有 dissolves. Both are defensible; both quietly re-import the maker-God or the engineer, the frame Laozi's razor is precisely cutting away. His cosmogony is gestation, not construction. The world was not fashioned. It was *borne*.

### The working register

生 will not hold still as one English word — it flexes by grammar, and we let it, so long as it never leaves the *organic* register:

- transitive and generative → **gives birth to / bears / brings forth** (道生之 → "the Tao gives birth to them"; 生而不有 → "gives birth without possessing")
- as a noun → **life / the living** (出生入死; 善攝生者)
- intransitive → **arises / comes forth / is born** (有生於無 → "being is born from non-being")

One register — sprouting, bearing, alive — and one standing prohibition: **never "manufacture," never "generate."** The word must stay warm.

### The tension, left open

Two honesties, so this doesn't harden into dogma.

First: 生 is not *always* the mother. In 出生入死 (50) it is simply *life* set against death; in 生生之厚 (50) it is *clinging to living*. We sound the maternal note where the text sounds it — in the cosmogony, in the refrain, wherever the Tao is the one giving birth — and we do not force it where the word is only plainly alive.

Second, on the feminine itself: Laozi's exaltation of 雌, 牝, 母, 柔 — the female, the receptive, the yielding — is real, distinctive, and for centuries muted by translators who preferred a sterner, more masculine Way. To honor it is not to make Laozi a modern feminist; it is to restore what he actually wrote — that the generative, receptive, low, and yielding is *stronger* than the assertive, and that the deepest name for the source of all things is the **mother**. We keep her at the center, because he put her there.
entries.render: give birth to / bear / bring forth

entries.body:
## 事 (Shì) — Affairs, and the Hand That Holds Them

*Say "shr," fourth tone, falling hard. The second hand in the book — and the one nobody notices, because English has scattered it across eight different words.*

**Locked: 事 → "affairs" or "undertakings" as a noun; "serve" or "attend to" as a verb.** *(Never "techniques," never "processes." Reasoning below.)*

Nineteen lines in fourteen chapters, and this edition had been rendering them as *work*, *affairs*, *actions*, *techniques*, *processes*, *non-interference*, *serve*, and *tend*. Eight Englishes for one character — and two of them, *techniques* and *processes*, are the mechanistic overlay this edition exists to strip. Nothing was holding 事 together, so its best line has been invisible: **事 is a hand, and it is standing beside another hand.**

### The character: a hand holding the badge of office

In the oracle bones, four characters that English keeps carefully apart were **one graph**: a hand (又, *yòu*) gripping an implement — a standard with a banner at the top, or a recording tool.

| Descendant | Became |
|---|---|
| **史** (*shǐ*) | the scribe, and then *history* — the hand that keeps the record |
| **吏** (*lì*) | the official — the hand that holds office |
| **使** (*shǐ*) | to send, to cause — the hand that dispatches |
| **事** (*shì*) | **the matter to be dealt with** — what the hand is holding |

So 事 is not "stuff that happens." It is **the thing you have been appointed to do**, the business in your grip. Its oldest sense is closer to *to serve in office* than to *an event*, which is why the verb sense in this book — 事天 (*shì tiān*, 59, serving nature) and 入事人 (*rù shì rén*, 61, entering to serve people) — is not a separate word but the graph read straight.

### The second hand

Here is what the scattering hid. The book's other great verb is **為** (*wéi*), whose oracle-bone graph is a human hand laid on the head of an **elephant** — handling something that has its own momentum. Put the two together and Laozi has **two hands**, and they are not doing the same thing:

- **為** — a hand on a living thing that was already going somewhere. To take that hand away is **無為**, *non-doing*.
- **事** — a hand closed around the implement of office. To open it is **無事**.

Chapter 63 sets them side by side on purpose, in a triple that has already decided one lock and now explains a second:

> 為無為，事無事，味無味。
> *do the not-doing · serve the not-serving · taste the flavorless*

Three ordinary verbs, each negated and then taken as its own object. That structure is why 無為 had to be **non-doing** rather than "non-action" — only a word that is both verb and noun survives all three members (`glossary/wuwei-無為.md`). And it is why 事 belongs in the same register: **not an abstraction, a gesture.** Something a person does with their hands and can stop doing.

### What the noun covers

事 is the matter itself, at every scale, and the range is worth seeing whole:

- **the business of governing** — 處無為之事 (2), *dwelling in the work of non-doing*
- **daily competence** — 事善能 (8), water is *skillful in its affairs*
- **the ruler's completed project** — 功成事遂 (17), *the work done, the undertaking finished*
- **what rebounds on you** — 其事好還 (30), of military force: *such undertakings tend to come back*
- **a ceremonial occasion** — 吉事 / 凶事 (31), auspicious and inauspicious **rites**, which is what sets the seating at a general's table
- **proliferating busyness** — 濟其事 (52), *multiplying your affairs*, and your life is beyond saving
- **the scale argument** — 天下難事 / 天下大事 (63), the world's *difficult* and *great* undertakings, both beginning small

That range is why no single English word can carry all nineteen lines, and the entry does not pretend otherwise. What it insists on is the **register**: every one of these is something undertaken, held, and capable of being put down.

### What is set aside

**"Techniques"** (30). 其事好還 became *"Such techniques inevitably cycle back."* A technique is a method you could refine; 事 is the undertaking itself. The line is not about doing warfare better — it is about the fact that taking up this particular implement puts something in motion that returns to you.

**"Processes"** (31). 吉事尚左，凶事尚右 became *"Life-generating processes amplify creative energy. Life-negating processes invoke destruction."* Two separate faults. **Process** is the mechanistic overlay — it turns a room full of people observing a protocol into physics. And 尚 (*shàng*) simply means *to honor, to place above*; nothing in the line says *amplify* or *invoke*. These are **rites**, and the chapter says so four lines later when it puts the generals in the places that funeral observance assigns them.

**"Actions"** (23) and **"work"** used loosely. Both are near enough to pass unnoticed and thin enough to erase the hand. 從事於道者 (23) is *one who takes up their undertakings within the Tao* — someone with business in their grip, conducting it in a particular way.

**"Non-interference"** for 無事 (48, 57). An interpretation, and a Latinate one, standing in a book that reaches for the plain and physical — and the only member of Chapter 57's quartet that was not a plain saying. Retired 2026-08-12 in favour of *meddle*; see below.

**"Tend"** for 無事, briefly tried and retired the same day. *Tend* is what you do to a garden to make it grow, so *not tending* implies neglect that kills — the reverse of the claim, which is that things flourish once the hand comes off (民自富, *the people grow rich of themselves*). A word that misdescribes the teaching is a worse fault than a word that is merely stiff.

### Working register

| The grammar | Where | Render |
|---|---|---|
| the matter undertaken | 8, 17, 30, 52, 63 | **affairs**, **undertakings** |
| a ceremonial occasion | 31 | **rites**, **occasions** |
| to serve, hold office under | 59, 61 | **serve** |
| to take up, conduct | 23, 64 | **attend to**, **take up** |
| 無事, naming the policy | 48, 57 | **meddle** (negated) |
| 事無事, the neutral verb | 63 | **serve** |

### 無事 — one character, two jobs

無事 renders **"meddle"** at Chapters 48 and 57, and **"serve"** at Chapter 63. That is not drift. The two places are doing different grammatical work, and the difference is visible in the Chinese.

**At 48 and 57, 無事 stands alone** as the name of a policy. Nothing in the line rhymes with it, so the English is free to name the failure it prevents — and *meddling* is exactly what the commentators describe. Wang Bi on 及其有事: 自已造也, *"it is manufactured by oneself."* Heshang Gong: 好有事，則政教煩，民不安 — *"fond of having undertakings, and governance and instruction turn troublesome, and the people are not at peace."* Officiousness, not violence, which is what makes it such a good diagnosis of bad rule.

> 48 · 取天下常以**無事** — *the world always comes to you by not meddling with it*
> 57 · 我**無事**，而民自富 — *I do not meddle, and the people enrich themselves*

That last line sits third in a quartet — 無為 / 好靜 / 無事 / 無欲 — and the plain verb keeps all four as plain sayings, which is what the Chinese has.

**At 63, 事 appears twice inside one line**, and the English has to hold in both positions at once:

> 為無為，**事無事**，味無味 — *do the not-doing, **serve the not-serving**, taste the flavorless*

Each beat is one character twice with 無 (*wú* — there is no) between. So the verb must be **neutral**: *do* is neutral, *taste* is neutral, and the paradox lives in the negation. *Meddle* fails twice over — you meddle *in* something, so the bare transitive is not English, and a verb that is already a rebuke flattens the line into a plain prohibition.

**"Serve" is 事's oldest verb sense**, the one the graph draws: a hand holding the badge of office is a hand *in service*. It is also already this edition's word for 事 at **Ch 59** (治人**事**天 → *governing people and serving nature*) and **Ch 61** (入**事**人 → *enter and serve people*). The middle beat therefore ties to the two chapters where 事 is unambiguously *serve*, and the triple keeps its even rhythm — one syllable against *do* and *taste*.

**The principle, stated so it holds elsewhere: the lock on 事 is on its register, not on a single English token.** A matter undertaken, held, and capable of being put down — never a *technique*, never a *process*. That is the same license 為 already carries as *do / handle / serve as*.

*(Note the loss the triple already accepts: 味無味 reads "taste the flavorless," using two English words for one character, because "flavorless" buys the chime with Ch 35's 淡乎其無味, where the Tao itself is bland and flavorless. The internal echo is worth having and is not sacred.)*
entries.render: affairs / undertakings (noun) · to serve, to attend to (verb)

## 士 (Shì) — In Service

*Say "shr," falling hard — the same sound as 事 (*shì* — affairs) and 恃 (*shì* — to rely on), which each have their own entry. Five appearances across three chapters, two of them on one identical phrase.*

**Locked: 士 → "in service."** *(Lowercase. Never "student," never "scholar," never "warrior.")*

A small word with a long reach: it is the first thing Chapter 15 says, the whole architecture of Chapter 41's opening, and the first of Chapter 68's four masteries. It had three Englishes until 2026-09-07 — *masters* (15), *student* (41), *warrior* (68) — **two of them on the identical phrase 善為士者**.

### The character, and the reading that was put on it later

說文解字 (c. 100 CE) opens with the definition that matters and then explains it away:

> 士，**事也**。數始於一，終於十。从一从十。孔子曰：「推十合一爲士。」
> *"A 士 is **事** (affairs, service). Numbers begin at one and end at ten; the graph is from 一 (one) and 十 (ten). Confucius said: to push the ten together into one is a 士."*

**The first two characters are the definition. Everything after them is philosophy.** 一 + 十 with a Confucius quotation attached is a moral reading of a shape — a person who gathers the many into one — and it is the same move Han scholarship made on 王 (*wáng* — ruler), where 董仲舒 read the three strokes as sky, earth and human joined by the king. `glossary/wang-王.md` dates that one to roughly fourteen centuries after the graph it explains. **This book's rank-words attract that treatment**, and the pattern is worth knowing before trusting any traditional etymology of one.

**The honest limit:** what the graph originally depicted is contested and this entry does not settle it. What is not contested is 說文's own gloss — **事** — and that is the whole of what the English needs.

### 士 is defined by a character this glossary already holds

**事 (*shì* — affairs / to attend to)** has its own entry, and its graph is **a hand gripping the badge of office**. So 說文 is saying: **a 士 is the person whose hand that is.** Not someone who studies affairs, not someone who owns them — someone who *handles* them on another's behalf.

Historically that is exact. A 士 was the **lowest rank of the Zhou nobility**, between the 大夫 (*dà fū* — grandee) and the commoner: a person with a sword, a post, and a lord. By the Warring States the word had widened to cover the courtier, the retainer, the man-at-arms and the man of talent looking for a patron — but the centre held. **A 士 serves.**

### How Laozi uses it — five lines, two shapes

**善為士者 — "masterful in service" (15, 68).** The identical four characters open both chapters' arguments, and they must read identically:

> 古之**善為士者**，微妙玄通 (15) — *the ancients who were masterful in service were faint, subtle, dark and unobstructed*
> **善為士者**，不武 (68) — *those masterful in service are not martial*

**上士 · 中士 · 下士 — ranked (41).** 上 (*shàng* — upper), 中 (*zhōng* — middle), 下 (*xià* — lower) grade the same people into three grades of hearer. 上 is a rank marker throughout this book — ch 38's 上德 is *the highest integrity*, ch 8's 上善 *the most masterful* — so the English takes the height and keeps the noun: *those highest in service*, *those middling in service*, *those lowest in service*.

### The commentators disagree about what a 士 is, and that decides the English

This is the entry's real finding, and it is why a narrower word cannot be used.

> 王弼 on 68: **士卒之帥也**。武尚先陵人也 — *"a 士 is **the commander of the troops**. 武 (martial) means prizing being first and overbearing people."*
> 河上公 on 68: **言貴道德，不好武力** — *"it says: prize the Tao and integrity, and do not favour martial force."*

**王弼 makes 士 an office. 河上公 makes it a disposition.** One is reading a rank in an army, the other a person of a certain character. 河上公 is equally concrete at 41, where the middle 士 治身以長存，**治國以太平** — *"governs the body for long life, governs the state for great peace"* — and the lowest are 貪狼多欲, *"greedy as wolves and full of desire."*

**"In service" is the English that leaves both standing.** It does not say soldier and it does not say sage; it says *someone whose position is to serve*, which is what a commander and a moral agent both are here. **Convergence is strong evidence; divergence is a finding, and it must not be averaged away by picking one commentator's noun.**

### What is set aside

**"Student"** — the rendering this replaced at 41, and the one furthest from the character. 說文 says 事, affairs. Nobody in Chapter 41 is at school; 河上公's middle 士 is *governing a state*, and his lowest are greedy, not slow. It also makes the chapter a lesson about pupils when it is a claim about how the Tao is received by people with power.

**"Officer"** — the strongest rival, and it lost on register rather than on meaning. It is concrete, takes 上/中/下 naturally, and matches 王弼's 士卒之帥 exactly. But in English it reads **bureaucratic**, and carries a negative valence for many readers that the Chinese does not have; it also picks 王弼's reading over 河上公's, which the section above forbids. *(It is separately spoken for: 官 (*guān*) is *officers* at ch 28.)*

**"Warrior"** — what 68 read before, and it made the line cancel itself: *"the master warrior is not martial."* The Chinese says something sharper — the person whose whole position is service is not the one who fights hardest.

**"Scholar," "gentleman," "knight."** *Scholar* is the standard dictionary gloss for later Chinese and imports the imperial examination system, a thousand years downstream. *Gentleman* belongs to 君子 (*jūn zǐ*), which is a different word in this book and a Confucian honorific — handing it to 士 would tangle two rank-words the text keeps apart. *Knight* imports European feudalism wholesale.

**"Servant."** A 士 held rank. The word marks the bottom of the nobility, not the top of the household.

### The register, and how it flexes

| Chinese | shape | English |
|---|---|---|
| 善為士者 (15, 68) | 善為 + 士 + 者 | **masterful in service** |
| 上士 / 中士 / 下士 (41) | rank word + 士 | **those highest / middling / lowest in service** |

**The rule for anything outside these five lines:** keep *service* as the root and let English grammar move around it. 士 is a **standing**, not an activity — so *in service* rather than *serving*, which would make it something a person does on an afternoon. Where a bare noun is unavoidable, *a person in service* before any rank word.

**The cost of the choice, stated plainly:** it is five English words for two characters at Chapter 41, and it is weak where the Chinese has a solid noun. That was accepted deliberately in exchange for not narrowing the word.

### The seam

**士 named a class of men.** Standing rule 2 governs: render toward the universal, and never erase the male default in silence. *In service* is neutral by design, and the fact that the original is not is recorded here rather than smoothed over.

士 belongs to a family the manuscript is still deciding — **大丈夫** (*dà zhàng fū*, ch 38), **君子** (*jūn zǐ*, ch 26 and 31), and 士 — three male rank-words that have been dissolved in opposite directions. `WORKLIST.md` T4-7 holds that question, and it is the same question as 民 / 人: what to do with a social category when the rank is often what the line is about.

### Left open

**Whether 上士 · 中士 · 下士 are three kinds of person or three grades of one office.** 王弼's 士卒之帥 implies a real hierarchy with posts in it; 河上公's greedy-as-wolves implies a moral spectrum. Our English takes the height words and stays silent on which, which may be more silence than the Chinese keeps.

**Whether ch 68's frame survives.** 善為士者 must match ch 15, but its three companion lines run 善▢者 as *"the master fighter," "the master of overcoming enemies," "the master of using people."* Four instances of one frame now wear two shapes. `WORKLIST.md` T2-47.

## 恃 (Shì) — To Rely On

*Say "shr," falling. Five lines across five chapters, and four of them are the same three characters.*

**Locked: 恃 → "rely on" — the heart putting its weight on something.** *(Not "presume," not "presuming," not "dependency.")*

為而不恃 (*wéi ér bù shì*) is conventionally read **"acts without presuming."** That is not a translation of 恃. It is an inference about what someone who 恃-ed would be doing — and it lands on *presumption*, a fault of manner, when the character is about **where your weight is**.

**恃 is the word for what a child does to a mother**, and the Tao Te Ching uses it in both directions.

### The graph: the heart's version of holding

恃 is **忄 (heart)** beside **寺**. The *Shuowen Jiezi* is one line:

> 恃，**賴**也。从心，寺聲。
> *"恃 is 賴 (lài — to rely). From 心 (heart), with 寺 as the sound."*

寺 is treated as phonetic there, but it is not a random noise. In its older form it is a **hand (又 / 寸) under a foot-graph (之)** — holding, attending, being posted at. And it seeds an entire family of words about holding, distinguished by *which part of you does it*:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **持** (*chí*) | 扌 hand + 寺 | to hold, in the hand |
| **侍** (*shì*) | 亻 person + 寺 | to attend upon, with the body |
| **待** (*dài*) | 彳 step + 寺 | to wait for, to await |
| **恃** (*shì*) | 忄 heart + 寺 | **to hold onto with the heart — to lean your weight on** |

That table is not decoration. **河上公 confirms it from inside the family**, glossing Ch 34 with a bare definition:

> 恃，**待**也。萬物皆恃道而生
> *"恃 is 待 (dài — to await, to depend on). The countless things all 恃 the Tao and so live."*

A Han commentator defines 恃 by its own cousin. The core is not calculation and not manner. It is **the heart resting its weight on something outside itself, and expecting that thing to be there.**

### The mother-word

The oldest use of 恃 in the language is a child's, and it is gendered with total precision. From the *Shijing* 《小雅·蓼莪》, older than the Tao Te Ching:

> 無父何**怙**，無母何**恃**
> *"With no father, whom do I 怙? With no mother, whom do I 恃?"*

怙 (*hù*) went to the father, 恃 to the mother — and classical Chinese later fossilized the pair into idiom: **失恃** (*shī shì*), "to lose one's 恃," is the euphemism for a mother's death. *(The Shijing line is ancient; the 失恃/失怙 idiom is a later crystallization of it. Neither text is vendored in `sources/` — flagged here as a classical locus, not as evidence from this repository's files.)*

**This matters for this book specifically.** 母 (*mǔ* — mother) is one of this edition's locked terms and one of its load-bearing images: 天下母 (*tiān xià mǔ* — mother of the world) at Ch 52, and Ch 20's closing 貴食母 — *"I prize feeding from the mother."* When Ch 34 says 萬物**恃**之以生, *"the countless things rely on it to live,"* it is reaching for the verb whose native object is a mother. The relation the Tao stands in to everything is the one an infant stands in to the person feeding it.

### The asymmetry — the whole finding

恃 occurs five times, and the direction reverses exactly once.

**Once, positive, of the Tao:**
- **34**: 萬物恃之以生而不辭 — *the countless things rely on it to live, and it refuses none.*

**Four times, negative, of the Tao or the sage:**
- **2, 10, 51, 77**: 為而不恃 — *acts yet relies on nothing.*

So the book's claim is a chiasm, and it is the mother relation stated as a principle: **be the thing that is relied on, and rely on nothing.** The mother is leaned on and does not lean back. Ch 34 supplies the other half of the picture in the same breath — 不辭 (*bù cí* — refuses none), 衣養萬物 (*yī yǎng wàn wù* — clothes and feeds the countless things) — and then refuses the credit: 而不為主, *and does not act as their master.*

**王弼 sharpens why the sage has nothing to rely on.** On Ch 10:

> 不禁其性，則物自濟，**何為之恃**
> *"If you do not block their nature, things sort themselves out — so what is there to rely on?"*

The sage cannot lean on their accomplishment because, done rightly, the accomplishment was not theirs. 王弼 finishes: 物自長足，不吾宰成 — *"things grow to their own fullness; I do not master them into being."*

**河上公 reads the unstated object as the repayment**, and does so identically in four places:

> 道所施為，**不恃望其報**也
> *"What the Tao gives out and does, it does not 恃望 (lean toward and watch for) its repayment."*

恃望 is the compound worth keeping in mind: the heart already tipped toward what is owed back. Ch 77 varies it only in the subject — 聖人為德施，不恃其報也, *"the sage gives out integrity and does not rely on its return."*

### The one thing you may rely on

**韓非** (*Hán Fēi*, d. 233 BCE), the oldest commentary in this repository, quotes Ch 64 with 恃 in the positive and names its object:

> **恃**萬物之自然而不敢為也
> *"Rely on the countless things being so of themselves, and do not push to act."*

That single line ties 恃 to two locked terms at once. 自然 (*zìrán* — so of itself) is the ground, and 敢 (*gǎn* — to push, to venture) is what you stop doing once you have that ground. **恃 is the hinge between them:** 無為 (*wúwéi* — non-doing) is possible because there is something that will hold your weight, and what holds it is things going of themselves.

Elsewhere 韓非 uses the word the other way, for the wrong supports — 入山不**恃**備以救害, *"entering the mountains, one does not rely on preparations to save oneself from harm"* (Ch 50); 夫**恃**貌而論情者，其情惡也, *"one who relies on appearance to argue about the substance — the substance is bad"* (Ch 38). And 王弼 on Ch 60 aims it at government: 夫**恃**威網以使物者，治之衰也 — *"to rely on the net of authority to manage things is governance in decay."*

The pattern across all of them: **恃 is neutral; what you put your weight on is not.**

### Why *rely on*, and what it costs

**Set aside: "presume," "presuming."** The retired reading, and the reason this entry exists. It renders an imagined attitude rather than the character, and it makes the line a warning against arrogance when the line is about load-bearing. It also collides with 敢 (*gǎn* — to push, to venture), whose entry already had to note that *presume* was blocked here.

**Set aside: "dependency."** Proposed at Ch 77 and rejected the same day. It is an abstract noun in a line of verbs, and in current English it carries addiction.

**Considered and set aside: "lean on."** This was the working choice for one draft, and it is the most faithful *picture* — it keeps the body and it keeps the mother. It lost on two grounds. First, **倚** (*yǐ* — to lean against) already holds *lean* in the manuscript, at Ch 58's 禍兮福之所倚 — *"disaster is what fortune leans on."* Using one English word for two characters the text keeps distinct blurs them for no gain. Second, 河上公's 不恃望其報 is about **counting on a return**, and *rely* carries that where *lean* underplays it.

**The cost of "rely on," stated plainly.** It is Latinate and its picture is dead: *rely* is *re-* + Old French *lier*, to bind — a body word once, an abstraction now. English readers will hear a mental act where the Chinese has a posture. **That loss is what this entry exists to hold**, and it is why the gloss above says *the heart putting its weight on something* rather than just repeating the dictionary.

There is one further risk. *"Acts yet relies on nothing"* can read as self-sufficiency — the self-made sage, needing no one — which would be an overlay, and a Stoic one. **Ch 34 is the guard against it.** There, the same character says that everything alive relies on the Tao, and the Tao turns none of it away. The sage relies on nothing not because relying is weakness, but because, as 王弼 says, there is nothing there that was theirs to lean on.

**Not forbidden, and deliberately: "depend."** Ch 2 renders 高下相傾 (*gāo xià xiāng qīng*) as *"high and low depend on each other,"* and 傾 sits in the same chapter as 恃. The checker gates on whether a character is present in a chapter, so it cannot express *right for 傾, wrong for 恃, same chapter*. That distinction lives here and in the reader. See `CLAUDE.md` → *The glossary is generated*.
entries.render: rely on — the heart putting its weight on something

entries.body:
## 守 (Shǒu) — To Hold To

*Say "show," dipping. Eleven lines across eight chapters, and it is the verb the book reaches for when it tells you what to do.*

**Locked: 守 → "hold to" — and *guard* where what is kept is ground or property.** *(Never "embrace," never "attune to," never "stay with." Never *keep* either — but that one is a ruling no check can hold, and it is the likeliest wrong word here, so it has a section of its own below.)*

### The graph: a roof and a rule, and no hand anywhere

> 守，**守官**也。从宀从寸。寺府之事者。从寸。寸，**法度**也。
> *"守 is to keep an office. From 宀 (mián — a roof) and 寸 (cùn — an inch). It is the business of a court, hence 寸; 寸 means **a regulation**."* — 說文解字

This is the one member of the holding family with **no hand in it.** 持 (*chí* — to grip) has 手, the hand. 執 (*zhí* — to seize) has 丮, a hand, and a set of manacles. 保 (*bǎo* — to keep safe) has a person with a child. 守 has a building and a measure.

What you 守 is therefore not in your fist. **It is a post you have been given and are answerable for.** The English has to carry a charge, not a grip — which is why *hold to* takes a preposition where *hold* would not. You hold a cup. You hold to a post.

### Two registers, and the dictionary has both

說文 gives 守官 (*keeping a charge*) and 寺府之事 (*the business of a court*, which in a walled town includes the sentry at the gate). The book uses both, and the split runs by **what is being kept**:

| what is kept | reading | lines |
|---|---|---|
| a stance, a principle, a way of standing | **hold to** | 守中 (5) · 守靜 (16) · 守其雌 · 守其黑 · 守其辱 (28) · 守之 (32, 37) · 守其母 · 守柔 (52) |
| ground, property, a position under attack | **guard** | 金玉滿堂，莫之能守 (9) · 以守則固 (67) |

Nine of eleven are the first. The two that are not are the two where 守 has stopped being contemplative and gone back to the gate: a hall full of gold and jade that no one can guard, and 以戰則勝，以**守**則固 — *"fight with it and you win, guard with it and you stand firm"* — where 戰 (*zhàn* — to fight) and 守 are the plain military pair, attack and defence. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads the second exactly that way, expanding the bare character into a compound: 以**守衛**則堅固, *"used to guard and defend, then solid and firm."*

### The instruction verb

守 is how the book says *do this*, and the shape recurs. Chapter 28 runs it three times as a template:

> 知其雄，**守**其雌 · 知其白，**守**其黑 · 知其榮，**守**其辱
> *"Know the rooster, hold to the hen · know the white, hold to the black · know the glory, hold to the disgrace."*

Knowing is the easy half. 守 is the half you have to keep doing, and the pairing with 知 (*zhī* — to know) is what makes the stanza a practice rather than an observation. Chapters 32 and 37 use one line verbatim — 侯王若能**守**之 — for the whole political programme, and chapter 52 uses it for the most consoling movement in the book: 既知其子，復**守**其母, *"know her children, return and hold fast to the mother."*

And at 52 the character carries the book's hardest paradox without breaking. 守柔曰強 — *"holding to the soft is called strong"* — draws 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) into a sentence that puts both valences of 強 (*qiáng* — strong) on one page:

> 守強不強，守柔乃強也。
> *"Holding to the strong is not strong; holding to the soft is truly strong."*

The verb is the same in both halves of his sentence. Only the object changes. That is the whole argument for one English.

### What is set aside

**"embrace" is 抱's** (*bào* — to embrace: chapters 10, 19, 22, 42, 54, 64), and the two characters are close enough that a Han commentator defines one by the other — 河上公 on ch 22's 抱一: **抱，守也**…聖人**守一**乃知萬事, *"抱 means to hold to… the sage holds to one and thereby knows the countless affairs."* That closeness is exactly why the English must keep them apart: 抱 takes the whole body and 守 takes a charge, and the two never share a chapter, so there is nothing to gain and a distinction to lose by letting them share a word.

**"attune to"** inverts both the register and the grammar. It makes 守 something that happens *to* you, a matter of resonance and sensitivity, when the character is a duty roster. You are not attuned to a post; you keep it.

**"stay with"** and **"abide in"** drop the effort. 守 costs something — that is why 王弼 can set 守強 against 守柔 and expect the reader to feel the difference — and a verb of dwelling has no cost in it.

**"preserve"** is a conservator's word, and it puts the emphasis on the object's condition rather than on the keeper's obligation. It also drifts toward 保 (*bǎo*), whose entry is `bao-保.md`.

### What no rule can enforce

***"keep"* is ruled out in the verse, and it is not on the `forbidden:` list, because it cannot be.** Those are two different facts and the difference matters: the ruling holds, and the enforcement does not exist. 保 stands with 守 in chapters 9 and 67, and **保's English is built on *keep* in both** — *keep safe* at 67, and **bare *keep* at 9**, where a declared flexion drops the qualifier (`bao-保.md`). A rule keyed to 守's presence would fire on 保's own line, and at chapter 9 it would fire on the exact word. So *embrace*, *attune to* and *stay with* are held by the build; *keep* is held only by this entry and by the reader. Likewise the two words a reader is most likely to confuse here sit two lines apart at chapter 9 — 守 at *guard*, 保 at *keep* — and again at chapter 67, where 保 takes *keep safe*. No check in this repository can tell them apart. See `bao-保.md`, `chi-持.md`, `zhi-執.md`.

### Left open

**Chapter 5's 守中.** 中 (*zhōng* — the middle) is rendered *the center*, and both commentators pull it toward emptiness rather than toward moderation — 王弼 reads 中 as the bellows' hollow two lines above. Whether the English should say *the center* or something that carries the hollow is unsettled, and 中 has no entry yet.

flexions.why: what is kept is ground or property, not a stance
