## 爭 (Zhēng) — Contend

*Say "jung," level. Nine lines across seven chapters, and every one of them is under negation.*

**Locked: 爭 → "contend / contention."** *(Not "compete," not "competes," not "competing," not "competition.")*

Every English Tao Te Ching renders 爭 as **compete**. The word arrives without friction because the sentences it appears in sound like advice about ambition, and *compete* is what English does with ambition.

It costs two things.

First, it imports an institution. Competition in English is **rule-governed rivalry** — sport, markets, examinations. It has a referee, an agreed prize, and a starting line, and it is broadly understood to be healthy. None of that is in the character, and a chapter that says *do not compete* sounds like advice against careerism rather than a description of what hands do.

Second, and fatally, it collapses at the one line where the book distinguishes 爭 from winning.

### The character is two hands and one object

爪 (*zhǎo*) sits on top — a hand, turned down, fingers grasping. 彐 sits beneath it — a second hand, coming from the other direction. Between them, in the oldest forms, is the thing: a vertical stroke that survives in the modern character as the hook down its middle. Some read it as a plowshare, gripped from both sides.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* (c. 100 CE) does not define it as rivalry at all:

> 爭，引也。从𠬪𠂆 — ***"爭 is to pull.** From 𠬪 (two hands) and 𠂆."*

Xu Xuan's note adds that 𠂆 is sounded as 曳 (*yè* — to drag), and that dragging is the whole principle of the graph. And the classical gloss makes the direction explicit:

> 凡言爭者，皆謂引之使歸於己 — *"wherever 爭 is spoken of, it means **pulling a thing so that it comes to oneself**."*

That is the term. Not rivalry as a condition, not ambition as a temperament: **the physical act of pulling a shared thing toward your own body.** Two hands, one object, opposite directions. It passes the pointing test, which *compete* does not — nobody can point at a competition, and anyone can point at two people pulling on the same rope.

### It appears only under negation — all nine times

爭 occurs nine times across seven chapters, and **every single occurrence is negated.** The book never once describes anyone contending. It names the word only in order to refuse it.

| Chapter | Line | |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 不尚賢，使民不**爭** | do not exalt the worthy, so the people do not contend |
| 8 | 水善利萬物而不**爭** | water is masterful at benefiting the countless things and does not contend |
| 8 | 夫唯不**爭** | precisely because it does not contend |
| 22 | 夫唯不**爭** | precisely because they do not contend |
| 22 | 故天下莫能與之**爭** | so no one in the world can contend with them |
| 66 | 以其不**爭** | because they do not contend |
| 66 | 故天下莫能與之**爭** | so no one in the world can contend with them |
| 68 | 是謂不**爭**之德 | this is called the integrity of not contending |
| 73 | 不**爭**而善勝 | does not contend, yet is masterful at overcoming |
| 81 | 為而不**爭** | does, and does not contend |

A word that exists in a text only as something not done is being used as a name for a disease.

### Chapter 73 decides it

> 天之道，不**爭**而善**勝** — *"nature's Tao does not 爭, yet is masterful at 勝."*

勝 (*shèng* — to overcome, to prevail) is not a word this book refuses. It endorses it, repeatedly and without irony: 柔弱**勝**剛強 (36, *the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong*), 牝常以靜**勝**牡 (61, *the female overcomes the male through stillness*), 自**勝**者強 (33, *to overcome oneself is strength*).

So the book draws a line, and the line falls between **爭** and **勝**. Prevailing is permitted. Pulling toward yourself is not.

**Under *compete*, that line disappears.** "Does not compete yet wins well" is barely a sentence in English, because competing and winning are two halves of one activity — you cannot win a thing you did not compete for, so the line reads as either a contradiction or a boast.

**Under *contend*, it survives intact.** Contending is the pulling; overcoming is what happens. The second does not require the first, which is precisely the claim.

### Chapter 3 says where it comes from

> 不尚賢，使民不**爭** — *"do not exalt the worthy, and the people will not contend."*

爭 is not a constant of human nature in this book. It is **manufactured**, and the mechanism is named: 尚 (*shàng* — to exalt, to raise up). Rank one thing above another and hands begin to reach for it. Remove the ranking and the reaching stops, because there is no longer a single object in the middle.

This is the same shape as Chapter 65, where the ruler's own guile produces the guile they then have to govern. The problem is upstream of the people every time.

### Chapter 68 defines it by what it is not

Four lines, each opening on 善 (*shàn* — masterful at), and then the name for all of them together:

> 善為士者，不**武**；善**戰**者，不怒；善**勝**敵者，不與；善用人者，為之**下**。是謂不**爭**之德。
>
> *"Those masterful in service are not martial. The master fighter does not rage. The master of overcoming enemies does not engage them. The master of using people puts themselves below them. This is called the integrity of not contending."*

Not martial, not enraged, not engaging, underneath. **爭 is the common name for what all four refuse** — and note how far that reaches past ambition. It covers the battlefield. *Compete* cannot carry a chapter about war; *contend* can, because English contends in arguments and in wars alike.

This chapter also fixes the boundary of the lock. It holds 戰 (*zhàn* — to fight) and 勝 (*shèng* — to overcome) **in the same chapter as 爭**, so neither *fight* nor *overcome* can be forbidden for 爭: both are legitimately owed to other characters standing a few lines away.

### What is set aside

**compete, competition** — the institutional frame described above, and the collapse at Chapter 73. It also flatters the thing being refused: competition is a word for something we approve of.

**struggle** — too broad, and solitary. A person can struggle against weather, illness, or themselves; 爭 requires a second hand on the same object. Also spoken for elsewhere in the manuscript.

**fight** — belongs to 戰 (*zhàn*), which has its own chapters and stands beside 爭 in Chapter 68.

**strive** — solitary again, and it loses the object entirely. Striving is about effort; 爭 is about direction.

**vie** — the right meaning and the wrong century.

**quarrel, wrangle, dispute** — verbal only. 爭 is bodily first and became verbal later; running the derivation backwards puts the argument before the hands.

### Working register

| Form | Chapters | English |
|---|---|---|
| 不爭, plain verb | 8, 22, 66, 73, 81 | does not contend |
| 使民不爭, causative | 3 | so the people do not contend |
| 莫能與之爭 | 22, 66 | no one can contend with them |
| 不爭之德, nominal | 68 | the integrity of not contending |

**"Contend with" is a live English idiom** and it does real work in the repeated formula 故天下莫能與之爭, which Chapters 22 and 66 share verbatim: *no one in the world can contend with them.* That is ordinary English for *nobody can take them on*, and it is nearer the Chinese than *compete with*, which suggests entering a contest rather than pulling against someone.

The **noun** is the pressure point. English has no clean nominal for the act — *contention* has drifted toward *a contested claim* — so 不爭之德 takes the gerund: **the integrity of not contending.** Where a noun is unavoidable, *contention* is permitted; it should not become the ordinary form.

### The register we lose

爭 is two hands, a plough, and dirt. *Contend* is Latin, *com-* plus *tendere*, to stretch against — physical at the root but three removes from a farmyard by the time it reaches modern English. The Anglo-Saxon words that keep the object are unusable at this register: **grab**, **grabbing**, **pulling toward yourself**. They are what the character says, and none of them can carry 不爭之德.

So the rendering trades the fingernails for the distinction, and the distinction is worth more. But the loss is real, and a reader who wants the character rather than the word should keep the two hands in view.

### What stays open

**Whether non-contention is an ethic or a tactic.** The book will not say, and two chapters make the question sharp:

> 夫唯不爭，故天下莫能與之爭 (22) · 以其不爭，故天下莫能與之爭 (66)
>
> *"precisely because they do not contend, no one in the world can contend with them."*

Read one way, that is a description of someone who has stopped wanting the object, and is therefore beyond the reach of anyone still pulling. Read another, it is an unbeatable technique — the strongest possible position in exactly the contest being renounced. Chapter 66 leans into the second reading and does not flinch: the sage goes low, and 天下樂推 — *the world gladly pushes them forward*. They end up on top. They simply did not pull.

Whether that is a moral difference or a very elegant route to the same place, the text does not resolve, and neither should the English.

**And Chapter 81 keeps the hardest form of it**: 為而不**爭** — *does, and does not contend.* The sage acts. 為 (*wéi*) is already a hand laid on an elephant. So the instruction is not to take the hand away but to keep it there without pulling the thing toward yourself, and where exactly that boundary runs is the working question of the whole book, put in four characters.

## 執 (Zhí) — To Grasp

*Say "jr," rising. Nine lines across seven chapters, and the most famous of them is a warning.*

**Locked: 執 → "grasp" — and *seize* at chapter 74, where the seizing is an arrest.** *(Never "cling," never "attachment," never "embody," never "control.")*

### The graph: a hand and a pair of manacles

The *Shuowen Jiezi* does not hedge:

> 執，**捕罪人**也。从丮从幸，幸亦聲。
> *"執 is **to seize a criminal**. From 丮 (jǐ) and 幸 (xìng), 幸 also giving the sound."*

丮 is a hand thrust out to take hold. The element written 幸 here is not 幸 *"fortunate"* but 㚔 (*niè*), and in the oracle-bone and bronze forms of 執 the picture is legible without a dictionary: a kneeling figure with both hands closed inside a wooden restraint. A person, and a pair of manacles.

So 執 is not holding. It is **taking into custody** — the hand that closes on a thing in order to keep it where you put it. Every other word in this family is about keeping something. 執 is about keeping something *that would otherwise get away.*

### The book uses it as a legal word twice, in plain sight

At chapter 74 the sense is the dictionary's, undiluted. 若使民常畏死，而為奇者，吾得**執**而殺之 — *"suppose the people always feared death, and I could 執 whoever steps out of line and kill them."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads it as statute:

> 以道教化而民不從，反為竒巧，乃應**王法**執而殺之，誰敢有犯者。老子傷時王不先道德化之而先**刑罰**。
> *"If they are taught by the Tao and the people do not follow, turning instead to cunning tricks, then it accords with **the king's law** to 執 them and kill them, and who would dare offend? Laozi grieves that the kings of his day did not transform them by the Tao and integrity first, but by **punishment** first."*

At chapter 79 it is an instrument rather than a person: 聖人**執**左契 — the sage 執s the left half of a split tally, the physical bond that made a debt enforceable before there were written laws.

> 古者聖人執左契合符信也，無文書法律，刻契合符以為信也。 — 河上公
> *"In antiquity the sage held the left tally and matched the token of trust. There were no documents or statutes; they carved tallies and matched them to make trust."*

說文 on 契 is 大約也, *"a great covenant."* Both of these are custody. Neither is a metaphor.

### Which is what 執者失之 has been saying all along

為者敗之，**執**者失之 (29, 64) is usually read as a caution against clinging — a counsel of inner detachment. The character says something harder and more political. The line's object is 天下 (*tiān xià* — the world), and the clause just before it names what the world is: 天下**神器**，不可為也，不可執也 — *"the world is a sacred vessel. It cannot be handled. It cannot be grasped."*

You cannot take a sacred vessel into custody. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) makes it a statement about what kind of thing the world is, not about the state of your heart:

> 萬物以自然為性，故可因而不可為也，可**通**而不可**執**也。物有徃來而執之，故必失矣。
> *"The countless things have what is so of themselves for their nature. So they can be gone along with but not handled; they can be passed through but not grasped. Things have their coming and going, and to grasp them is necessarily to lose them."*

And he brackets 執 with the book's other blade-word: 不施為**執割**也 — *"imposes no handling, no grasping, no cutting"* — 割 (*gē* — to sever) being ch 28's 大制不割, *"the great carving severs nothing."*

河上公 draws the distinction that matters, on the same line, and refuses to let the verb take the blame:

> 執利遇患，執道全身。
> *"Grasp advantage and you meet trouble; grasp the Tao and you keep your body whole."*

### The two "positive" instances are not exceptions. They are the point.

執古之道，以御今之有 (14) and 執大象，天下往 (35) are instructions, and they use the custody word without apology. Read against chapters 29 and 64 they are not a contradiction but a joke with a straight face: **you cannot take the world into custody, so take the one thing that will not break in your hand.** An English that softens 執 to *hold* in these two lines and hardens it back to *grasp* in the others resolves a tension the Chinese leaves standing, and severs the link between the four chapters.

| ch | line | English |
|---|---|---|
| 14 | 執古之道 | grasp the ancient Tao |
| 29 | 不可執也 · 執者失之 | it cannot be grasped · those who grasp it lose it |
| 35 | 執大象 | grasp the great image |
| 64 | 執者失之 · 無執 | those who grasp it lose it · does not grasp |
| 69 | 執無兵 | grasping where there is no weapon |
| 74 | 執而殺之 | **seize** whoever steps out of line and kill them |
| 79 | 執左契 | grasps the left half of the tally |

**The flexion at 74 is not an exception to the character. It is the dictionary headword.** English *grasp* covers the hand and the metaphor but has no judicial sense at all; *"I could grasp whoever steps out of line and kill them"* is not English. 捕罪人也 is, in three characters, *seize a criminal* — so the one line in the book where the state actually arrests somebody takes the one English word that says so.

### What is set aside

**"cling" and "attachment"** import *upādāna* — the second link of the Buddhist chain of dependent origination — into a text written before Buddhism reached China, and they relocate the problem. Clinging is a condition of the heart; 執 is a thing you do with your hands to something outside you. Chapters 29 and 64 are about **governing**, and a ruler who has stopped clinging has still seized the state.

**"embody"** deletes the hand and reverses the direction: 執 puts the object in your grip, *embody* puts it inside you. At 執大象 (35) the great image is precisely what does not fit inside anybody.

**"control"** is the mechanistic temptation this edition watches for. You control a system; you grasp a vessel, and you can break it. 神器 and 不可執 are one gesture, and an abstraction cuts it in half.

**"possess"** belongs to 有 (*yǒu* — to have), which is locked in `wu-you-無有.md`.

### What no rule can enforce

***"hold"* is not on the forbidden list, and cannot be.** 持 (*chí* — to hold in the hand) stands in chapter 64 beside 執, and *hold* is 持's word on that page. A rule keyed to 執's presence in a chapter would fire on 持's own line. This is the standing limit of the harness — right for that character, wrong for this one, same chapter — and the distinction lives here and in the reader instead. See `chi-持.md`, `shou-守.md`, `bao-保.md`: four characters, four different hands.

### Left open

**Whose half is the left half.** 執左契 keeps 左 (*zuǒ* — left) in the English without saying which party held it. The Han commentators describe the practice without settling the side, and the traditions disagree: on one reading the sage holds the creditor's half and declines to press it, on the other they hold the debtor's half and have no claim to press. The line 而不責於人 — *"and never asks for the other"* — is pointed under the first reading and merely descriptive under the second. 王弼 says only 左契防怨之所由生也, *"the left tally prevents what gives rise to grudges."* We render the character and leave the side to the reader.

flexions.why: the seizing is an arrest, which is the dictionary headword: 捕罪人也

entries.body:
## 治 (Zhì) — To Govern

*Say "jr," falling. Twelve lines across nine chapters — the book's ordinary word for what a ruler does, and 說文解字 files it as a river.*

**Locked: 治 → "govern," with *order* at chapters 8 and 64.** *(Never "control," never "manage," never "administer." Never *rule* either — but that one is a ruling no check can hold; see* What no rule can enforce *below.)*

### The graph: a river in Shandong

> 治，**水**。出東萊曲城陽丘山，南入海。从水台聲。
> *"治 is **a watercourse**. It rises at Mount Yangqiu in Quchang, Donglai, and runs south into the sea. From 水 (shuǐ — water), with 台 (tái) as the sound."* — 說文解字

The dictionary's headword sense is not *to govern* at all. **It is the name of a particular river.** Everything the character later means — to regulate, to put right, to keep in working order, to rule a state — grows out of what one does to moving water: dredge it, bank it, let it run where it should run.

That path is not a curiosity of this one word. It is the oldest governing metaphor China has: 大禹**治**水 (*dà yǔ zhì shuǐ*) — Yu the Great **治**-ed the floods, and was given the realm for it. He did it, the story insists, by **channelling** rather than by damming. So when the Laozi reaches for a word for governing, the word it reaches for already carries a theory of governing inside it.

**And the book puts it in the water chapter.** 政善治 stands in chapter 8, which opens 上善若水 (*shàng shàn ruò shuǐ* — *"the most masterful are like water"*). 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses 治 there through water and nothing else: **无有不洗清且平也** — *"there is nothing it does not wash clean and level."* Washing, clearing, levelling. He is reading the river in the character.

### Where it stands

| ch | line | now |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 是以聖人之**治** · 為無為，則無不**治** | governs · nothing is left ungoverned |
| 8 | 政善**治** | **order** |
| 10 | 愛民**治**國 | governing the state |
| 57 | 以正**治**國 | govern the state |
| 59 | **治**人事天，莫若嗇 | governing people |
| 60 | **治**大國，若烹小鮮 | governing a large state |
| 64 | **治**之於未亂 | **order** it |
| 65 | 民之難**治** · 以智**治**國 · 不以智**治**國 | hard to govern · govern ×2 |
| 75 | 民之難**治** · 是以難**治** | hard to govern ×2 |

Ten of twelve are *govern*, and the two that are not are the two where the object is **not a polity**.

### What 治 is, by what it is not

**說文 defines 亂 (*luàn* — disorder) as 治** — 亂，治也 — so the two characters are each other's definition, and **chapter 64 prints them in one clause**: 為之於未有，**治**之於未**亂**, *"handle it before it exists; order it before it falls into disorder."* That line is the whole argument for keeping the English pair visibly related. See `luan-亂.md`.

**And 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) says what the governing consists of, at chapter 60:**

> 治大國若烹小鮮 → **不擾也。**躁則多害，靜則全真。故其國彌大，而其主彌靜。
> *"治 is **not to disturb**. Agitation (躁 zào) brings much harm; stillness (靜 jìng) keeps the genuine whole. So the larger the state, the stiller its ruler."*

烹小鮮 (*pēng xiǎo xiān*) is cooking a small fish: turn it too often and it falls apart. **So 治 in this book is not intervention.** It is keeping a thing in its course — which is exactly what one does to a river, and exactly what 亂 is the failure of.

### The flexion, and why it exists

**Chapters 8 and 64 take *order* rather than *govern*, and in both the object is not a state.**

At **64**, 治之 (*zhì zhī* — *"治 it"*) has for its object something 王弼 calls 㣲脆 (*wēi cuì* — *"faint and brittle"*): a situation while it is still a thread or two. *Govern it* would be strange English for a brittle small thing, and it would also drop the pairing with 亂 standing three characters away.

At **8**, the line is 政善治, and **政 (*zhèng* — government) is already in it.** 說文 makes them near-twins — 政，正也。从攴从正 (*"政 is 正 (zhèng — upright); from 攴 (pū — a hand holding a rod) and 正, which is also the sound"*) — and modern Chinese fuses the two characters into 政治 (*zhèngzhì*), the ordinary word for *politics*. Chinese can print the doublet; English cannot say *"in government, masterful at governing"* without sounding as though it has stuttered. **The flexion here is forced by English, not by the Chinese**, and it is recorded rather than hidden for that reason.

### What is set aside

**"rule"** puts a person on a throne. 治 is what you do to the thing, not authority over it, and the book is at pains to say the sage does not 宰 (*zǎi* — lord over, ch 10 and 51). *Rule* also imports the ruler-word 王 (*wáng*), which has its own entry.

**"control"** and **"manage"** both invert 王弼's 不擾 (*bù rǎo* — not to disturb). A controlled river is a dammed one, and the metaphor inside the character is the other kind of engineering.

**"administer"** is bureaucratic, which is the register this edition keeps out, and it is 政's territory rather than 治's.

**"order" as the primary** was weighed and declined. It suits 8 and 64 and fails the other ten: *"the people are hard to order"* (65, 75) is not English, and *"ordering a large state is like cooking a small fish"* (60) loses the office the line is about.

### The working register

- of a state or a people → **govern** (治大國 → "governing a large state"; 民之難治 → "the people are hard to govern")
- as the state's own condition → **ungoverned** (無不治 → "nothing is left ungoverned")
- where the object is not a polity → **order** (治之於未亂 → "order it before it falls into disorder")

### 政, settled — and 正, which is not

**政 (*zhèng* — government) is settled as of 2026-09-23: *government* in all three of its lines**, so chapter 8 reads *"In government, masterful at order."* It had been *"In governing"* here and *"the government"* at chapter 58 twice (其政悶悶 · 其政察察).

**The decision turned on part of speech, not on consistency.** 其政 (*qí zhèng* — ***its*** government) can only be nominal, since 其 takes a noun — so the book's own two unambiguous uses of 政 are nouns. And chapter 8's other six first slots are each rendered by **their own** part of speech: 居 (*jū* — to dwell), 與 (*yǔ* — to give) and 動 (*dòng* — to move) as verbs, 心 (*xīn* — heart), 言 (*yán* — speech) and 事 (*shì* — affairs) as nouns. **The stanza alternates three and four, and that mix is the thing to keep.** Making 政 the one slot rendered against its own part of speech was the error, and it is what pushed 治 onto *order* in the first place.

**正 (*zhèng* — upright) is in the room and stays untouched.** 說文 defines 政 *as* 正 — 政，正也。从攴从正, *"from 攴 (pū — a hand holding a rod) and 正, which is also the sound"*; our base at chapter 8 reads 政 where 河上公's reads 正, a fork already logged; and 正 stands at chapter 57 inside another 治 line, 以正治國 (*"govern the state with uprightness"*). **正 is one of the calls Shalom has deferred** (`WORKLIST.md` T4-2, 正/奇), so 政 was settled without reaching into it.

### Left open

**居 (*jū* — to dwell) reads at least four ways and is unrendered twice.** It stands beside 治 in this very stanza, and chapter 8 gives it *settling* — correctly, because 處 (*chǔ*) holds *dwell* four lines above at 處眾人之所惡. But elsewhere 居 is *stay* (ch 2 ×2), *at home* (ch 31), *homes* (ch 72), and **nothing at all at chapter 38**, where 不居其薄 and 不居其華 are folded into 處's verb. `WORKLIST.md` T2-57.

### What no rule can enforce

***"rule" is ruled out in the verse, and it is not on the `forbidden:` list, because it cannot be.*** Those are two different facts: the ruling holds, and the enforcement does not exist. **宰 (*zǎi* — to lord over) stands with 治 in chapter 10**, where 長而不宰 legitimately reads *"growing them without **ruling** them"* — so a rule keyed to 治's presence would fire on 宰's own line. *Control*, *manage* and *administer* are held by the build; *rule* is held only by this entry and by the reader.

flexions.why: the object is not a polity — 政 already stands in the line at 8, and at 64 it is a small brittle situation

entries.body:
## 知足 (Zhī zú) — Knowing You Have Enough

*Say "jr dzoo." A lock-note: one recurring phrase, one settled rendering, so it stops drifting.*

**The characters.** 知 (zhī) = to know, to recognize. 足 (zú) is a picture of a **foot** — the lower leg and foot — and its first meaning is exactly that: *foot, leg*. The very same character also, from very early, means **"enough, sufficient, ample."** We won't pretend the bridge between the two senses is settled, but the resonance is worth keeping: your foot is *what you stand on* — your footing, your ground. To have 足 is to have ground enough to stand. So 知足 — "know-enough" — is, almost literally, **knowing the ground under you is already enough to stand on.** Contentment as sound footing, not as resignation.

**The lock.** Render 足 as **"enough"** — plain, concrete, unstuffy — and 知足 as **"knowing you have enough."** Where a line needs a *noun for the inner state*, use **"contentment."** That is the whole rule: the plain verb is *enough*, the state-noun is *contentment*, and nothing else. Retire **"sufficiency"** (stiff), **"fulfilled"** (drifts — it slipped into Ch 33), and **"satisfaction"** (too psychological). Two faces of one plain word.

**How it reads, locked, across the book:**

- **Ch 33** — 知足者富 → *"Those who know they have enough are rich."* (contentment as the only durable wealth)
- **Ch 44** — 知足不辱 → *"Know when you have enough, and you are never disgraced."*
- **Ch 46** — 禍莫大於不知足 → *"no greater disaster than not knowing when you have enough"*; and the triple-足 close, 知足之足常足矣 → *"the **contentment** of knowing you have **enough** is **contentment** forever"* — the plain verb and the state-noun working together to echo the original's three hammered 足.

**Don't confuse it with its sibling.** 知足 travels beside 知止 (*knowing when to stop*, Ch 32 & 44). They rhyme but they are not the same: **知足 is about *having*** — being at peace with what you already hold; **知止 is about *doing*** — halting the action before it overreaches. *Enough*, and *stop*. Keep them distinct in English, too.

## 眾 (Zhòng) — The Crowd

*Say "jong," falling. Nine appearances across six chapters — and until this entry it was rendered four different ways, including once as nothing at all.*

**Locked: 眾 → "the crowd" (of people) / "the many" (of things).** *(Not "the masses," not "the multitude," not "the people.")*

The word had drifted into four Englishes: *all* in Chapter 1, **dropped entirely** in Chapter 8, *the masses* six times in Chapter 20, *the many* in Chapter 21. The drop is the worst of them — Chapter 8's 處眾人之所惡 (*it dwells where the crowd will not go*) had become simply *"it seeks the lowest places,"* which keeps the water and loses the people the line is measuring the water against.

### The character, read slowly — worked and watched

The *Shuowen Jiezi* (~100 CE) analyses 眾 as **多也。从乑目** — *many; from 乑 and 目* — where 乑 is a stack of three 人 (*rén* — person) and 目 is an eye.

But the oracle-bone form is more specific and more uncomfortable. There the element above the people is **日** (*rì* — the sun), and the figures beneath it are **labourers**: a gang of people working in the open, under the sun. The eye of the later graph appears to be the sun's replacement, and it does not soften the picture — it adds an **overseer**. Either way, 眾 in its earliest use names not simply *a lot of people* but **the many who are worked, and watched while working.**

Three people is enough. Classical Chinese uses three for *innumerable* — the same convention that makes 森 (three trees) a forest.

This matters for the register. **"The masses"** imports a nineteenth-century class politics Laozi has no word for, and hands the reader Marx on the way to a text about water. But the oracle bone is a reminder that the neutral-sounding alternatives can under-translate too: 眾 is not an abstract plurality. It is a crowd of specific bodies with someone standing over them.

### The evidence — the crowd is what the sage is not

**Chapter 20 is the word's home**, and it uses 眾人 six times as one half of a contrast, with 我 (*wǒ* — the self seen) as the other:

> 眾人熙熙 · 眾人皆有餘 · 眾人皆有以
> *the crowd is merry · the crowd all has surplus · the crowd all has purpose*

Against which: 我獨若遺 (*I alone seem to have been left out*), 我獨昏昏 (*I alone am dim*), 我獨頑似鄙 (*I alone am stubborn and seem crude*). The crowd is **bright, full, and busy**; the speaker is dim, empty, and useless. The chapter needs the crowd to be genuinely enviable for its reversal to cost anything, which is one more reason to avoid a word that pre-judges them.

**Chapter 8 measures water by them.** 處眾人之所惡 — *it dwells in what the crowd finds distasteful.* 惡 (*è*) is *to dislike, to find repugnant.* Water's virtue is located precisely where the crowd will not stand.

**Chapter 64 sends the sage back to them.** 學不學，復眾人之所過 — *learning to be unlearned, returning to what the crowd has passed by.* Not above the crowd; back over the ground they walked past.

**Chapter 31 counts the dead.** 殺人之眾，以悲哀泣之 — *when the killed are many, weep for them in grief.* Here 眾 is predicative — *many* — and the line is one of the most humane in the book.

**And twice 眾 modifies things, not people.** Chapter 1's 眾妙之門 (*the gate of all subtleties*) and Chapter 21's 眾甫 (*the origin of the many*). In both, "the crowd" would be absurd and **the many** or **all** is right.

### The lock: what is set aside, and why

**"The masses"** carries a modern political charge — a bloc, a demographic, an object of policy — and a faint condescension the Chinese does not have. Chapter 20's crowd is *merry at a spring festival*, not a proletariat.

**"The multitude"** fails the hymn test outright. *The multitudes* is King James English, and it arrives with loaves and fishes attached.

**"The people"** belongs to a different and far more common character: **民** (*mín*), which appears in thirteen chapters and means the **governed populace** — the ones a ruler acts upon (愛民治國, 民之難治, 使民不爭). 眾 is a plurality; 民 is a political relation. Chapter 17's 百姓 (*bǎi xìng* — the hundred surnames) is a third thing again. Blurring them costs the political chapters their precision.

**"Everyone"** is a reasonable near-miss and is right in some lines — it is arguably the best English for Chapter 8 — but it loses the massed quality that Chapter 20 depends on. A crowd moves together; everyone does not.

### The working register

- of people, as a body → **the crowd** (眾人熙熙 → "the crowd is merry"; 處眾人之所惡 → "where the crowd will not go")
- of things, as a modifier → **all** or **the many** (眾妙之門 → "the gate of all subtleties"; 眾甫 → "the origin of the many")
- as a bare predicate → **many** (殺人之眾 → "when the killed are many")

**Never** "the masses," "the multitude," and never the word that belongs to 民.

### The tension, left open

**Is Laozi contemptuous of the crowd, or one of them?**

Chapter 20 can be read either way, and the reading changes the whole voice of the book. Take 我獨 (*I alone*) as pride and the chapter is an aristocrat's complaint: the crowd is shallow, I am deep. Take it as loneliness and the chapter is an admission: everyone else knows how to live and I do not. The Chinese supports both, and the same six-fold contrast carries them equally.

Two things weigh toward the second. The self-descriptions are **not flattering** — 昏昏 (*dim*), 頑 (*stubborn*), 鄙 (*crude*), 若遺 (*as if left out*) — and Laozi elsewhere claims 愚 (*yú* — simple, foolish) for himself as a good. And Chapter 64 has the sage **return** to what the crowd walked past, which is a movement toward them rather than away.

But Chapter 20 also says 我獨異於人 — *I alone am different from people* — and difference is not humility. We keep "the crowd," which is neutral enough to let a reader hear either, and we do not decide for them.

## 自然 (Zìrán) — Of Itself

*Say "dzuh rahn," the first falling, the second rising. Five appearances only — 17, 23, 25, 51, 64 — and one of them is the last line of Chapter 25, where the Tao is said to take its model from this and nothing further. Few words in the book carry more weight per occurrence.*

**Locked: 自然 → "of itself" / "of themselves" / "so of itself."** *(Never capital-N "Nature." Never "self-so" — see below.)*

**Revised 2026-08-24.** This entry previously locked **"the self-so,"** and Shalom reopened it on the grounds that the word felt wrong. It was. The reasoning is in *Why "the self-so" was retired*, below, and it is worth reading before the rest, because the error it describes is one this entry itself was written to prevent.

There are two dangers here, and the second is subtler than the first.

The **obvious** danger is "Nature." In modern Chinese 自然 does mean *nature* — the natural world, forests and weather and wildlife. But that meaning is a **late arrival**, shaped in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries as Chinese absorbed Western scientific vocabulary. Reading it back into a text from the fourth century BCE is an anachronism, and in Chapter 25 it is a catastrophic one. More on that below.

The **quieter** danger is inconsistency. 自然 appears only five times, and if each is rendered to suit its local sentence, the term goes **invisible** — a reader cannot see that five passages are saying one thing when the English never repeats. Rare words need consistent rendering more than common ones do, not less.

### The characters, read slowly — a nose, and a fire

**自** (*zì*) is a **nose**. The oracle-bone graph draws one, and the *Shuowen Jiezi* says so flatly: 自，鼻也 — "*zì*: the nose; a picture of a nose." The meaning *self* came from the gesture, and the gesture survives: a Chinese speaker indicating themselves points not at the chest, as Europeans do, but at the **nose**. The word for "self" is the part of you that you point at.

**然** (*rán*) began as fire. Its parts are meat, dog, and flame — a picture of roasting. It meant *to burn*, and was then borrowed for its **sound** to serve as a grammatical word meaning *so, thus, in that manner*. The original sense needed a new character, and got one: 燃, "to burn," which is 然 with a fire radical added back on. So 然 in classical Chinese is not an image at all; it is a pure connective — **"so," "thus," "that way."**

**And 然 does that work alone, three times, in one formula.** Chapters 21, 54 and 57 all close on 吾何以知…**然**哉？以此 — *"how do I know it is **so**? By this."* (Ch 21's is a witness reading; our base text has 狀 there, and the Manuscript Notes carry the argument.) The question Laozi asks about the world, about the origin of the many, and about his own claims is not *what is its shape* but **is it so** — and he asks it in the word he builds 自然 out of. So the formula and the term are the same thought at two scales: *is it so?* / *it is so of itself.* The answer, 以此 (*yǐ cǐ*), is the same two characters in all three, and since 2026-08-30 the same two words: **by this.**

Put them together and 自然 is, literally, **self + so**: so because of itself and nothing else. It is not a place, not a realm, not a collection of trees and animals. It is a **way of being so** — the condition of a thing whose being-that-way comes from nowhere but itself.

### Chapter 25 — the ladder that must terminate

The book's most famous ascent closes on this word:

> 人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然。
> *Humans model themselves on earth; earth models itself on sky; sky models itself on the Tao; and the Tao models itself on being what it is.*

**法** (*fǎ*) is *law, pattern, to take as one's model*. Each rung takes its pattern from the rung above. And then the ladder stops — and *how* it stops is the entire point.

Render 自然 as "Nature" and the line says *the Tao follows Nature*, which places something **above the Tao**. That contradicts the book at its foundation: this same chapter says the Tao was 先天地生 — *born before sky and earth* — and Chapter 4 calls it older than any ancestor. Nothing precedes it. A translation that puts Nature on top has not made a small slip; it has inverted the cosmology and broken the chapter it appears in.

Read correctly, the ladder is a **regress that dissolves**. Each thing patterns itself on something further up, until you reach the Tao, which patterns itself on — *being what it is.* There is no fifth term. The climb ends not by arriving somewhere higher but by discovering that the top of the ladder is standing on its own ground.

**Both commentators say this outright, and they say it in the same word.** 王弼: 道不違自然乃得其**性**…自然者，無稱之言，窮極之辭也 — *"the Tao does not go against 自然 and so attains its **nature** … 自然 is a term that **designates nothing**, an expression of the ultimate."* 河上公, blunter: 道**性**自然，無所法也 — *"the Tao's **nature** is 自然; **there is nothing it takes as a model**."* Both gloss the line with 性 (*xìng* — inherent nature), and both insist the ladder has no fourth rung above it.

**So the English at this one place refuses to supply a noun** — *"the Tao models itself on being what it is"* — and that is the deliberate exception the working register records below. 法 stays *models itself on* through all four rungs, so the pattern holds; what changes is that the object stops being a **name** (earth, sky, the Tao) and becomes a **clause**. The dissolution is made grammatically visible. A ladder that ends in *A is A* has ended. *(Shalom's rendering, 2026-08-24.)*

#### The closest rival, and why it was refused

Anyone working on this line arrives sooner or later at:

> *"The Tao models itself on **its own nature**."*

**It is the strongest alternative there is, and it should be understood before it is dismissed.** It is not a paraphrase — it is 性 (*xìng* — inherent nature), the exact word **both** commentators reach for here: 王弼's 道不違自然乃得其**性** and 河上公's 道**性**自然. It reads cleanly. And it carries the **自** lexically, in *its own*, which is the one thing the chosen rendering does not do with a dedicated word. *(Tested and set aside by Shalom, 2026-08-24.)*

Three things defeat it.

**1 · *Nature* is already spoken for, by 天 — though more loosely than first stated here.** `concordance.py --english "nature"` returns nine lines across the book and **not one is backed by 自然**. Seven render 天 (*tiān*) where it acts as an agent: *the way of nature* (9, 47, 73), *serving nature* (59), *when nature would rescue someone* (67), *nature's net is vast* (73). *(The other two are Ch 16's "returning to your original nature," which renders 復命 — fù mìng, returning to the allotted course — and is a separate looseness, flagged in `WORKLIST.md`.)*

**This objection is real but weaker than the two below, and the correction is worth recording.** 天 is **split** in this edition, coherently: **as a cosmic tier it is *sky*** (天地; 39's 天得一以清; both ascent ladders), and **as an agent that gives, hates or judges it is *nature***. So on the page of Chapter 25 the third rung reads **sky**, not *nature*, and there is no collision in the line itself. The collision is at book level — a reader who has met *the way of nature* knows the word points at 天 — and it puts the alternative one syllable from *"the Tao follows Nature,"* the mistranslation this entry exists to prevent. That is enough to weigh, not enough to decide. *(Caught by Shalom, 2026-08-24: the first version of this paragraph claimed all nine lines and read the split as though 天 were only ever *nature*.)*

**2 · 河上公 reaches for 性 in order to *cancel* the modelling, not to supply it.** His sentence does not stop at 道性自然. It runs 道性自然，**無所法也** — *"the Tao's nature is 自然, **and so there is nothing it models itself on.**"* The alternative keeps the modelling relation intact and fills its empty slot with a noun, which is the opposite of the conclusion he draws from the word he is being quoted for.

**3 · It re-posits a thing.** *Its own nature* is a possessed noun, so there are now two items — the Tao, and the nature it conforms to. That is milder than *the self-so*, since a possessive is weaker than a definite article, but it is **the same axis**, and it is the axis this line was rewritten to clear. 王弼's 無稱之言 — *a term that designates nothing* — tolerates neither.

**And the 自 is less lost than it looks.** English carries the reflexive in its pronouns where Chinese carries it in a morpheme: *models **itself** on being what **it** is* holds the self-reference twice, and *what it is* sits close to *how it is*, which is 然. The chosen line does more of the work than a first reading credits.

### Why this is the ground beneath 無為

Here is the structural point that makes 自然 more than a curiosity, and it is worth stating plainly.

**無為** (*wúwéi* — "non-doing") asks you to take your hand off the elephant. But why would that be wise rather than negligent? Only if the elephant is going somewhere on its own. **自然 is that guarantee.** Things are so of themselves: they have their own direction, their own unfolding, their own sufficiency. Non-doing is not abandonment because there is something there to trust.

Chapter 64 puts both words in a single line, and it is the most compact statement of the whole ethic:

> 以輔萬物之自然，而不敢為。
> *…to support the countless things in being so of themselves, and never push them.*

**Assist**, not manage. 輔 (*fǔ*) is the word for a support strut, a brace on a cart. You may prop something up in the direction it is already going. You may not steer it.

And Chapter 17 shows what this feels like from **inside** — the only place in the book where 自然 is spoken by ordinary people rather than the philosopher:

> 百姓皆謂：「我自然」。
> *Everyone says: "We did this ourselves."*

The best ruler is the one whose work is invisible, because those who lived through it experience their own flourishing as **self-caused**. That is 自然 as a lived political fact, not a metaphysical abstraction.

### The wider thread — 自 running through the book

The nose-character does not appear only in this compound. It threads through some of the book's most important lines, and once the lock is in place a reader can follow it:

- **Chapter 57**, four times in four lines, each ending in 自: 民**自**化 · 民**自**正 · 民**自**富 · 民**自**樸 — the people transform, right, enrich, and simplify **themselves**.
- **Chapters 32 and 37**: 萬物將**自**賓 · 萬物將**自**化 — the countless things submit, transform, *of themselves*.
- **Chapter 73**: 不召而**自**來 — *not summoned, yet it comes of itself.*
- **Chapter 51**: 莫之命而常**自然** — *no one commands it. It is always so, of itself.*

The pattern is the argument: nobody is in charge, and things happen anyway. Better, in fact, than when someone is.

### Why "the self-so" was retired

This entry locked **"the self-so"** from its writing until 2026-08-24, and the case against it is the entry's own case against "Nature," turned around.

**It is a noun, and both commentators say there is no thing there.** 王弼's 無稱之言 — *a term that designates nothing* — and 河上公's 無所法也 — *there is nothing it models itself on* — are refusals to name an entity. English **"the self-so"** is a definite noun phrase, and *the* is an instruction to the reader to go looking for a thing. Once they look, 自然 becomes something the Tao defers to: a fifth rung. That is the same structural error as "Nature," smaller in degree and identical in kind. This entry diagnosed the disease and then carried a milder strain of it.

**It fails the pointing test, and 河上公 shows what passing looks like.** Glossing Chapter 23 he writes 雲從龍，風從虎，水流濕，火就燥，自然之□也 — *"clouds follow the dragon, wind follows the tiger, water flows toward the damp, fire goes toward the dry — this is 自然's [way]."* He points at **water finding the low ground.** Nobody can point at *the self-so*. It is a calque: it lives only inside sinology, and in the verse it survived only because a note explained it. A term that needs its own footnote to be read has failed the poetry half of this edition's brief.

**And the lock had already lost.** Its stated fear was that local renderings would make the term invisible. Three of the five lines paraphrased anyway — 17, 51 and 64 — and those three read *well*. What the lock actually preserved was the calque in the two lines it damaged.

**What is kept is the analysis, which was right and which produced the answer**: the nose, the roasting-fire borrowed for its sound, and the 吾何以知…然哉 formula. Retiring the calque in fact makes that analysis *audible in the verse for the first time*. The claim of `DISCOVERIES.md` §2 is that 然 means **so** — and *things go of themselves*, *always so of itself*, *so of themselves* all say **so**. A hyphen had buried it.

### What we set aside

**"The self-so."** Forbidden. A calque that names a thing where the Chinese and both commentators refuse to. Retained nowhere.

**"Nature," capitalized.** An anachronism and, in Chapter 25, an inversion. It also drags in Romanticism — Nature as a numinous presence to commune with, the sublime, the wilderness — which is a European inheritance, not a Chinese one. Laozi is not a nature poet; he is describing a *mode of causation*.

**"Naturalness," "the natural."** Better, and occasionally usable in adjective position, but they slide toward the same noun and toward "unaffected charm," which is a matter of manners.

**"Spontaneity."** The most defensible alternative, and often used. Its trouble is that English "spontaneous" has drifted toward *impulsive, unplanned, whimsical* — the opposite of what a river or a seed does. A seed is not being spontaneous. It is being exactly what it is, reliably, on its own. Keep "spontaneous" available as an adjective where it fits; do not let it carry the term.

**"The way things are."** Too flat; it loses the *self* — the whole force of 自 is that the being-so comes **from the thing itself**.

**And any systems rendering** — 自然 as autonomy, self-organization, frictionless process. A self-organizing system is still a *system*, still designed, still explained from the outside. 自然 is precisely the refusal of an outside explanation.

### The working register

**The rule: 自然 is rendered as a movement, never as a name.** Four of the five occurrences are adverbial and take the plain English; the fifth is the exception, and it is an exception in the direction of *less* noun, not more.

| Ch | Chinese | Rendered | Slot |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17 | 我**自然** | "We did this by ourselves." | in the people's mouth — keep the plain human voice |
| 23 | 希言**自然** | "Brevity in speech happens of itself." | the locked wording, in a plain predicate — see below |
| 25 | 道法**自然** | "The Tao models itself on being what it is." | the one noun slot, answered with a **clause** |
| 51 | 常**自然** | "It is always so, of itself." | adverbial |
| 64 | 萬物之**自然** | "in being so of themselves" | possessed — a gerund, not a noun |

**Chapter 23 — revised 2026-09-03, and the strain is now paid differently.** This entry long read 希言自然 as *"Speak sparingly, for things go of themselves,"* defending *for* on the ground that 自然 is **the ground, not the consequence** — 河上公's 愛言者自然之道. **That reasoning stands.** What it could not do was supply a subject without inventing 物 (*wù* — things), which is not in the line. The entry's own verdict on the line was correct — *"A-自然 compressed to four characters, and English has no predicate slot that fits it; a strain case"* — and the strain is now paid by **letting 自然 be a plain predicate on a plain subject**: *"Brevity in speech happens of itself."* (Shalom's line, 2026-09-03.) **The 故 that follows is printed and left unrendered** — our base is the only witness that has it (〔案河上公注本及各本俱無故字〕) — so the line stands beside the two storm lines in juxtaposition rather than asserting an inference the English cannot carry. *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-04: it also leaves the reader room to make the connection.)*

**Why not a fresh local rendering.** ch 17 and ch 25 already depart from the lock's wording, so **two of five occurrences do not show the phrase**. A third departure produces exactly the invisibility this entry was written to prevent, which is why ch 23 keeps *"so of itself"* and explains itself instead of paraphrasing.

***On its own* was declined for *of itself*** — the same idea in a sixth wording, and a sixth wording is the invisibility this entry exists to prevent. *(Shalom caught both defects in the intermediate drafts: that *"Speech barely heard"* named **volume**, which neither commentator does, and that the line did not set up the *therefore* following it.)*

**The trade to keep in view.** Chapter 25 spends the 自 — *"being what it is"* names the state but not its provenance, and the whole force of the nose-character is that the being-so comes **from the thing itself and nowhere else**. That loss is accepted there and paid back everywhere else: the four adverbial cases all carry *itself / themselves*. **The one place the term is a noun is the one place we decline to translate it as one** — which may be the truest thing this entry can say about the word.


### A note on Alan Watts

Watts did more than almost anyone to bring this idea into English, and his central intuition sits close to ours: that the Chinese cosmos is **grown rather than made** — not an artifact assembled by a maker but something that unfolds from within, the way a plant does. That distinction is exactly what 自然 protects, and it is why the machine metaphors had to go. A made thing has a maker outside it; a grown thing is *so of itself*.

Two honest boundaries. Watts's work remains **in copyright** (he died in 1973), so we do not draw on his phrasing, only note the affinity — the same rule that governs our use of any modern interpreter. And he was a popularizer with a Zen-inflected ear; where his emphasis and the classical Chinese diverge, the characters decide.

### The tension, left open

If everything is self-so, why does the book need to be written?

Chapter 64 answers with a strut, not a rule: 輔 — *assist*. There is apparently a difference between propping something in the direction it is already going and taking hold of it. But the text never says where that line falls, and any honest reading has to sit with the fact that Laozi is himself intervening — writing instructions, advising rulers, making a case — in a world he says runs perfectly well without instruction.

Perhaps that is the joke he is in on. The book that counsels non-doing is itself a doing; the argument for the self-so is an argument, which is to say a hand extended. Chapter 17 may be the closest he comes to resolving it: the best work is the kind that leaves people saying *we did this ourselves* — including, presumably, the work of the book you are holding.
